Speaking after Borussia Dortmund's hard-fought 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich on Saturday, Nico Schlotterbeck said he believes the Black and Yellows are better than they are often given credit for in Germany.

The draw ensured Dortmund remain level on points with league leaders Bayern, trailing only on goal difference, and Schlotterbeck hopes a genuine title race will emerge as the season progresses.

“I think we're still underrated in Germany, partly because people keep saying that we don't play the best football. But we are good, and we know it. If we keep playing like this, I'm confident that we can keep things open for a very long time," Schlotterbeck told Kicker.

While acknowledging that Bayern are favourites to retain the title, the centre-back believes the Black and Yellows can challenge them if they continue to perform at their best.

“However, if we perform over the coming weeks as we did today – or as we have done in certain halves of games this season – then we're in a good place and can certainly give ourselves a chance of keeping the title race open for a long time.”

While admitting that “not everything was perfect” in Saturday's draw against a side he himself has described as the best Bayern team of the last 10 or 15 years, Schlotterbeck believes Dortmund proved they can cause the Bavarians problems.

“We are good too. We showed that again today. The point was deserved. It's only one point, with plenty more still up for grabs in the title race, but it's already one more point than we managed to get against Bayern last season. #2796. Utah Jazz vs San Antonio Spurs: Recap and final score

At the start of the season, Jazz fans were hyped. With the #2 pick in Darryn Peterson, Keyonte George on a new contract, and Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. healthy and ready to play, the season was extremely promising.

After tonight's 119-97 loss to the San Antonio Spurs, the Jazz are now 1-6 and are in last place in the Western Conference.

Tonight was easily the worst showing from the Jazz all season, with the Jazz looking disjointed and chaotic on both ends of the floor for most of the game. As a team, Utah shot 35.4% from the field and 35.3% from three. Yes, the Jazz are young, and they're missing Jaren Jackson Jr. to injury, but nothing looks easy with this offense. Credit goes to the Spurs for their excellent perimeter defense, but Utah never looked like it had an offensive rhythm. There are a lot of actions with the Jazz offense that come from a lot of movement, but those ended up in some pretty odd endings. Jaxson Hayes, for example, had 9 shots in this one but was just 4/9. Svi Mykhailiuk was 1/7 in this one as well. That's not the worst thing in the world, but it feels like there are too many times when Utah's offense doesn't flow through the most important players: Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson, Lauri Markkanen, and Ace Bailey. That's not to say Utah didn't get shots for those players. Markkanen led the team with 16 shots, Peterson was next with 13, Keyonte George 12, and Ace Bailey 11, but at times the offense feels like it has no clear order, and a lot of role players hijack possessions that turn into bad plays.

Now, you could argue those shots being spread around were justified, given the bad shooting from those core players on the Jazz. Keyonte George has now had two bad shooting games in a row (3/12), and Ace Bailey is still finding his stroke from three (1/5), for example. But something has to be done to improve shot quality. Are there offensive tweaks that could give them more opportunities for easier shots? Can they simplify things somehow? The reality is something has to improve because Utah is not a very good team right now.

Tonight's game had some really weird energy. Could it have had something to do with the news that Isaiah Collier had the team option declined on his contract?

Maybe it was that? Or maybe it was a residual effect of Will Hardy's decision to bench Darryn Peterson for Brice Sensabaugh and Isaiah Collier? Speaking of that, it's not great that Peterson was benched for a player who won't even be on the team next year. It's not a great sign. There's no way to know as an outside observer, but the team did not look happy. Now, winning cures all, and Utah could really stand to get some wins soon to turn the season around, but if they play like they did tonight, it'll take some time.

That's not to say there weren't some bright spots. Utah apparently made it clear they were not playing Collier and had Darryn Peterson running the show with the second unit. Things weren't perfect, but Peterson and the second unit clawed their way back into the game. Peterson was just a -4 in a blowout loss, and those minutes with the bench were a big reason why. It's a great sign for the future and confirmation that Will Hardy force-feeding Isaiah Collier minutes wasn't the best play.

The takeaway from this game, besides learning to compartmentalize the difficult things in life, is to remember the team is only going to get better. The Jazz are evolving game by game in how they are running, and eventually those moves will lead to winning. It also looks like this season will turn around as soon as Darryn Peterson takes off as a player. That may take time though, so Jazz fans might need to find some patience.

#2795. 2027 South Side Sox Top Prospect No. 98: Abraham Núñez

Abraham NúñezCenter Fielder6´2´´175 poundsAge: 212024 South Side Sox Top Prospect Ranking 372025 South Side Sox Top Prospect Ranking 522026 South Side Sox Top Prospect Ranking 832026 High Level Kannapolis (Low-A)Age relative to high level -0.3 yearsSSS rank among all center fielders in the system 9Overall 2026 stats 63 games ⚾️ 5 HR ⚾️ 22 RBI ⚾️ .270/.356/.395 ⚾️ 29 BB ⚾️ 59 K ⚾️ 17-of-27 (63.0%) SB ⚾️ .975 FLD ⚾️ 1.0 WAR

Abraham Núñez was a Jan. 15, 2023 signing out of the Dominican Republic as a 17-year-old, and he hit the ground running in his first pro season.

The son of former Royal and Marlin Abraham Sr., Junior posted a .299/.427/.442 line in his DSL debut along with a .869 wOBA and a 136 wRC+. As that swollen on-base percentage suggests, his plate discipline numbers were also stout: Núñez walked in just fewer than 18% of his 185 PAs while striking out in just 12%. He did have a 70% contact rate and a SwStr% of 17%, so he didn't go without whiffs, it just appears that Núñez was apt at putting the ball in play with two strikes. The lefty featured some pull-side pop as well with a line drive rate at 26%. Núñez also stole 12 bags and played 43 games in the outfield (32 in center field) without making an error.

One year later, Núñez moved Stateside and held steady, albeit with a more muted performance. Núñez logged a similar speedy profile as ascendant star ACL teammate Javier Mogollón, but without any of Mogollón's power. Núñez's slugging percentage fell short of .400, and sat worse than his on-base. Concerning, but that's what the weight room is for, right?

The 2025 season, Núñez's first in full-season pro ball, continued some worrisome, downward trends. Again, his slugging was waifish and unbecoming even for a center-field speedster. And it's not as if Núñez was some sort of dastardly demon on the basepaths: Swiping two-thirds of the bags he attempts is actually a poor showing.

Núñez repeated Kannapolis in 2026, and fared much better, recovering some gap power and running up a 270/.356/.395 slash that prevented him from slipping out of our Top 100 entirely. What is becoming a bigger concern than on-field performance is his tendency toward injury; 2026 represented the second straight year Núñez couldn't even get into 70 games, as he started the year on the IL and later missed a month in the second half of the season.

Núñez will be moved up to Winston-Salem in 2027, as there is little point to placing any player in Low-A ball for more than two summers. With the Dash, Núñez will be age-appropriate for High-A, and the White Sox will give him plenty of run in Winston-Salem. If his offensive uptick was a mirage or the injury bug bites again, Núñez will move from an intriguing prospect to an expendable one.

#2792. Horse Tracks: ‘Mile High Magic’ wins again

It's been more than 24 hours since the Broncos' five-play goal-line stand against the Chiefs and I still can't get enough of it. As I said on the post-game pod, this Bo Nix era is bringing back John Elway vibes — when you knew you always had a chance to win no matter the odds.

With less than two minutes remaining and followed by a 44-yard kickoff return from Emmett Johnson, Patrick Mahomes marched the Chiefs to the Broncos' 4 in just four plays.

But Denver's defense refused to give up the end zone. For 5 plays. FIVE!

Kenneth Walker III picked up three yards on first-and-goal before the Broncos slammed the door.

Under pressure from Que Robinson, Mahomes threw incomplete on second-and-1, and JL Skinner stuffed Walker for no gain on third-and-1.

Then the magic happened. Mahomes threw a touchdown on fourth-and-1, but a Kansas City false start negated the win and instead pushed the Chiefs back to the 6-yard line, setting up one final chance with four seconds remaining.

This time Malcolm Roach delivered the knockout blow, sacking Mahomes for a 6-yard loss to cement what I would consider an historic goal-line stand in Denver.

And it all started with the Mile High crowd.

The third quarter was ugly – three possessions, three punts, zero first downs and the Chiefs holding the ball for 9:26 of the 15 minutes — and the Mile High crowd let the team know it.

"I just know there are other cities where that adversity would be greater and longer," Payton said of the boos. "This is anything but that. You feel their disappointment with that reaction as much as anything else. It's pro sports, but man, it's a special place. It's something else."

And maybe it made a difference because the fourth quarter belonged to Denver.

Bo Nix led an 80-yard drive that ended with a two-yard touchdown pass to Nate Adkins on fourth down and a two-point conversion to Jaylen Waddle.

Alex Singleton sacked Mahomes on third down forcing Chiefs to settle for a field goal attempt, and Harrison Butker crumbled under the pressure.

Then rookie Jonah Coleman broke the game wide open with a break-away 51-yard catch-and-run before punching in a 5-yard touchdown.

That's 15 unanswered points in the fourth quarter and a 28-24 lead with 1:56 on the clock.

Then it was nothing but defensive grit and Mile High Magic.

"Obviously our fans are incredible," said Singleton, who finished with 14 tackles and a huge third-down sack to force Butker's missed field goal.

Singleton said that confidence has been building with the defense — especially inside the red zone.

"I think from last week, Houston last year, now this week, and then just short-yardage in general, we've played really good football," he said. "There's a lot of confidence in our defense in those situations. I think we're almost more comfortable there than we are in the open field sometimes."

A week earlier in Arizona, the Broncos allowed the Cardinals just one score on five trips inside the 20.

Nix, whose fourth-quarter heroics put the Broncos in a position to win, had to wait and watch from the sidelines to see if the defense could hold onto it.

"The fourth down was another crazy play by our defense," Nix said, admitting he was exhausted after that game. "It was just an incredible stand by them. They just battled and battled on that drive and came out on top."

Mike McGlinchey was saying his prayers from the sideline.

"I was saying a few Hail Mary's on the sidelines, I was praying to some guardian angels, and they came through and our defense did, too," he said.

Wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr. admitted his nerves were shot.

"My heart was racing," he said. "Out of all the games we've had, that's probably the toughest one to actually like to sit there and watch because my heart was just pumping the whole time."

But the defenders on the field knew they had to stay level.

Cornerback Riley Moss said the message was to not be too hot or too cold.

"So finding that go-zone," he said. "We were all in that zone, even if they're driving down, even if they're in the one yard line—finish, finish, finish."

For edge rusher Nik Bonitto, it came down to preparation and grit.

"It's just the grit of the team, man. We wanted to win this game bad and, you know how much it meant for us," Bonitto said. "VJ' talked about toughness and mentality all week, and that showed itself right there."

Que Robinson noted that it really just came down to "ball out or go home."

"And I don't want to go home without the dub."

#2791. Rockets keep rolling with 109-93 win over Celtics

Well, this is pretty fun. The Rockets are not only winning, they're rolling over most teams. Yes, they lost a winnable game in Dallas, with perhaps the wrong players missing, but they followed that up with a win over a depleted yet still dangerous OKC the next night. Now they've taken down Boston, admittedly on a back to back of their own, dropping their record to 5-2. That is to say, Boston had been very good so far, and beating them, even with a schedule advantage is no easy feat.

And yet, the Rockets are making it look pretty easy in most of their wins. Boston wasn't depleted tonight, and the Rockets were fairly close to full strength as well, with recent absentees Reed Sheppard, Fred VanVleet and Marcus Smart playing tonight. Clint Capela was out, and that proved surprisingly troublesome at points in the game, as Boston is pretty big and physical at center, if generally fairly small elsewhere. Adams or Clint might have helped in that regard, but alas. Boston was without Classic Celtic Paul George, who was sitting on the second night of a back to back.

This game started out disjointed, and it more or less stayed that way. Lots of odd calls, anticipatory calls, and an illegible standard for fouls. Not terrible, but it did kill any hope of free flowing basketball. Until fairly late in the 3rd quarter the Rockets would step out to a small lead, of say 6-8 points, but couldn't build on it. Boston would close the gap to a few points. The Rockets would build a small lead again. And repeat. In the fourth quarters the Rockets pulled away, and with the lead pushing 20 points, a bad shooting Boston could never catch up.

Boston lives or dies by three point shooting, and tonight, they died by it, going 12-42 from deep. Some of this was surely tired Celtic legs, but some of it has to be credited to the Rockets. It was a dismal shooting night from pretty much all the Boston stalwarts and quondam Rocket killers. Peyton "I cut my own hair." Pritchard was 0-5 from deep. Jason "MSFT" Tatum was 1-7, Derek "Beardo" White was 1-5, and Sam"Snuggy" Hauser was 0-5. Only Baylor "Nebraksa!" Scheierman and Luka "The Other Luka" Garza had good shooting nights with any volume.

If you'd asked who'd be the high scorer tonight, Jason "Microsoft" Tatum, Kevin Durant or Alperen Sengun, would you have automatically picked Sengun? Possibly not, but Sengun has played not like an All Star, but an All NBA player this season. Tonight he went for 26pts on a very tidy 12-15 shooting, grabbed 7 boards, dished 10 assists to 1 TO, and made 1 of 2 of his 3pt shots, maintaining his great, though low volume, 3pt% percentage.

Tatum only scored 19, went 5-16, with nearly half his output coming from the free throw line. He had 6 boards, and 9 assists to 5 turnovers. Some in TDS land aren't happy with Amen Thompson lately, but a lot of Amen's value so far, in my view, has come from shutting down opposing stars fairly well. He's still posting stats, he still is having trouble scoring inside, and also having any sort of effective mid range game. He seems to be struggling to find his place in a new order where even Kevin Durant isn't notching high volume attempts.

We saw another great game from Jabari Smith, who is somehow turning into the "go to" guy for the Rockets when they simply have to have 3pt shot. Jabs was 5-10 shooting tonight, and 4-5 from three point range. He added 10 rebounds, and I think played some excellent defense, especially on the perimeter.

We also saw the Rockets Dr. Jeckyll and Mr Hyde player, Marcus Smart, in Mr. Hyde form tonight. He could not shoot it much at all, unlike last game, going 2-10 and 2-8 from three point range (though the makes came late to help seal the win). Smart did however open almost the entire Dark Arts Grimoire that so annoyed me when he played for Boston. I've never seen a player pick up not one, but two, fouls in a sequence with the ball not yet inbounded, but Smart did that tonight. I'm fairly sure both of those fouls were on Boston, but whatever the case, he definitely annoyed the hell out of Boston's players. Even "Cap" himself, Jason Tatum showed human emotions at times. Did playing Boston mean something to Ime Udoka and Marcus Smart? Yes, I'd say it did.

Fred VanVleet continues his good playing, maculate shooting, and immaculate distribution. We also saw another quiet night, at a lowish 33 minutes from Kevin Durant, who took only 6 shots. He did add two blocks and a steal, and seems perfectly content. Opponents now have a tough choice with Sengun, Durant, and Smith. It's really impossible to do what opponents did last season, and utterly pack the paint and dare the Rockets to make shots. It seems almost impossible to grab and blanket Durant as is the usual scheme against the Rockets and win. That message hasn't permeated the NBA yet, and it will be interesting to see what the adjustment to the Rockets will be.

We saw a late return to shooting form from Reed Sheppard who played a pretty worthless stint in the first half, but contributed some good passing, defense, and two valuable three pointers as part of a Rockets run that buried Boston for good. Hopefully this will continue in his role off the bench. Tari Eason continues to be a force from the bench, mostly a force for good. Tonight he had 13pts on 5-8 shooting and a very strong 3-6 from three, and added 4 rebounds, 3 assists (2TO) and 2 blocks in his 27 minutes.

It's all going very well, and I think we should not let the perfect (which the Rockets nearly are) be the enemy of the very good indeed.

Anyway, the Rockets are alone at number one in the West, as Memphis was knocked off in OT by the Pelicans. I will admit that I didn't think the Rockets would be #1 in the West at any point before the season started.

The Rockets play Antless Minnesota on Wednesday in Houston.

The Eagles have lost six in a row and rank 30th in the NFL in points per game, but Nick Sirianni said Monday that he isn’t making a change at offensive coordinator or quarterback.

Sean Mannion will continue to call plays, and Tanner McKee will remain the starting quarterback with Jalen Hurts out for the year.

“I’m not making any changes there,” Sirianni said about his coaching staff, via Tim McManus of ESPN. “It is on all of us to figure out how to get things going in the right direction. Hurts played five games before going on injured reserve with blood clots; Johnson retired after three games; Jurgens played four games with the Eagles before a trade to the Ravens; Barkley has missed two games and been limited in others with injuries; Smith has missed four games with a hamstring injury; and Wicks has missed two games with an ankle injury.

The Eagles are averaging 17.1 points a game.

McKee has started the past three games, completing 63.2 percent of his passes for 639 yards with two touchdowns and two interceptions.

We’re looking at everything as far as what we can do differently as coaches.”

McKee’s backup, Joe Milton, only arrived in Philadelphia on Oct. 16, signing from the Cowboys’ practice squad.

#2788. Bills show different defensive tendencies against Ravens

Two weeks ago, I wrote an article about the qualitative differences between the (thus far) 2026 version of the Buffalo Bills defense and the 2025 iteration under former head coach Sean McDermott. In short, the 2026 version is:

running a less diverse selection of coverages

The results, specifically in pass defense through six games, were suboptimal. Before the Bills faced the Baltimore Ravens this past Sunday, their defense rankings were:

Then the Bills rolled out a differently looking defense to face off against Lamar Jackson, Derrick Henry, and the expected-to-be-explosive Baltimore offense…or maybe they would have. We can't be sure. Jackson injured the thumb on his throwing hands on the Ravens first play from scrimmage and was promptly replaced by former Pro Bowl backup Tyler "Snoop" Huntley (who then was replaced by emergency quarterback and undrafted free agent Joe Fagnano).

This means that while we can (and should) discuss the changes we saw for the Bills defensive tendencies against the Ravens, all of them must be heavily couched through the lens of Jackson's injury. The Bills set season-high marks in man coverage rate (54.8%), blitz rate (61.3%), and middle-of-field closed coverages (67.7%) while rolling from two-high pre-snap looks to one-high post-snap looks at the season's highest rate (25.8%). They also completed abandoned the idea of pressing opposing receivers (0.0% after a previous season-low of 7.9%). In addition, Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard spent the game calling plays from the booth and commented that it helped him smooth out the operation.

The only one of the changes mentioned above that we can definitively say is likely to continue moving forward is Leonhard's presence in the booth, confirmed by head coach Joe Brady during his press conference on Monday. Every other differentiation could have been influenced heavily by the immediate removal of Jackson from the Baltimore offensive equation after one snap. Would the Bills have blitzed as much if they had one of the greatest rushing quarterbacks of all time across the line of scrimmage? Would they have run as much man coverage and turned their backs to the signal caller if that signal caller was Jackson?

The Bills had a defensive identity against the Ravens: off man and a high blitz rate. We'll keep an eye on it moving forward to see how much of it was "new-look Bills defense", how much of it was "the Ravens don't have Lamar", and how effective it can be (if it persists).

#2782. Bears QB Caleb Williams blacks out logo on cleats, says he wants 'to calm things down' after risking $12,000 in NFL fines

Just a few days after saying that he would keep facing NFL fines to wear his cleats of choice, Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams is slightly changing direction, and meeting the league in the middle.

Williams, who was facing fines nearing $12,000 per week for wearing an unauthorized logo, instead showed up on Monday in all-black cleats that did not have any visible logo. Williams debuted the logo-less cleats on his way to leading the Bears over the Seattle Seahawks.

Postgame, Williams said that he wore the cleats because he didn't want the media attention to be a distraction.

"Just to calm things down," he said when asked why he changed his cleats. "It was a big week and I'm not here to create any B.S. towards the team, I wanna keep that to a minimum from my side. Obviously I get a lot of media, and so just trying to minimize that as much as possible."

Caleb Williams opted for matte black cleats without a logo in order to avoid fines from the NFL.

Williams wears cleats made by Caddix, a company that says it designs cleats to help reduce ACL and ankle injuries, based on the way that the studs release more quickly and limit the torque associated with those injuries. Williams does not have an endorsement deal with the company, but says he believes in the science behind them.

However, the NFL has a long-standing partnership with Nike, and does not allow players to wear gear from other sports apparel brands. Williams was reportedly fined $11,941 after both Week 6 and Week 7 for wearing Caddix cleats, which the league counted as displaying an "unauthorized logo."

Last week, Williams said that he would keep wearing the cleats throughout the rest of the season, risking a huge number of fines from the league. Williams also wore the brand during Week 1 and Week 2, before missing time with a hamstring injury, but he was only fined over the past two weeks.

Monday's cleats, which Williams described as "matte black," appeared to be a compromise.

Though Williams is not the only player to wear Caddix cleats, he's become the most high-profile wearer thanks to the ongoing fines. It's unclear whether the NFL will decide to let his shoe choices rest, given this compromise.

If he is fined, though, he'll have some help: Caddix CEO Jack Rasmussen has offered to pay Williams' fines, and Cincinnati Bengals quarterback and longtime Caddix wearer Joe Flacco also told ESPN that he would pay any fines Williams receives.

#2780. Windsor softball sweeps top CHSAA awards after historic unbeaten title

A state-championship season always brings the accolades, especially when it's a historic unbeaten run.

Windsor is enjoying the spoils of a perfect 29-0 season that finished Oct. 24 with a long-awaited Colorado Class 4A softball state championship.

The Wizards swept the top 4A awards on CHSAA's all-state softball teams released Nov. 2.

Windsor senior pitching ace Jenna McGinnis was named 4A Player of the Year, while coach Haley Hanson took 4A Coach of the Year honors.

McGinnis went 18-0 and allowed just 14 runs (10 earned) while striking out a ridiculous 162 hitters in just 89 innings of work.

She's been a dominant force in the circle since her freshman season, finishing with a 44-4 career record, a 1.33 ERA and 473 strikouts in 332 innings.

McGinnis pitched four games this postseason, going 4-0 while allowing just one earned run with 36 strikeouts.

McGinnis paired with fellow senior standout Shannon Nielsen (10-0, 0.56 ERA, 4 ER and 65 Ks in 50 innings) to give Windsor an untouchable duo in the circle.

This is a full-circle moment for Hanson, played for the Wizards program and now has finally led Windsor back to the top after 4A runner-up finishes in 2024 and 2025.

Freshman Taylor Nixon joined McGinnis on the 4A first team. Windsor put three players on the 4A second team in Nielsen, Breckyn Billadeau and Maizie Magaña. Addison White and Gabriella Wagner were also 4A honorable mentions.

There was little doubt that the Wizards would lead the 4A all-state teams after a remarkably dominant title run.

Windsor went 29-0 against a schedule that was nearly half top-10 state seeds across all three classifications, including a win over 5A No. 1 Cherokee Trail and five of the other 11 state semifinalists.

Windsor was the first unbeaten and untied Colorado 4A or 5A softball team since Legacy in 2010.

The full picture: 10 stats that show how dominant Windsor softball was in perfect season

The Wizards run-ruled 21 of 29 teams and outscored opponents 347-26, a Colorado record average scoring margin in the MaxPreps era, which dates back to 2006.

Speaking of 2006, this was also Windsor's first state softball title in exactly 20 years after three runner-up finishes since, including two straight in 2024 and 2025.

Chris Abshire covers high school and community sports for the Coloradoan.

#2776. Lions, Vikings Song of the Game: ‘Soldier’s Poem’ by Muse

It didn't feel like a Victory Monday, and it sure as hell didn't feel like a divisional Victory Monday this week.

There's a dark cloud hovering over Allen Park these days, and as we continue to await actual, tangible good news on the health of Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell, I've officially moved into the anger stage of grief.

Jack Campbell has given everything to this team. He's committed nearly his entire life to football.

And, yes, that has resulted in wonderful, amazing opportunities only a few of us could dream of. He got a college education and was drafted in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft. In May, he signed a contract worth more money than most of us will see in 10 lifetimes.

But on Sunday, we got a terrible reminder that football can take nearly all of that back in an innocent-looking instant.

No amount of money or fame can prepare you for that kind of physical and emotional trauma. We justify the violence and terrible, long-term impacts this game has on its players because we give them fame and fortune. Then we convince ourselves that they know the implicit danger they are heading into, and it's not our fault they made that decision.

But do they really know the risk? Is an NFL prospect who's not even old enough to buy beer really capable of understanding just how life-altering even a short career in football can be? At that age, you feel invincible. And showing any sort of vulnerability or doubt will cost you your roster spot. Do you think most college players even saw the study a couple of months ago that found that among 235 former NFL players who donated their brains posthumously from 2016 to 2021, 91.5% of them had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)?

As someone who has not only paid thousands of dollars to watch this bloodsport, but now actively profits off of it—while putting zero of my life at risk—it forces me to rethink a lot of things. Jarring reminders like Sunday provide a glimpse into how ugly this whole operation is, and it's hard not to feel complicit.

When you know damn well that this is wrong?I would still lay down my life for you

And yet, despite all of that, I'm confident that a fully informed Jack Campbell would change very little in his life up until this point. The man loves football, and more importantly, he loves the process. He loves putting in a full day of work and throwing everything into the task in front of him.

One of Campbell's most remarkable quotes came in his press conference after signing an $81 million deal. In a moment in which he became one of the highest-paid linebackers in NFL history, he, instead, admired the work, not the profits.

"I've just got a deep appreciation for people who show up to work every single day, even if no one notices, even if no one writes stories about them," Campbell. "(They) get to work, do their job, and take care of their families and keep their families first. Just a great appreciation. It's literally what the city of Detroit epitomizes, so that's what I'm going to try to epitomize."

Campbell followed through on that promise. He sacrificed so much of his time, effort, and now his body to this game that he loves, and there's something tragically beautiful about that.

But in this moment, nothing feels beautiful about it. His sacrifices feel fruitless.

In an outstanding story for The Athletic, Campbell talked about his ultimate goal to give back to the people who awarded him financial stability for the rest of his life.

"How can I bring a Super Bowl to Detroit? How can I do everything in my power, with every waking second inside and outside of the building, to do that?"

Now, despite putting more into that goal than arguably any other player on the team, he may never get that opportunity. His days of putting in that work he so admires may be over forever in Allen Park.

It may be callous to compare Campbell's plight to that of a soldier. He gets paid millions for our entertainment, while a soldier barely gets paid enough to eat in exchange (in theory) for our safety. But it sucks all the same that the people who give up so much of their own life for us rarely seem to get the kind of recompense they deserve.

There's no justice in this world,and there never was.

#2774. Analyst warns Panthers offense could struggle the rest of the season

So said Ray Liotta's Henry Hill in Goodfellas, "This is the bad time," as he descended into drug abuse, paranoia and legitimate fear of his "friends" in the mob, who may or may not have been planning to kill him.

The Carolina Panthers can probably relate right now, as they have lost two games in a row to NFC opponents—and it's been their own mistakes that have doomed them. From bad pass protection to turnover problems and a total lack of a pass rush, the Panthers are in free-fall mode going into their Week 9 matchup against an elite Denver Broncos team.

Following last week's 27-19 loss on the road to the Green Bay Packers, the Panthers have earned a 'C' grade for the week by John Breech at CBS Sports. Breech writes:

The Panthers' offensive line has struggled to protect Young all year and it only got uglier on Thursday night with two more starters out (RT Taylor Moton and LG Damien Lewis). Young tends to struggle when he's under pressure and he faced a lot of pressure while facing a Packers team that sacked him six times. If the Panthers can't figure out how to protect Young, this offense might struggle for the rest of the season.

The Panthers have a lot of problems, but the biggest by far is this issue of pass blocking—which has been horrible all year and is only getting worse by the week. Over the last two games, quarterback Bryce Young has been sacked 11 times—an unsustainable number for any team, especially one that doesn't have the weapons or the defense to counteract that kind of pressure.

It's a bit late in the game to fire offensive line coach Joe Gilbert now, but they have to do something to shake up their lineup—or you can kiss a second straight playoff appearance goodbye.

#2770. Browns defensive front problem, and missed tackles, need to improve

With this Browns' defense, I can tolerate a few big runs being given up if the defense took a chance and was burned. But the 3rd-and-13 resulting in a 51-yard run was a back-breaker, and then the sheer number of missed open field tackles, both against the run and on screen passes, is embarrassing. I don't expect perfection in the open field, but it's becoming a consistent problem that is helping extend drives. I've also seen various stats out there, indicating the Browns missed between 14 to 16 tackles on the day, which sounds about right from the eye test.

Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on defense for the Cleveland Browns' Week 8 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

2 tackles, 2 assists (4 combined). 1 TFL.

1 tackle, 1 assist (2 combined). 1 sack, 1 TFL, 1 QH.

Teams are starting to expose the Browns' defensive interior, which has proven to be threatening when teams have to pass, but has been susceptible to runs like this (see below). And then, the second- and third-level haven't been making tackles in open space to limit the damage a bit more.

While Todd Monken noted that they will have to make an adjustment, it is a concern when you factor in the personnel Cleveland has. However, it also seems like a bit of a scheme issue too, because the intent of the linemen seem clear in trying to rush up the field. I thought the Browns have played smarter at times this season by letting their talented secondary and cover corners make a play, instead of trying to force a big play via a rush up front.

Mike Hall returned this week and was one of the team's top-graded defenders, ranking third by PFF, with a grade of 72.2. However, tackling grades were poor for much of the team, including Hall, Jared Verse, Adin Huntington. In these loses, the frustration from the fan base continues to build toward Verse, who barely makes a visible impact on the game. The biggest story with him in this game was getting dumped on his head after talking in the media about Pittsburgh being dirty.

Maliek Collins left the game for a bit with an elbow injury.

2 tackles, 3 assists (5 combined). 1 TFL, 1 pass defended, 1 FF.

This wasn't the finest day at the office for Carson Schwesinger. Although he had 10 tackles, he received a grade of 30.5 from PFF, grading poorly in run defense, tackling, pass rush, and coverage. He appeared to be the man responsible on both of Darnell Washington's wheel routes that were successful for big gains. He denies that his ankle injury isn't holding him back, but you know that injuries like that can certainly be a factor.

Quincy Williams was back atop the PFF rankings with a grade of 90.0 and a solid run defense grade, for what it's worth.

1 tackle, 1 assist (2 combined). 1 INT, 2 passes defended.

1 tackle, 4 assists (5 combined). 1 pass defended, 1 FF.

Denzel Ward had a fortunate interception, with a PFF coverage grade of 90.1 on the day. His overall grade was only 63.5, though, as he also suffered with tackling and run defense.

Tyson Campbell was the Browns' top-graded defender by PFF, grading out to a 90.8, with some impressive work against DK Metcalf. Campbell left at the end of the first half with an injury, but returned. It's not his fault of course, but him being injured forced Cleveland to burn a timeout on that final drive of the first half, which may have been the difference in Pittsburgh getting a touchdown vs. only a field goal try.

2 tackles, 2 assists (4 combined). 1 TFL.

Emmanuel McNeil-Warren played 53% of the snaps this week.

#2769. Jeffery Simmons: Felt great to get my first sack as a Chicago Bear

It didn’t take long for Jeffery Simmons to get his first sack as a Bear.

Simmons took Sam Darnold down on the Seahawks’ fourth offensive play on Monday night, and he said afterward that as soon as he saw that they were blocking him one-on-one, he knew a big play was coming.

“If you block me one-on-one, I need to win the one-on-one. If I don’t win a one-on-one, the coaches should be on me. I hold myself to a high standard,” Simmons said. “It felt great to get my first sack as a Chicago Bear in my first game.”

Simmons always drew a lot of double teams during his All-Pro seasons with the Titans, and he drew plenty on Monday night in his first game since the Titans traded him to the Bears as well. He said he challenged his fellow Bears defensive linemen to take advantage of it when he was getting double teamed.

“If I’m getting a double team, I expect them to win their single block,” Simmons said. “We don’t need to blitz. I feel like if we can win at the line of scrimmage without the blitzes, that makes the guys’ jobs on the back end that much easier.”

Simmons played 55 defensive snaps, by far the most of any Bear in the game. He played 87 percent of the Bears’ defensive plays, which was exactly his snap count percentage for the Titans this season before he was traded. The Bears made a big investment in Simmons, trading two first-round draft picks for him, and they got a big return immediately.

In the moments before kickoff, Simmons said he was trying to keep his emotions in check by reminding himself, “It’s just football.” But it was hard not to be emotional.

“The emotions, especially during the national anthem, the emotions were coming and coming,” Simmons said.

Simmons said after the game that it means a lot to him to be playing meaningful football. The Titans are 1-7 and the Bears are 6-2 and Simmons knows the blockbuster trade was an opportunity for him to compete for a Super Bowl.

#2768. What Michael Malone said after North Carolina's win to open season

The North Carolina Tar Heels opened up the 2026-27 season with a win, kicking off the Michael Malone era in a positive way. However, it wasn't easy.

After grabbing an early lead, the Tar Heels watched as Western Carolina kept it close and made it a game. It took a late run for the Tar Heels to get the 80-72 win. And while it's a win, there are some concerns with this first game.

It's early but this is a game North Carolina should have won by a lot more. They are certainly going to have to play better if they want to achieve their goals this season. But nonetheless, a win is a win.

Following the first win of his college coaching career, Malone met the media where he discussed his team's performance and what's next. Here is what Malone had to say about the team's win.

"(That Western Carolina had) 13 more offensive rebounds is definitely a concern, and you can't have your power forward and your starting center only have four combined. Terrence (Brown) had five by himself. Neo (Avdalas) had seven by himself. But we'll have to watch it because one thing I do know is that both Jarin Stevenson and Sayon Keita, it's not like they're not playing hard. It's not like they're out there not giving effort. So we we will watch some film, see what what's really causing it. But big picture, yes, we need Sayon and Jarin to be seven to 10 boards every night."

"We were nine of 30 from the three-point line, 30%, and I'm going to make a guess here, I bet you 25 of those were open or wide open. I thought we generated a ton of good looks tonight that just did not go down. Aside from that, one thing I told our guys that right now we're a team that takes two steps forward, three steps back. We can't sustain anything. We have really good stretches, but we're unable to sustain it for long stretches, and we have to find a way to build those habits where we can start putting longer stretches together, putting halves together, putting a full 40 minutes together."

"Before you can run, you have to rebound, and so we can't worry about guys whether it's leaking out right now. I think it's four games now where our field goal percentage defense has been terrific, in my eyes. So you do all that hard work only to see the shot taken, and then they get an extra opportunity — 13 more tonight. So I think it's something where we just have to continue to harp on it, drill it, demand it, and I'm going to keep on pounding that rock."

"Coach Williams is the best. He sent me an amazing text last night, a touching text, and you know how he and his wife Wanda have welcomed me into this family means the world to myself, my wife Jocelyn, and just kind of reminded me that I'm sharing the seat that Dean Smith sat in, and and how fortunate you are to be doing that.

"I have to remind myself constantly that this really is going to be a process. And I'm thankful we got the win tonight. Always much easier and better to clean up things after a win. But the emotions were, I'm thankful to get that first one. And the fans here have been just so kind to me and welcoming. I love that and I appreciate that. And I just want to make sure I'm doing my job to make the Carolina family proud. I don't take this opportunity lightly, and that's a huge responsibility."

"Each game is an opportunity to look at different lineups, different combinations. We're always looking at the analytics. The best two-man, three-man, four-man, or five-man combos out there, and that's not just in our games, but we use that tracking from our practices as we try different groupings of players together to see what may help. The way I coach, we have our starting lineup. We have a sub chart going into each game as a reference, but the game will take on its own personality, and I'll read that and act accordingly."

"I had no idea it was coming. I'll be honest. Eric Hoots says, 'Hey, Coach, they want to give you the game ball.' I said, 'I don't want to do that right now. I just want to go in the back locker room.' And then I looked over, and they had to grab Coach Williams. I said, 'Well, Coach Williams is out here. I'm definitely going to do it.' No disrespect to Steve Newmark, but Roy Williams is one of the greatest to ever do it, and for him to just to take the time to be here for the game — he told me, 'Coach, you will not see me at any exhibition games, I'll only come to the games that count.' But I shook his hand before the game. I gave him a hug after the game, and obviously somebody that I look up to and respect, and thankful for his relationship."

#2767. The Lakers’ starting lineup is crushing teams to start the season

LOS ANGELES — If an 82-game season can guarantee a team one thing, it's disruption. And the Lakers have already had their fair share in just eight games.

Los Angeles forward Ziaire Williams missed the last three games with left foot soreness before being made active ahead of their 138-117 win against the Miami Heat on Monday. Williams, who impressed in the starting lineup to open the season, came off the bench for Jake LaRavia.

It could have been injury management. It could have also been matchup-dependent against the ever-so-powerful Giannis Antetokounmpo. LaRavia started in Williams's place during the three games he missed. Not only did the starting lineup with LaRavia hold up, it outperformed the opening night lineup.

Head coach JJ Redick is aware of what the numbers say, but assures that it's more about the team's overall balance rather than LaRavia simply being a better fit with the lineup than Williams.

"I just feel like there's balance with those lineups," Redick said pregame on Monday. "With Luka [Dončić] and [Austin Reaves] being the primary creators and [Walker Kessler]'s rim rolling and running. The other guys being able to guard multiple positions. … It's not surprising to me that Jake being in that lineup with those guys is good for us, because there's intrinsic knowledge with what we're trying to do. Just having another guy out there who knows our stuff has been helpful."

It's the balance Redick has been trying to manage since the Lakers turned over their roster this offseason: meshing the new with the old. It's a process that will take patience and time, as he's been lamenting so often this season.

But the results have been good nonetheless. In 51 minutes over four games when Williams shares the floor with the starters (Dončić, Reaves, Kessler and Matisse Thybulle), the Lakers have a 135.5 offensive rating and a 115.1 defensive rating for a 20.4 net rating. When LaRavia has been in Williams' spot, those numbers surge to a 144.3 offensive rating, a 90.0 defensive rating and a 54.3 net rating in 37 minutes.

For all the talk of balance and lineup optionality, it really all just boils down to Dončić continuing to be the best player in the world. The "supernova" — as Redick called him on Sunday — added another 42 points and 13 assists to his season total on Monday, dicing up every look Miami gave him on offense.

Dončić is now averaging 38.8 points, 8.1 assists and 21.3 assist points created in seven games, meaning Dončić is responsible for 60.1 points per game.

Redick added on Dončić postgame, "It's a really good offense that we're playing right now, and a lot of that, of course, is Dončić and what he's able to do. Bend the defense and his shot making creates a lot of problems, and then he can make every pass."

Williams, who scored nine points in fifteen minutes against Miami, is one of the biggest beneficiaries of Dončić's galatctic playamking. In Brooklyn last season, without a player of Dončić's shot-creating ilk, Williams shot 34.3% from deep with an overall 3-point shot quality that ranked in the league's 49th percentile, according to BBall Index.

In five games this season, Williams is shooting 47.6% from beyond the arc.

"Very easy looks. Way easier than in the past," Williams said Monday. "They're sending two to Luka, two to AR every time. So, it's just swing, swing, one more, and I get to set my feet, get to square up the ball. And I put a lot of work in this summer. I trust my work. I'm confident in my shot, my shot feels great."

It's not just Williams. Kessler is averaging 14.4 points on 71.4% from the field, the best percentage since his rookie season. Thybulle is on pace for a career-best season from on 3-pointers (45.9%). Reaves is putting together the best shooting splits of his career (53.9/44.4/86.5), taking advantage of the pressure Dončić attracts.

Los Angeles's offense is humming at a rate that rivals any other in the league. It's spearheaded by perhaps the best player in the world and bolstered by a bevy of guards, wings and bigs that can shoot, pass and dribble.

Rob Pelinka and Redick's had a clear plan this offseason, but even they may not have imagined it working this quickly and this effectively.

#2764. Position grades from the Patriots’ win over the Dolphins

It's not about how you start, it's about how you finish.

The New England Patriots took that saying to heart on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Going against a one-win opponent and enjoying the benefit of some extra rest, they played arguably their worst half of the season to star the Week 8 game. The result was a 13-3 deficit and a team looking less like a playoff contender and more like a middling team struggling to get above .500.

Luckily for the Patriots, the second half saw them do a 180-degree turn. They looked much improved especially on offense and defense — special teams we'll get to — and were able to score 21 unanswered points en route to a 24-19 victory.

Let's take a look at the film and hand out some grades.

Quarterback: If the Patriots were to come back from their 10-point deficit at the half, it needed to start with their most important player. Drake Maye answered the call, and delivered a near-perfect performance down the stretch: in the third and fourth quarters, when the team became more comfortable attacking Miami's defense vertically, he went a combined 9-for-10 for 146 yards with two deep passing touchdowns and a rushing score on a well-executed fake pitch as well. Overall, he finished the game with +0.42 expected points added per play, and continued to look every bit as impressive as he had in October. And let's not forget that Maye did all that while being without his nominal WR1, WR2, WR 4, TE1 and RB2, and with backups manning the left and right guard spots. | Grade: A

Running back: Aided by a good battle plan drawn up by offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, the Patriots had one of their best rushing days of the season so far. The main man, once again, was Rhamondre Stevenson: the veteran did not have any explosive runs, but he did have a success rate of 47.4% on his 19 carries for a combined 82 yards and caught all three of his pass targets. He also was again competitive in pass protection, despite giving up one hurry. Corey Kiner and Lan Larison also had their moments, with the former having the game's longest run — a 20-yarder in the first quarter — and the latter earning his first two career carries for six total yards. | Grade: A

Wide receiver: Down A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins, and losing tight end Hunter Henry in the second quarter, the Patriots relied heavily on Efton Chism, Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas. The trio did have some ups and downs, including when Chism had the ball punched out on a short throw to the flat, but overall performed well. Chism made up for his turnover by catching all five of his targets, including a 12-yard reception on a 4th-and-3 in the second quarter. Williams scored a massive 43-yard touchdown on his only target in the third, serving predominately as a space-clearer for the underneath routes. Douglas extended just enough on a crucial fourth-down conversion and later showed some tremendous speed, quickness and vision on a 48-yard catch-and-run touchdown. The Patriots needed them to step up, and they did. | Grade: A-

Tight end: The tight end group was big part of the Patriots' game plan, but losing Hunter Henry to a foot injury in the early second quarter forced the team to adapt; at that point, Henry had already caught three passes for 30 yards. Eli Raridon took a majority of snaps down the stretch, and primarily operated in the short and intermediate area while catching one 5-yard pass on three catchable targets. He also showed some improvement as a blocker in the run game, but was flagged for two false starts and unable to create movement on a pair of stuffed runs. The depth tight ends, Cameron Lomu and Tanner Arkin, both served as blockers and mostly did a serviceable job. | Grade: C

Offensive line: Have you heard Will Campbell's name lately? No? That's because he continues his ascent from offseason question mark to offensive pillar; he was very good against Miami and allowed just one hurry while also helping clear the way on some successful runs. Not everybody up front was quite that successful. Left guard Walter Rouse surrendered two quick pressures before getting benched for Ben Brown at the half, and center Jared Wilson again looked shaky with the snap. The right side had its ups and downs as well, with guard Matt Pryor failing to generate a consistent penetration in the run game but not giving up any quarterback disruptions, and right tackle Morgan Moses struggling at times with the speed rush around the edge. | Grade: C+

Defensive line: The Patriots' run defense came to play on Sunday, and the play along the defensive line had a lot to do with it. The standout name among the group was Cory Durden, who registered three pressures including 1.5 sacks and helped stuff a pair of runs. The other DTs also had their moments, with Milton Williams and Christian Barmore — who both lined up inside and outside — challenging the interior offensive line beyond their five combined credited pressures, and Leonard Williams continuing to positively contribute in limited snaps. On the edge, Gabe Jacas' knee injury forced him to miss most of the second half, but he continued showing his speed and power in his limited reps and helping create two sacks. Elijah Ponder played some off-ball linebacker to open the game and also looked good dropping out on an incompletion intended for tight end Will Kacmarek; he also was at the point of attack on a sack. Dre'Mont Jones, meanwhile, notched a team-leading five pressures even though him lining up offsides negated a Christian Elliss interception. | Grade: A

Linebacker: Speaking of Christian Elliss, he was disruptive coming downhill and like fellow starter- Robert Spillane did a good job finishing tackles; a point of emphasis at One Patriot Place after last week's loss in Chicago. The two were moved out of the way on a 16-yard Ollie Gordon run in the fourth quarter — Spillane was pushed wide on a run blitz, Elliss unable to create a proper tackling form reaching around center Aaron Brewer — but in general the pair continues to be solid guarding the second level of New England's defense. | Grade: A-

Cornerback: The Patriots relied heavily on zone coverage against one of the league's most productive scramble quarterbacks, Malik Willis. The plan worked, with Willis gaining only two yards on his lone run of the day, but it created some openings in the passing game. New England did mix and match its coverages, including by the introduction of more quarters looks to complement their heavy usage of Cover 4, but Miami still found some openings. Two of those came in the direction of Christian Gonzalez, whose deep-zone drops created space underneath for gains of 23 and 18 yards in the second quarter. Gonzalez was his usual stout self in New England's limited man reps, which is where returnee Carlton Davis showed some rust. He allowed a pair of third-down conversions when receivers were able to create some separation at the top of their routes. Marcus Jones limited the damage in man, while Charles Woods tripping over his own feet in Cover 4 allowed Kevin Coleman Jr. to get open for a 35-yard touchdown. | Grade: C+

Safety: Kevin Byard caught his first interception of the season when a pass intended for Caleb Douglas, who was open underneath New England's Cover 2 structure, bounced off of defensive tackle DaQuan Jones' helmet and into the safety's waiting arms. It was a right place/right time-type of play, and some good finishing by the captain. Byard also was beaten in a tough 1-on-1 red zone matchup for a touchdown versus Malik Washington. Craig Woodson dropped an interception in the early third quarter and was a bit too hesitant on a 19-yard catch by tight end Greg Dulcich, but otherwise solid. Third option Jaylen Reed was on the field for 13 reps as well, and did get to the quarterback on a delayed rush. | Grade: C

Special teams: New England's kicking game operation was not at its best last week in Chicago, and it again had some negative moments against the Dolphins. Among them was a 43-yard kickoff return in the first quarter, when Leonard Taylor was too aggressive getting downfield and an Andy Borregales shoe-string tackle prevented further damage. Speaking of Borregales, he missed a 40-yard field goal attempt and has now been unable to make four of 34 combined place kicks to bring his success rate to 88.2%. On the plus side, Marcus Jones averaged 11.7 yards on his three punt returns. | Grade: C-

How would you grade the Patriots' performance against the Dolphins? Do you agree with our assessment? Please head down to the comment section to discuss with the rest of the community.

#2763. Colorado football rises in ESPN FPI rankings after Week 9 win

After snapping their five-game losing streak with an overtime win over Kansas State, the Buffaloes saw their standing improve in ESPN's Football Power Index after all the Week 9 action.

#2762. Wil Lutz has made 113 straight extra points, most in the NFL since the 2015 rule change

It’s been three years since Broncos kicker Wil Lutz missed an extra point.

After hitting both his extra points in Sunday’s win over the Chiefs, Lutz has now made 113 consecutive extra points without a miss. That’s the longest streak in the NFL since the 2015 rule change that moved extra points back by 13 yards. The previous record of 112 consecutive extra points was set by Justin Tucker with the Ravens.

“I’ve [said] a hundred times how much I value the extra point. I value them a lot. But my goal isn’t to break the record, it’s to make every one the rest of the season, so whatever that number is at the end of the season,” Lutz told Chris Tomasson of the Denver Gazette.

Lutz’s last missed an extra point when he doinked one off the upright against the Bills on November 11, 2023. Lutz made up for that with the game-winning field goal as time expired in a 24-22 victory.

The 32-year-old Lutz first entered the NFL as an undrafted rookie in 2016 with the Ravens, who weren’t seriously considering him for a roster spot as they had Tucker, who was the best kicker in the NFL at the time. But Lutz impressed then-Ravens coach John Harbaugh enough that when it came time to cut Lutz at the end of the preseason, Harbaugh personally called then-Saints coach Sean Payton to recommend Lutz. Payton brought Lutz to New Orleans, and then traded for Lutz when Payton became coach of the Broncos.

By having faith in Lutz, Payton has ensured that he’ll have nothing to worry about on extra points.

#2760. Mike Macdonald: We lost in all three phases

Monday night’s game in Seattle featured a pair of 2025 NFC playoff teams who would like to be back in the postseason this year and it ended with the Bears celebrating a 34-17 win over the defending Super Bowl champions.

The Seahawks had made it a three-point game early in the fourth quarter, but a 39-yard screen pass to Kalif Raymond converted a key Bears third down on the next drive and the roof caved in on the Seahawks from there. The Bears ended the night with 111 more offensive yards than the Seahawks and their defense thwarted Seattle on 10 of their 11 third down attempts over the course of the night, which led Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald to say after the game that “there’s no other way to sugarcoat” the way his team got beat.

Seahawks kicker Jason Myers missed an extra point and had a field goal blocked and the Seahawks committed several personal fouls to add to their woes on a night when the Bears were clearly better across the board.

“They made it happen, and we didn’t,” Macdonald said, via the team’s website. “It’s a team effort; we lost as a team. In all three phases, we can have better plans, we can coach it better, prepare our players better, and we can play better. We’ll go back to work and go attack the heck out of it. The margins in our league are too small, and when you don’t do the things that it takes to win, that’s how a game like that shapes up. It was a team effort. We lost in all three phases.”

The Seahawks overwhelmed the Chiefs in a Week 7 win, but Monday night was the kind of step back that explains why they’re 4-4 on the season. Having it happen against another NFC contender at home makes the blow more painful and Macdonald said the Seahawks “have some work to do” if they’re going to position themselves for another run at the end of this season.

#2759. 3 things from Charlotte's 124-91 defeat to Detroit

The Charlotte Hornets dropped their fourth consecutive game Monday, losing by 33 points to the Detroit Pistons. In five home games to begin the season, the Hornets have now suffered two blowouts at the Spectrum Center, losing by 47 points to the Atlanta Hawks and now 33 points at the hands of the Pistons.

A former two-time All-NBA selection, Cade Cunningham was dominant, finishing the game with a team-high 33 points to go along with seven assists, five rebounds and five steals. Duncan Robinson poured in 24 points as well, converting on six of his nine 3-point attempts. Ausar Thompson, Paul Reed and Ron Holland II also finished in double figures. For the Hornets, Brandon Miller finished with 17 points and Naz Reid added 13. Sion James and Grayson Allen tallied 11 each. Before Charlotte faces the Nets Wednesday, here are three things to take note of.

While it doesn't help that the Hornets lead the NBA in turnovers per game, when they are able to put together a quality offensive possession, they've had trouble scoring. After another sub-100 performance Monday, the Hornets are the only NBA team to average fewer than 100 points per contest (97.4). At 40.5% from the field, the Hornets are dead last in field goal percentage, headlined by Sion James who is shooting 27.7% in eight starts.

On paper, the pairing between the Hornets and Naz Reid seemed like a perfect match this summer. However, eight games in, it hasn't looked too pretty. While Reid is averaging a career-high in points (15.5) and rebounds (8.3) in his first season as a starter, he hasn't been as advertised on offense. Reid is shooting a career-low 39.5% from the field, a tough pill to swallow, considering Reid's size. He's also shooting 34.5% from beyond the arc on 6.9 3-point attempts per game. While the former LSU forward can certainly turn things around in support of Miller, Coby White and Kon Knueppel, his performance has been a bit disappointing in an increased role to begin the year.

Why were the Hornets so great offensively a season ago? They led the league in 3-pointers made while finishing third in 3-point percentage. After loading up on 3-point shooters to take a similar approach this season, things haven't gone to plan. Despite leading the league in 3-pointers attempted (44.4), Charlotte is tied for 16th in makes (13.1). At 29.6%, Charlotte is 29th in the league in 3-point percentage, one of only two teams shooting below 30%.

#2757. Warriors vs. Suns player grades: Steph Curry saves the day, Charles Bassey has career night

The Golden State Warriors won an odd game on Monday, beating the Phoenix Suns 116-113. They once again dug themselves a first-quarter hole, and this time it took them a bit longer to climb out of it. But a win is a win is a win, and the Warriors have now won five straight … something they didn't do at any point last season.

It was a game that featured some great performances and some awful ones, so let's grade them! As always, grades are based on my expectations for each player, with a "B" grade representing the average performance for that individual.

Note: True-shooting percentage (TS) is a scoring efficiency metric that accounts for threes and free throws. Entering Monday's games, league-average TS was 57.2%.

28 minutes, 6 points, 5 rebounds, 1 block, 1 turnover, 3 fouls, 2-for-7 shooting, 2-for-5 threes, 42.9% TS, -17

Richard got the start in this one, for the second time this season. It was a play to get more perimeter defense on a team starting Jalen Green, Devin Booker, and Miles Bridges, and Richard took turns defending all three. As we've grown accustomed to, he played good defense, though it wasn't the best he's been on that side of the ball. There were definitely plenty of moments where he got beat, or was a little over eager and out of position.

He did some good things on offense, but not too much. He's there for defense, though, and he played it.

Grade: BPost-game bonus: Worst plus/minus on the team.

29 minutes, 16 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, 1 steal, 1 block, 2 turnovers, 4 fouls, 3-for-10 shooting, 2-for-6 threes, 8-for-9 free throws, 57.3% TS, -11

Poor Yaxel. Sunday was the first time this season that I didn't write a grades article and, fittingly, he had his best game of the season. Obviously that's his biggest concern, so I'm sorry, Yaxel. Please know that you would have gotten an A with two plus signs had I penned some grades.

For this game the grade has to be a little bit lower, though. Lendeborg got off to a slow start (as did the entire team), and picked up two quick fouls while struggling to get anything going on offense.

As the game went on, though, the rookie picked things up considerably, and he ended up having a very strong second half. I remain in awe of his restraint: you just don't see a lot of rookies who are so comfortable picking and choosing their shots, and not hoisting an unnecessary number of jumpers. Critically, even after his tough start, the team turned to him on multiple possessions down the stretch, and he very often delivered, while also having a glass-check block late in the game that was probably the defensive highlight of the contest.

I'm still struggling to grade him, though, because I'm struggling to figure out what my expectations should be. This guy genuinely might be the first rookie All-Star since Blake Griffin, so how do I grade him? With all respect to Draymond Green and Brandin Podziemski, Lendeborg is far and away the second-best player on the team (until Jimmy Butler III returns, at least, and maybe after, too), and that makes grading difficult. But who cares, the show is a hell of a lot of fun to watch.

17 minutes, 4 points, 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 1 turnover, 1 foul, 1-for-2 shooting, 2-for-2 free throws, 69.4% TS, -6

The Warriors over the last week have had the best vibes they've possessed since the first round of the 2025 playoffs. And Green put that in jeapoardy. Two minutes into the third quarter, he got into it with Phoenix center Khaman Maluach. After being pushed to the floor, Green got up, committed a hard foul, and kind of threw Maluach to the floor. What followed was an altercation with Dillon Brooks, in which Green shoved Brooks around the neck area. He received a technical foul for each act, and was subsequently ejected for the first time this year.

Ejections come with the territory with Green, and I'm usually one to defend him more quickly than others. After all, these are grown adults playing a high-stakes contact sport … some pushing and shoving and yelling never hurt anyone. But this was too far, and, while not as bad as his incidents a few years back with Rudy Gobert, Domantas Sabonis, and Jusuf Nurkić, these started to cross over the line from "aggressive basketball" to "violence."

Thankfully for Green, the team responded to his absence well, but it didn't need to go that way. His absence didn't end up costing the Warriors the win, but it could hurt them down the road, as it's possible he'll get a one-game suspension for his actions.

I've giving Green a harsh grade for taking himself out of the game and possibly the next one, and not playing particularly well before then, either. But it's worth noting that the Warriors players spoke after the game about how Green's ejection fired them up, so … take that for what it's worth.

33 minutes, 20 points, 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 3 turnovers, 2 fouls, 7-for-15 shooting, 3-for-8 threes, 3-for-4 free throws, 59.7% TS, -4

The Warriors, over the course of this nice winning streak, have developed a habit of starting slow and finishing strong. And Podziemski completely embodies that. Podz has really been struggling out of the gates lately, but as soon as he emerges from the locker room at halftime, he's a completely different player.

That was again the case in this game. He couldn't get anything going in the first half, and then he was bailing the Dubs out time and time again in the second. If he had paced his performance over the course of the game, I'd probably give him a "B" for a very solid, if not noteworthy performance. But because he had so many big plays on both ends of the court with the game on the line, we'll bump him up a half grade.

33 minutes, 34 points, 6 rebounds, 7 assists, 1 steal, 3 turnovers, 2 fouls, 9-for-21 shooting, 5-for-13 threes, 11-for-12 free throws, 64.7% TS, +21

I'm sure that when the game ended and the Dubs retreated to the locker rooms, Green was waiting with a big hug for Curry. Golden State was losing when Green was ejected, and had the score held, the biggest story — maybe the only story — would have been Draymond's transgressions. Instead, Curry went ballistic as soon as Green left the court, and scored 18 points in the third quarter alone as the Dubs rattled off 42 in the frame to tie things up.

Curry looks better this year than in the past few years, and this was his third consecutive game with at least 30 points and five made threes. He seems energized, and that's a joy to behold, and a harbinger of how good this team can be.

Grade: APost-game bonus: Led the team in points and assists; best plus/minus on the team.

20 minutes, 2 points, 2 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 steal, 2 turnovers, 4 fouls, 1-for-3 shooting, 0-for-2 threes, 33.3% TS, +3

Not surprisingly, GPII got a lot of run against a team with Booker, Green, and Bridges. And also not surprisingly, he handled those assignments really well. He hasn't had one of his bursts of offense yet this season, and he had a few sloppy plays in this one, but overall, solid performance.

22 minutes, 13 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 foul, 5-for-6 shooting, 1-for-2 threes, 2-for-3 free throws, 88.8% TS, +20

Well that was a damn fine performance. Niang showed everything the Warriors are looking for from him: he drained open shots, passed to the open man, played strong defense while guarding a variety of positions, crashed tho glass, made the smart play, and hustled. He's very quickly building a strong rapport with Curry, which is huge; the result is that he's a very trustworthy player to have on the court down the stretch.

It's not always going to work this well, but when it does? Yeesh.

28 minutes, 2 points, 7 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals, 2 fouls, 1-for-9 shooting, 0-for-5 threes, 0-for-1 free throws, 10.6% TS, 0 +/-

Remember when I said, just a few words ago, that it isn't always going to work this well with Niang? Well, that's the case for all players in that sort of role … and Melton is living proof. Melton has had some really good games lately but this one was a bit of a clunker … at least scoring the ball, as he could not get any shots to fall.

He did some other good things though. He took care of the rock, rebounded really well, and played decent enough defense. But it's hard to impact the game when you shoot 1-for-9 from the field, and he just looked a step behind on a lot of plays.

23 minutes, 19 points, 8 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 turnover, 4 fouls, 7-for-10 shooting, 5-for-6 free throws, 75.2% TS, +10

What a performance by Bassey! His role has been very undefined this year, which makes sense. He's still trying to carve out a role in the NBA, he's recovering from a preseason injury, and the Warriors needs fluctuate based on who they're playing, how Green and Lendeborg are performing, and whether or not Al Horford is playing.

But Bassey got a decent-sized role in this one, and then that role expanded because he was playing so damn well. He was crafty around the rim, finding ways to contort his body to score around and through contact, en route to a career-high 19 points. He not only grabbed a bunch of boards, but did so emphatically, patrolling the paint every time a shot went up.

He even had a great memeable moment, when the ball went out of bounds and he hugged a fan.

Re-signing him is just one of many fantastic moves that the Warriors made this offseason. Hindsight is 20/20, as no one was saying they made good moves a few months ago!

Grade: A+Post-game bonus: Led the team in rebounds.

Ike somewhat surprisingly got some run in this game, especially after Green was ejected. He didn't do anything statistically — he didn't log a single stat — but I liked what we saw from him on defense.

39 seconds, 0 points, 0-for-1 shooting, 0-for-1 threes, 0.0% TS, 0 +/-

Cryer briefly got onto the court for an end-of-quarter offense situation, but that was all we saw of him.

Monday's inactives: Jimmy Butler III, Al Horford, Moses Moody, Kristaps Porziņģis, Gui Santos, Brandon Williams
