#2752. Steph Curry, Charles Bassey help Warriors to fifth straight win

A Golden State Warriors season doesn't truly begin until Draymond Green gets kicked out of a game. This year, they have Charles Bassey to pick up the slack.

Bassey scored a career-high 19 points and collected eight rebounds, holding down the fort inside as the Warriors erased a 17-point deficit to beat the Phoenix Suns, 116-113. Golden State put up 42 points in the third quarter, Steph Curry exceeded 30 points for the third straight game, and De'Anthony Melton made two huge defensive plays late to lock down the victory.

Let's get the ejection out of the way early. It's become exhausting to write about Green losing control on the court, which coincidentally tends to happen when he's playing badly or the Warriors are losing. Early in the third quarter, Green took exception to contact from second-year Suns center Khaman Maluach, which left him on the ground. To be honest, it looked like Green was flopping for a call.

Green jumped up, grabbed Maluach around the waist, and threw him to the ground. When his longtime nemesis Dillon Brooks ran in to defend his teammate, Green grabbed Brooks by the jersey and jammed a fist into the side of his neck. The result? One technical foul for Brooks, and two for Green, which meant his 23rd regular-season ejection (he's been kicked out of two playoff games and suspended for two more). He finished with four points, four rebounds, and two assists.

Brooks claimed he was running in to de-escalate the situation, something Brooks is known for never, ever doing, but he really wasn't in the wrong there. I've watched the replay multiple times and I strongly support anyone who would grab Draymond and yell, "What are you doing?" at him. There's no word that Maluach was injured in the altercation, but he also didn't really play afterward.

After the game, Curry said Green's ejection "lit a fire beneath us," but what lit up the Warriors right away was Bassey's energy. They missed their first two shots after Green's ejection, but Bassey tipped in a miss and drew a foul, then found Curry for one of his four third-quarter triples.

Bassey scored six points in the quarter and 10 after halftime, getting to the line for five free throws and making four. He was opportunistic, setting screens and rolling hard to the rim while also taking advantage of mismatches with smaller Suns defenders.

Of course, Steph Curry scoring 18 points in the quarter was a pretty big factor as well. He shot 6-for-9 in nine minutes, putting up double-digit points in the third quarter for the third time in his last four games (he had 8 in the other one). In the four games Curry played during the Warriors' five-game winning streak, he's scored 55 points in the third quarter, perhaps because he's gone back to his old habit of reading critical tweets about his first-half performance during halftime.

Graham Ike played seven minutes and twenty-three seconds Monday night and did not record a single stat. That's officially known as a "7 trillion," with the seven referring to Ike's minutes, followed by 12 consecutive zeroes in the other categories. He was -1 in those seven minutes, which means that while Ike did not have an individual moment statistically regarded for posterity, at least he didn't foul, turn the ball over, or get in the way of better players. Plus, he had a sweet hockey assist on Curry's corner three.

Curry finally missed a free throw in the final seconds of the game, one that could have iced the game, but it's hard to judge him too harshly when he started the season 51-for-51. Curry is also averaging 8.7 free throw attempts per game, which is 37% more than his previous single-season high. Maybe the referees are finally showing some respect to the baby-faced assassin Dangerfield.

The Warriors got Green and Curry back after they sat out Sunday's win over the L.A. Clippers, while Will Richard made his first start of the season in place of the injured Gui Santos and the too-slow-to-guard-Devin-Booker Georges Niang. Or Steve Kerr simply wanted The Minivan to run all over the Suns' reserves, as he did by shooting 5-for-6 and putting up 13 points, finishing +20 in his 23 minutes.

It was a rough start, mainly because the Warriors kept settling for, and missing, three-pointers, finishing 2-for-15 from behind the arc in the quarter. A typical slow Warriors start involves a lot of turnovers, reckless fouling, or indifferent defense, but this one was simple: They could not buy a bucket, even with just two turnovers. It could have been worse, but Bassey drew some fouls and hustled his way to seven points.

Phoenix blocked the Warriors' first three-point attempts of the second quarter, meaning they started the game going 2-for-17 from deep. After a Miles Bridges three, Phoenix led by 17 points with 8:29 to play. Even after Yaxel Lendeborg made two threes, Phoenix was still up by 16 points with 3:45 to go in the quarter. After Devin Booker (26 points) hit a short jumper, Kerr called timeout, Curry and Green came back in the game, and ESPN declared the Suns had a win probability of 88.6%. Do they do election predictions?

The Suns wouldn't make a field goal the rest of the half, as Brandin Podziemski (20 points) led a 12-0 run that got the Warriors firmly back into the game (Suns win probability down to 62.3%). Kerr also won a challenge after Curry forced a turnover and the referees awarded Phoenix the ball, which was reversed and turned into a Curry bucket on the ensuing inbounds play.

Golden State finally tied the game in the third quarter on a Curry bucket, but didn't take the lead until early in the 4th, on a bucket from (who else?) Bassey.

The game went back and forth throughout the final quarter. The Warriors led by as many as seven points, then lost their lead, and finally went ahead for good on a Niang three-pointer with under four minutes to go. The rest of the way, they did it with defense.

Curry stole the ball from Booker. Melton stole the ball from Jalen Green. Then, with the Warriors clinging to a five-point lead, Melton drew an offensive foul on Booker, his sixth. Not a great closing effort for Booker, who had the same number of turnovers as points in the 4th: Two.

The Warriors made it interesting, of course. After Booker's ejection, Lendeborg blocked a Jalen Green layup out of bounds, but the Suns got a dunk after inbounding the ball. With 20 seconds left, Curry traveled, and the Suns, who were out of timeouts, cut the lead to a single point on Green's dunk. But Curry made two free throws, Green missed the rim entirely trying to miss on purpose, and Collin Gillespie's last-gasp 37-footer missed at the buzzer.

Curry is always the MVP of this team, but honorable mentions for Monday go to Bassey, Podz, and the security guy who dragged Draymond to the bench before he could start throttling Brooks' windpipe.

Brooks had 18 points, with four turnovers. Jalen Green had eight assists, with four turnovers. Miles Bridges had 21 points and four steals and remains a domestic abuser who has no place in the NBA. However, he did only turn the ball over once.

It was a big win for the Warriors, who didn't win five straight for all of last season. It was also a big win for Warriors assistant coach Frank Vogel, who has seen the Dubs defeat the two most recent NBA teams to fire him within four nights. #2749. Why Honda’s power unit lasted barely five laps in F1 Mexico GP

In its Mexico Grand Prix preview, Honda's Shintaro Orihara had described Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez as "a very challenging track for the power unit", but he perhaps didn't expect Aston Martin's weekend to go so awry.

Despite decent pace and mileage in free practice – Fernando Alonso was just 0.769s down on pacesetter Charles Leclerc in FP2, with the AMR26s covering a whopping 144 laps across all three sessions – it all went wrong in the competitive sessions.

Honda did fix some driveability and turbo lag issues between FP3 and qualifying, but Alonso encountered "abnormal signals on the water systems" on Saturday afternoon, which didn't prevent him from outqualifying Lance Stroll; still, both cars were out in Q1, four tenths down on the Q2 cut-off time.

Aston Martin claims Lance Stroll is "unbeatable" at many F1 tracks

In the race, the pair retired after five laps due to cooling issues.

"We knew that with the special high-altitude circumstance of Mexico City, we would face some additional challenges compared to other racetracks for the cooling," said Orihara, Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer, following the race.

"However, we found that our ERS cooling circuit was under heavier stress than anticipated and this is why we had to stop the car in different sessions.

"Despite completing a series of laps during the practice sessions, the issue occurred today and during qualifying yesterday.

"At each race this year, we need to learn for 2027, even the hard lessons. We have a lot of data that we can bring back to this circuit next year, including on the turbo lag, and we will work on the solutions."

Orihara pointed out on Thursday that in previous years the MGU-H supported the turbo, therefore reducing lag, but the new, simpler power units no longer feature that device – and that too was a problem with the thinner air at Mexico City's high altitude.

While a frustrated Stroll only gave laconic answers to the media at the end of the weekend, Alonso was slightly more loquacious and underlined the scale of the challenge for Aston Martin and Honda.

"The car is very good," the Spaniard said. "The problem is just, we cannot do more laps than a certain number, apparently, with the engine. Hopefully we learned a lesson and we come next year more prepared."

But the Adrian Newey-designed machine had potential – even in Mexico. It's fair to say Alonso and Stroll didn't get much of a chance to show what they could do in the race; yet, putting the Spaniard's quickest three sectors together on Sunday (he pitted on lap three, which prevented him from completing a decent lap), he was nearly as quick as Williams' Carlos Sainz, despite presumably having a much heavier car with a full tank of fuel.

"On Thursday, when we sat together, we said this is a track that has a lot of low-speed corners," Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said. "And if we get the driveability under control, that we can be competitive. For example, corners like the stadium section, [Turns] 4-5-6, low-speed stuff."

Reliability therefore is the crux of the issue – as well as keeping morale up. "It's difficult for everyone to keep the motivation high in such situations, and we are struggling all year already," Krack admitted.

"We had a very difficult start of the year, then the period when we introduced the upgrades and the ADUO, we [had] a bit better results. Now, we have more trouble in terms of reliability. In Texas, we had different issues with incidents. You know, it's part of racing.

"The thing is, everybody tries his best, everybody is motivated to do better, and I have no doubt about the motivation. We don't have to motivate them, it's motivating them the highest possible."

And if anyone is staying motivated, that will be Alonso. "I'm doing my best every time, every lap I do, every morning I wake up, every preparation I do, every food I take – everything is focused on performing at my best behind the wheel," he insisted again despite his seventh retirement of the season.

#2747. Why are there no NBA games today? League promotes the midterm vote

In a push to get more people out to the ballot box, for the fourth time in five years, the entire NBA will go dark.

The league did not schedule any games Tuesday, Nov. 3, the day of the fiercely contested 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Because the first slate of polls close on the East Coast at 6 p.m. ET, with many more at 7 p.m. ET, holding games would severely interfere with the ability for people who choose to vote in person to do so.

It's one of the three days that the NBA typically avoids scheduling games, joining Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve.

The NBA has also published a website with several resources for fans interested in voting to learn more about their polling sites, ballots, and the league even has a link to check voter registration status.

Although the entire league is off Tuesday, each team played Monday, Nov. 2. And at each of those 15 games, players wore T-shirts that said "VOTE" across the chest.

"No games have been scheduled for Election Day (Tuesday, Nov. 3) as the league will encourage fans and the broader NBA community to make a plan to vote and to participate in the civic process," the NBA said in August when it issued its official release announcing the schedule.

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr spoke on the importance of voting before their game against the Phoenix Suns on Monday, Nov. 2.

"I hope everybody votes," Kerr said. "I voted today, dropped my ballot off in a ballot box near my house, and, you know, I always encourage everybody to get out there and vote. And sometimes there's a tendency to stay away in the midterms and only vote in the presidential elections, but there's a lot of really important issues here in California.

"I hope everybody gets out there and cast their ballot.  That's what democracy's about."

The NBA first began the initiative of not scheduling games on Election Day in Nov. 2022. At the time, the league also encouraged its teams to promote voting initiatives. The NBA also declined to schedule games on Election Day 2023 and 2024.

And since Tuesday will be an off night, the league will return to action in full force Wednesday, Nov. 4, with a slate packed with 14 games.

#2745. If you're nervous about the Ravens' fantasy outlook, you should be

With Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley indefinitely sidelined, and with third-string QB Joe Fagnano a question mark heading into Thursday Night Football, the Ravens are in complete fantasy disarray. Sometimes disarray can be cleaned up -- like a messy closet or bedhead. Baltimore's problems should force fantasy managers to accept the almost inevitable pain to come.

The Ravens were one of only two teams this summer with three fantasy players inside the ADP top 40: Jackson, Derrick Henry, and Zay Flowers. Jackson was overvalued at his QB2 ADP, which assumed a return to greatness—something rarely done by frequently injured, dual-threat quarterbacks facing declining rushing attempts and advancing age.

Henry's only significant obstacle entering the season was limited usage in the passing game. He's almost always made up for it with high rushing volume and elite TD totals. But what happens when an offense descends from "great" to "struggling"? Henry has scored only once in his last three games while averaging just 8.3 points. If he doesn't score, he usually needs 20+ carries to be a must-start RB. His rest-of-season production likely will drop significantly.

But not as much as Flowers' rest-of-season production. The Ravens' #1 WR was on pace for an incredible 113-1,723-9 receiving line entering Week 8, which translated into 20+ fantasy points per game. He'll be lucky to have 10 points going forward. Over the years, we've seen what happens when third- or fourth-string quarterbacks helm an offense. It's often a fantasy disaster.

If you're rostering any of these guys, it's probably too late to unload them unless you're willing to part ways at a huge discount -- and that might be the best move you can make.

#2743. Celtics’ shooting woes got the best of them — as did Marcus Smart

The Boston Celtics already had their hands full on Monday night. No Paul George. No reprieve on the second night of a back-to-back on the road. Then came Marcus Smart.

Former beloved friend of the program, Smart embraced his new Houston Rockets uniform. Like a gray wolf circling wounded prey, he watched his former team struggle through a miserable 38.6 percent shooting performance before sinking his teeth in at every opportunity. Whenever the Celtics tried to put out the fire, Smart poured kerosene on it, leading Houston to a 109-93 victory and bringing Boston's Eastern Conference-best five-game winning streak to an end.

"He woke up everybody's ass," Rockets teammate Alperen Şengün told Ryan Hollins postgame.

It didn't take long for Smart to make his presence felt.

HOUSTON, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Marcus Smart #36 of the Houston Rockets shoots a three point basket during the game against the Boston Celtics on November 2, 2026 at the Toyota Center in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Logan Riely/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

After noticing Jayson Tatum expressing his frustration with referee Matt Kallio with 3:11 left until halftime, Smart immediately fled Houston's bench and instigated, urging the official to issue Tatum a technical foul. He was all laughs, while Tatum — considerably less amused by the antics — remained visibly frustrated as he stared Smart down for a brief second and walked back to Boston's bench.

Smart was still all smiles, as he put his arm around Mike Conley and began plotting his scheme.

In the third quarter, Smart got Tatum again. He drew a charge on Tatum, handing him his fourth personal foul. Seconds later, Tatum was whistled for a second straight offensive foul, bringing his total to five and forcing Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla to remove him with 1:39 remaining in the frame. Tatum, visibly frustrated once again, made another unhappy trip to Boston's sideline.

Payton Pritchard also fell for Smart's bait, earning a third-quarter offensive foul himself. Smart did his signature Shawn Michaels-inspired kip-up to get back on his feet.

By then, it was official. Smart's plan was in full effect.

Much like the menace who wore No. 36 for nine seasons in Boston, Smart reminded the Celtics why it's great to play alongside him and a pain in the ass to compete against him. He went scoreless in the first half and missed his first seven shots before finally making Boston pay.

Rockets head coach Ime Udoka kept Smart on the floor to begin the fourth quarter, and the 13th-year veteran rewarded that decision with two timely shots.

Smart drained back-to-back 3-pointers, extending Houston's lead to 90-79 with over eight minutes remaining. He raised both middle fingers in celebration, later claiming the gesture was directed at a select few seated on Boston's bench.

"Just a lot of pent-up, I guess you can call it emotions," Smart told reporters. "Plus, certain guys on the (Boston) bench was talking. Didn't know who. I just heard them say something, so I let them hear it back."

Smart finished with eight points, four rebounds, four assists, and two steals in over 19 minutes.

"You always wanna do good against your former team," Smart added, "and show them that you still can go out there and do what you do, right? So it definitely felt good. Energy was there. They know what I can do, and I reminded them again tonight."

The energy Tatum once benefited from having alongside him had finally come back to haunt him. Smart's swagger was contagious, and everyone in Houston fed off it.

The Rockets shot 40 percent from three and 54.4 percent overall, having their way with Boston.

Meanwhile, the Celtics couldn't get anything to go.

Boston's top outside-shooting threats — Pritchard, Derrick White, Sam Hauser, and Baylor Scheierman — combined to go 4-for-21 from beyond the arc. Luka Garza, coming off the bench to play over 17 minutes, was the Celtics' leader in 3-point makes (four), although that contribution was largely overshadowed by the rest of the team's shooting woes.

They were a hair better from three (29 percent) than they were 24 hours earlier (27 percent) against the Orlando Magic on Sunday night.

Tatum went 1-for-7 from distance and 5-for-16 overall, finishing the night with 19 points and a season-high five turnovers in Houston.

It's difficult enough to play two games in two nights, especially on the road, but Tatum believes the Celtics didn't do themselves many favors either throughout the game.

"Everybody plays back-to-backs," Tatum told reporters, per NBC Sports Boston. "We're not the only team that's gotta travel and play a back-to-back. Are they tough? Yeah. But a lot of us been doing this for a long time. There were moments where we cut it to six or seven (points) and couldn't get a rebound, and they hit a three. It's moments like that where we gotta dig deeper a little bit."

It's been three years since the Celtics traded Smart, originally sending him to the Memphis Grizzlies. In the years since, the 32-year-old has struggled to make his former team pay, whether because of his on-court performance or availability. But Monday night in Houston, Smart finally got his get-back, and Boston felt it.

#2741. Where will Jonathan Taylor land? Breaking down the Colts’ most likely trade partners

The Indianapolis Colts have already made it clear that significant changes are coming, trading two of their most accomplished veterans in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner following the dismissal of general manager Chris Ballard. With the team now sitting at 2-6 after Sunday's humiliating 42-7 defeat against the Jacksonville Jaguars, attention has increasingly shifted toward the future of another franchise cornerstone: Jonathan Taylor.

A little over two weeks ago, I examined Taylor's hypothetical trade value, projecting that Indianapolis could realistically receive a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 third-round selection in exchange for its star running back. That evaluation came before the Colts began moving key veterans, and with several teams now reportedly expressing serious interest, the market appears to be considerably more competitive than initially anticipated.

According to reports from ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, Indianapolis has been engaged in trade discussions involving Taylor, with the Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Seattle Seahawks, New York Giants and Green Bay Packers among the interested teams. Cincinnati has also reportedly entered the conversation, leaving the Colts with several potential trade partners ahead of the November 10 deadline.

Perhaps the most important development concerns the asking price. Indianapolis is reportedly seeking compensation comparable to what Carolina received for Christian McCaffrey in 2022, and reports have indicated that the Colts have discussed a package involving a first-round pick and a defensive tackle. While the exact minimum price remains uncertain, I believe it will take a first-round selection, or an exceptional alternative package, to convince Indianapolis to move Taylor.

That is a significant investment for a running back, particularly one who will turn 28 next season and is scheduled to earn approximately $34 million over the final two years of his contract. However, Taylor remains one of the league's best players at his position, and acquiring him would give a contender an immediate offensive centerpiece for the remainder of 2026 and two additional seasons.

With just over a week remaining before the deadline, the timing of these discussions is particularly important. Teams aren't evaluating what their backfields looked like during training camp or even a month ago. Recent performances, injuries, divisional standings and the pressure to win immediately will all influence whether an organization is willing to surrender a premium draft pick.

So, which teams actually make the most sense, and where do I believe Taylor will ultimately end up?

Denver has been widely linked to Taylor over the past several days, and there are certainly reasons to understand the interest. The Broncos are 6-2 following Sunday's crazy 28-24 victory over the Kansas City Chiefs, a result that moved them into first place in the AFC West. With one of the league's stronger defenses and an offense led by Bo Nix, adding an elite running back could make Denver an even more dangerous contender.

However, the emergence of rookie Jonah Coleman has complicated the situation considerably. The former Washington running back produced 104 yards from scrimmage and scored the game-winning touchdown against Kansas City, including an impressive 51-yard reception that helped set up the decisive score. Coleman finished with 11 carries for 41 yards and four receptions for 63 yards, outproducing veteran J.K. Dobbins while demonstrating the explosiveness and versatility Denver had been searching for in its backfield.

Coleman's performance was not an isolated development, either. He had already shown encouraging signs during the previous week's victory over Arizona, and his increasing workload suggests the coaching staff is becoming more comfortable giving him meaningful opportunities. Denver also has Dobbins available as a veteran complement and RJ Harvey, who remains an intriguing receiving weapon despite recently landing on injured reserve with a knee injury.

There is no question that Taylor would represent an immediate upgrade, but the Broncos would effectively be committing premium draft capital and substantial future salary to a position where they already have multiple capable options. Coleman is still a rookie, and one impressive performance should not eliminate interest in a proven star, although it does make the decision considerably more difficult than it appeared a few weeks ago.

Denver's interest appears legitimate, with local reporting suggesting the organization is strongly motivated to pursue Taylor. I simply have a difficult time believing the Broncos will ultimately surrender a first-round pick when their current backfield is beginning to show encouraging signs of improvement.

Seattle is another team that has been heavily connected to Taylor, and the Seahawks' previous trade with Indianapolis could certainly help facilitate discussions. Just last week, Seattle acquired Quenton Nelson for a third- and fifth-round selection, demonstrating its willingness to invest additional resources in improving an offense that has struggled with consistency.

The Seahawks are 4-3 heading into Monday night's matchup against Chicago, and their running game has been a concern following the offseason departure of Kenneth Walker III. However, the situation has changed somewhat in recent weeks, particularly with Emanuel Wilson emerging as a capable contributor. Wilson rushed for 100 yards against Kansas City in Week 7 and has accumulated 403 rushing yards this season, providing Seattle with a dependable option while other members of its backfield have been sidelined.

More importantly, Zach Charbonnet is expected to make his season debut Monday after recovering from a torn ACL, while rookie Jadarian Price has also returned to practice following a chest injury. Seattle selected Price with the 32nd overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, making him an important part of the organization's long-term plans. George Holani provides additional depth, leaving the Seahawks with four running backs who could reasonably factor into the rotation once everyone is healthy.

Taylor would immediately become the most accomplished player in that group, but acquiring him would require Seattle to make another substantial investment at a position where it has already spent a first-round pick this year. If the Colts insist on another first-round selection, the Seahawks would effectively be committing consecutive first-round picks to running backs while also taking on Taylor's expensive contract.

There is an argument for doing so. Seattle is attempting to defend its Super Bowl title, and another elite player could help compensate for an offense that has become too dependent on Sam Darnold. The addition of Nelson also creates an interesting opportunity to reunite Taylor with one of the offensive linemen who helped him become such a productive runner in Indianapolis.

Still, I believe Seattle has enough options to avoid making a desperate move. Charbonnet's return and Price's continued development could provide much of the improvement the Seahawks are searching for without surrendering additional premium draft capital.

Minnesota is where I believe the conversation becomes considerably more interesting.

The Vikings are 6-1 following Sunday's narrow 19-15 loss to the Detroit Lions, remaining near the top of a highly competitive NFC North. They have already demonstrated that they can compete with some of the league's strongest teams, although the running game remains an area where a significant upgrade could make an enormous difference.

Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason have provided Minnesota with a respectable backfield, but neither is an ideal long-term centerpiece. Jones is now 31 years old and approaching the later stages of his career, while Mason has generally been more effective as a complementary power runner rather than someone capable of consistently carrying an offense.

Their performance against Detroit reinforced those concerns. Jones managed just 22 rushing yards on five carries, while Mason added only 20 yards on eight attempts. Minnesota's inability to establish a consistent ground attack placed additional pressure on quarterback Kyler Murray, who was forced to carry much of the offensive responsibility against a strong Detroit defense.

Taylor would immediately change that dynamic.

His ability to handle a substantial workload, generate explosive runs and consistently produce in short-yardage situations would provide Minnesota with a legitimate offensive centerpiece alongside Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. He could also take considerable pressure off Murray, allowing the Vikings to operate a more balanced offense rather than relying so heavily on their quarterback and receiving corps to generate production.

Financially, Minnesota is in a relatively favorable position to absorb Taylor's remaining contract, particularly considering the value of adding a proven veteran to a roster that is already capable of competing for the NFC's top seed. A first-round pick would be expensive, but the Vikings could reasonably argue that their championship window is open right now and that Taylor provides a substantial enough upgrade to justify the investment.

The NFC North is also unlikely to become any easier. Detroit remains one of the conference's strongest teams, while Chicago and Green Bay are both capable of competing for playoff spots. Minnesota cannot afford to assume its current position in the standings will be enough to carry it through the remainder of the season.

Of the teams reportedly interested in Taylor, the Vikings have one of the clearest combinations of immediate need, financial flexibility and championship aspirations. I believe they should be considered among the favorites to acquire him, particularly if the organization is willing to sacrifice future draft capital for a legitimate opportunity to win now.

The New York Giants might be the most fascinating potential destination because their current situation is almost the opposite of what many expected entering the season.

Under first-year head coach John Harbaugh, New York has surprisingly climbed to first place in the NFC East with a 4-2-1 record. The Giants are certainly not a complete football team, and injuries have created significant uncertainty at several important positions, but the division has been considerably weaker than anticipated. With Philadelphia, Dallas and Washington all struggling, New York has a legitimate opportunity to win the NFC East and secure a home playoff game.

That opportunity could be enough to convince Harbaugh and the front office to pursue an aggressive move.

The Giants already have an intriguing young running back in Cam Skattebo, whose physical running style has provided the offense with an important dimension. However, the backfield becomes much less convincing beyond him, particularly following Tyrone Tracy Jr.'s recent hamstring injury that landed him on injured reserve. Devin Singletary and Gregory Desrosiers provide depth, but neither offers anything close to the explosive ability and consistency Taylor would bring.

A combination of Taylor and Skattebo could give New York one of the league's more physical rushing attacks, allowing Harbaugh to establish the offensive identity he has traditionally favored throughout his coaching career. Taylor would handle the primary workload, while Skattebo could continue contributing as a complementary runner capable of punishing defenses and providing fresh legs throughout games.

The quarterback situation makes that possibility even more appealing. With Jaxson Dart sidelined and J.J. McCarthy attempting to establish himself following his arrival from Minnesota, having a dependable running game would take considerable pressure off an offense that has been forced to adjust repeatedly this season. Taylor would provide stability at a time when the Giants desperately need it, particularly with several important divisional games approaching.

New York has also demonstrated interest in acquiring a premier running back before, reportedly pursuing Kenneth Walker III during free agency. Harbaugh has made it clear that he values having a legitimate workhorse in the backfield, and Taylor would provide exactly that.

There are certainly financial and draft-capital concerns. The Giants remain a team with several roster weaknesses, and surrendering a first-round selection could make it more difficult to address those needs in the future. However, with an unexpected division title within reach and a head coach who has consistently emphasized the importance of a physical running game, I believe New York has a stronger incentive to make this move than several of the teams currently receiving more attention.

Green Bay is another intriguing possibility, particularly given the continued struggles of its rushing attack.

Josh Jacobs recently returned to action after missing the beginning of the season, but his performance has not been especially encouraging. In Thursday's 27-19 victory over Carolina, Jacobs managed just 39 rushing yards on 21 carries, averaging fewer than two yards per attempt against a defense that had struggled considerably against the run. Although he scored twice, Green Bay's inability to consistently move the football on the ground remained one of the most concerning aspects of an otherwise important victory.

The Packers are now 5-3 and remain firmly in the NFC playoff race, but their offense has become increasingly dependent on Jordan Love and the passing game. Taylor would give Green Bay a more explosive and dependable option in the backfield, potentially restoring some of the offensive balance that helped make the team so dangerous in previous seasons.

The biggest issue, however, has relatively little to do with Taylor's ability or his potential fit within the offense.

Green Bay does not own its first-round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft, having surrendered that pick to Dallas as part of the Micah Parsons trade. If Indianapolis is genuinely insisting on first-round compensation, the Packers would therefore have to offer their 2028 first-round selection or construct an alternative package involving multiple picks.

I have a difficult time seeing either option as particularly attractive for the Colts.

A 2028 first-round pick would not arrive until an additional year into Indianapolis' rebuilding process, and there is a reasonable possibility that Green Bay will remain a competitive team throughout that period. If the Packers continue performing at their current level, the selection could fall somewhere in the 20s, significantly reducing its appeal compared with a 2027 first-round pick from a team facing more uncertainty.

There is no guarantee where that pick would eventually land, and future first-round selections can occasionally become extremely valuable when an unexpected collapse occurs. However, the combination of the delayed return and Green Bay's relatively stable organizational situation makes this a difficult trade to justify from Indianapolis' perspective.

I wouldn't completely rule the Packers out, particularly if their running game continues struggling over the next week, but I believe the lack of immediate first-round draft capital makes them a less realistic destination than Minnesota or New York.

Cincinnati is perhaps the most underrated team in the entire discussion.

The Bengals are 5-2 following Sunday's wild 43-36 overtime victory over Tennessee, a game in which Joe Burrow threw for 462 yards and five touchdowns. With Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins continuing to provide one of the NFL's most dangerous receiving combinations, Cincinnati has demonstrated that its offense is capable of producing at an exceptionally high level.

However, the running game has not consistently matched that production.

Chase Brown remains a useful offensive contributor, particularly because of his receiving ability, but I don't believe he has demonstrated the consistency necessary to be considered an elite feature back. Against Tennessee, Brown finished with 55 rushing yards on 12 carries, although he added another 46 yards on eight receptions. Those numbers illustrate why he remains a valuable player, but also why he might be better suited to a complementary role alongside a more established runner.

Adding Taylor could potentially elevate Cincinnati's offense into the same conversation as the most dangerous units in football.

Burrow would no longer be required to carry such a substantial share of the offensive burden, while Taylor's presence would make it considerably more difficult for opposing defenses to concentrate primarily on Chase and Higgins. Cincinnati could also continue using Brown as a receiving back and change-of-pace option, giving the Bengals greater versatility without forcing either player into an unfamiliar role.

The AFC North provides another reason to consider making an aggressive move. Pittsburgh, Baltimore and Cleveland have all emphasized physical football and strong rushing attacks at various points in recent seasons, and Cincinnati could benefit from adding a legitimate workhorse capable of helping the Bengals control games rather than relying almost exclusively on Burrow's arm.

Unlike Green Bay, Cincinnati has the draft capital necessary to make a first-round offer, and the organization could reasonably accommodate Taylor's contract over the next two seasons if it views him as an important part of its championship window.

The biggest question is whether the Bengals would actually be willing to commit that level of resources to a running back while already carrying several expensive offensive contracts. Cincinnati has traditionally been somewhat selective about major in-season trades, and it may prefer to address other areas of the roster, particularly a defense that just surrendered 36 points to Tennessee.

Still, I believe the potential offensive impact is substantial enough to make Cincinnati a legitimate contender in these discussions, even if the market has generally treated the Bengals as a long shot.

New England has also been mentioned as a possible destination, although I have a difficult time envisioning the Patriots becoming serious contenders to acquire Taylor.

The Patriots have generally favored a committee approach at running back, rotating different players depending on the situation rather than consistently relying on a single workhorse. That approach has continued with Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson, both of whom provide different strengths and offer enough ability to maintain a functional rushing attack.

Stevenson is coming off a solid performance against Miami, rushing for 82 yards on 19 carries in Sunday's 24-19 victory. Henderson missed the game because of illness, but he remains an important part of the organization's plans and should continue receiving opportunities as he develops.

Taylor would obviously be an upgrade from a pure rushing standpoint, but I don't believe the difference is significant enough to justify surrendering a first-round selection when the Patriots already have two capable backs. New England has invested considerable resources in building around Drake Maye, and those assets would likely be better spent strengthening other areas of the roster rather than replacing a backfield that has generally been serviceable.

The Patriots could theoretically become involved if Taylor's asking price falls dramatically, but with Indianapolis apparently seeking premium compensation, I would be surprised if New England emerges as a particularly aggressive bidder.

There is still a possibility that Taylor remains with the Colts beyond the deadline, although I believe that outcome has become increasingly unlikely.

Indianapolis has already traded Nelson and Buckner, two of its most respected veterans and longtime leaders, suggesting that the organization is willing to make difficult decisions in order to improve its long-term position. Taylor is also approaching the later stages of his prime, and with the Colts potentially several years away from genuine contention, the timeline for his remaining high-level seasons may not align with the organization's rebuilding process.

Taylor has maintained that he is proud to represent Indianapolis and has not requested a trade. He also remains under contract through 2028, meaning the Colts are not facing the same immediate contractual pressure that existed with Nelson and Buckner.

That gives Indianapolis leverage in negotiations, but it also creates an important decision for ownership. If another organization is willing to surrender a first-round selection for a 27-year-old running back who may be entering the final few seasons of his prime, turning down that offer would require a considerable amount of confidence in the Colts' ability to rebuild quickly.

Given the amount of reported interest, I believe Indianapolis should eventually find a team willing to meet its asking price, or at least come close enough to make a trade worthwhile. However, with reports indicating that ownership would still prefer to retain Taylor, the possibility of the Colts deciding to keep him cannot be dismissed entirely.

After examining each team's current situation, I believe Minnesota and New York are the two most logical destinations.

Both organizations have immediate opportunities to compete for division titles, legitimate reasons to upgrade their running games and the draft capital necessary to satisfy Indianapolis' asking price. The Vikings have a more established roster and could benefit enormously from pairing Taylor with Murray and their talented receiving corps, while the Giants have an unexpected opportunity to seize control of the NFC East under Harbaugh.

Denver and Seattle remain serious possibilities, but their recent backfield developments make me somewhat skeptical that either organization will ultimately surrender a first-round pick. Coleman's emergence gives the Broncos reason to be patient, while Seattle has already invested heavily in Price and is preparing to welcome Charbonnet back into the lineup.

Cincinnati is the team I would watch most closely outside of the leading contenders. The Bengals have an exceptional passing offense, a legitimate opportunity to compete in the AFC and a backfield that could benefit considerably from adding an elite runner. If their front office decides to become aggressive, they have the resources and offensive infrastructure to make the trade worthwhile.

Here is how I would distribute the probabilities of Taylor's destination based on the current market, roster situations and reported interest:

These are subjective estimates rather than probabilities generated by a statistical model, and they could change considerably based on injuries, upcoming performances and developments in trade negotiations. The market has generally been more optimistic about Denver and Seattle than I am, while I believe Minnesota, New York and Cincinnati deserve more attention.

Ultimately, the biggest obstacle remains Indianapolis' asking price. Taylor is a tremendous player, but surrendering a first-round selection for a running back approaching 28 is a major commitment, particularly when the acquiring team would also inherit two expensive future seasons.

However, championship windows can close quickly, and several teams currently in contention have legitimate reasons to believe Taylor could make the difference between a good season and a deep playoff run.

If I had to make a prediction today, I would narrow the race to Minnesota and New York, with the Vikings perhaps holding a slight advantage because of their overall roster strength and more established championship aspirations.

The Colts have already demonstrated that few veterans are untouchable. With November 10 approaching and several contenders reportedly involved in discussions, Taylor could become the next major piece of Indianapolis' increasingly dramatic roster overhaul.

#2739. Shannon Sharpe urges the Eagles to cut ‘hothead’ who makes too many mistakes

The Philadelphia Eagles could be in for a long end to the 2026 season after injuries have seriously hindered their hopes of making it to the playoffs.

Nick Sirianni's team lost again at the weekend against NFC East rivals the Washington Commanders. The Eagles are heading into Week Nine at the bottom of their division with a 2-6 record. Any hopes of their season being saved are now extremely slim.

With Jalen Hurts watching the remainder of the year from home following his serious health scare, there is very little for the fans to get excited about. Given the expectations on the Eagles are now so little, Shannon Sharpe is already urging Howie Roseman to cut one of his players ahead of the offseason.

Riq Woolen played down trade rumours just last week after speaking to the media in Philadelphia. Sharpe, however, is urging Philly to just get rid of the cornerback, who they acquired earlier this year after Woolen left the Seattle Seahawks.

"I don't really like to say this: I would cut Tariq Woolen," Sharpe said on Nightcap.

"You watch him. Every game, what happens? Holding calls, gets beat. What am I getting out of him, Ocho? He just wastes a roster spot. You mean to tell me I can't find somebody else that I can move forward with?

"They're not re-signing him after this year. You know that, I know that. I told you in the middle of the season. I said, "He gone. They're not gonna sign him." Too many mistakes. Hothead. Costly penalties like they cost him last year. Remember the playoff game? You remember the playoff game, don't you? Yeah, you remember."

Seahawks fans will know exactly what Sharpe means with this after his taunting penalty almost cost Seattle in their NFC Championship game against the Los Angeles Rams. After being penalised for taunting, Woolen gave up a touchdown on the literal next play.

"And I told you during the season, he makes dumb plays. He doesn't think. All he thinks about is that moment; he doesn't look at the big picture. He doesn't think, "Man, if I get a 15-yard penalty, this might kill our momentum and give them momentum." He doesn't think like that," Sharpe added.

#2737. Falcons Week 8 snap counts from a horrendous loss to the Buccaneers

The snap counts this week aren't going to help you feel any better about the game. Sorry about that.

If you absolutely have to run and you think trickery or your running back's guile alone won't get the job done, bringing on extra offensive linemen is a smart play. The Falcons did roll out Levin on seven snaps and Hinton on a further two to try to bully Tampa Bay's front, and that largely worked. Levin did a nice job, and had the Falcons committed to running more often, having him out there more often likely would've been a smart decision.

The Falcons also could've leaned more heavily on their usage of Nick Muse alongside Charlie Woerner, given that Muse has proven again and again this season to be a useful blocker. The fact that the Falcons ran the ball 23 times with their two backs and only had Muse and Levin on the field for a combined 17 snaps is, in my opinion, a missed opportunity, given that the only way to beat a run defense as good as Tampa Bay's is to block as effectively as possible and give Bijan a lane he has a prayer of working with. Bijan still had a couple of special runs in this one—disappearing into the pile and emerging for a first down, for example—but it's a long season and he needs a bit of breathing room that he wasn't getting Sunday.

That said, the Falcons also threw the ball 24 times (?) in this one and put a third receiver on the field often, so that explains things to some extent. Why they did that on a day where the Bucs threw three passes and the rain made passing treacherous and clearly extremely difficult for Penix is, I think, something I'd like to hear more from Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees about this week.

The Falcons clearly prioritized stopping the run up front, giving London a season-high number of snaps, prioritizing work for Harrison, and getting Woods on the field as time went on given that he's been a fairly consistent presence against the run. Sadly, aside from Cameron Thomas I don't think you can say anyone was truly great against the run on Sunday, with lapses and missed tackles bubbling up almost across the board. The Falcons missed 16 tackles after having one of the better missed tackle rates in football coming into the week.

The rookie linebackers both had their worst day at the office at the same time, which was unfortunate, combining for five missed tackles and a lot of chasing the play. Daniels has been so good—and Perkins so good in coverage—that I'm just chalking this up as an aberration on a very aberrant day. Perkins did get a sack, as well, which was really nice to see.

I think this one comes down to execution and how guys were lining up more than the actual personnel usage, but this Falcons run defense has been exposed in recent weeks. While getting James Pearce Jr. back is going to help the pass rush, it's not likely to give the run D the lift it badly needs, and the Falcons are simply going to have to be much better with what they have. It's fortunate they're getting a little break coming up between the bye and their opponents being kind of crummy at running the ball.

Aside from the missed field goal, this was one of the cleanest days for special teams yet this season. There were no missed tackles, solid enough returns, and good punts. Even the errors—you could argue the Falcons messed up by not fielding a couple of deep punts—were excused by the fact that fielding them in recent weeks had been catastrophic. Let's build on that, fellas.

#2736. Heat defense under scrutiny after Lakers rout

LOS ANGELES – Off to the side, beyond the end of the bench, Heat players Bam Adebayo and Davion Mitchell were standing on the baseline, talking with their hands on their hips.

The sober looks on their faces, however, gave the impression that it was something else. It looked like more of a debrief. As in: how did it get like this?

Just to their right, one seat from the end of the bench, sat Giannis Antetokounmpo, who draped a towel over his shoulders. He was staring blankly ahead, his head resting on his hand.

Once again, an opposing team had bombarded the Miami Heat. This time, it was Luka Dončić and the Los Angeles Lakers on Monday, Nov. 2 in a 138-117 torching. Miami jumped out to a 4-0 lead in the opening minutes. It was the last time the Heat would be ahead.

And as these remade Heat seek to build a contender around Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, it's not the offense or perimeter shooting that has become the problem. It is – surprisingly – the team's defense. All of which raises a question, and a significant one, even this early in the season.

Is this a fatal flaw that will prevent Miami from making the playoffs?

Realistically, it's far too early for such sweeping pronouncements. The lack of cohesion, however, is significant enough to be a serious concern.

"We're not playing hard enough," Antetokounmpo told reporters after the game. "We've got to play hard, have some pride. Individual pride, first of all, and then we've got to keep one another accountable and trust one another defensively. Right now we don't trust one another. We're not giving that extra effort.

"Effort, individual pride and trust. We've got to have those three things."

More: Watch: LeBron James takes a sip of 76ers fan's wine mid-game

The Heat have a collection of stellar individual defenders. Adebayo is an elite stopper, a six-time All-Defensive selection and a player who can guard any position. Antetokounmpo is six years removed from his Defensive Player of the Year award but remains a force in the paint. Mitchell, the starting point guard, has the nickname "Off Night" because convention goes that when he's guarding a prominent offensive player, said player will have an off night. Andrew Wiggins is a defensive-minded wing with plenty of length.

Yet, the sum has not been greater than the parts, and it shows.

"A lot of times I feel like when fatigue sets in, we stop communicating, and that's when mistakes happen," Adebayo said. "That's when bad habits set in. The lack of effort is there. We've got to figure it out."

The Lakers made eight of their first nine shots. They dropped 79 points in the first half. Entering the night, NBA teams had been averaging 113.7 points per game; Los Angeles had already reached 111 by the end of the third quarter.

Dončić flamed the Heat to the tune of 42 points and fellow guard Austin Reaves dropped 27.

And after the Lakers converted on 19-of-43 (44.2%) attempts from beyond the arc, no team in the NBA is allowing more made 3-pointers per game (17.3) than the Heat. Making matters worse, Miami also ranks second-to-last in opposing 3-point percentage at 41%; by comparison, the last-place team, the Suns, are giving up 3s at a 41.1% clip.

It's not just perimeter defense, either. Time after time Monday night, Lakers players blew past Heat defenders on closeouts, as L.A. outscored Miami in the paint by a margin of 60-40.

To a certain extent, this lack of trust does make some sense. The Heat traded four players to land Antetokounmpo and the group is still figuring out how to play together. So, in practical terms, what does this lack of trust actually look like on the floor?

"Like, when a guy beats you off the dribble, sometimes you don't close out all the way to Luka, and that is because you don't feel like somebody has your back," Antetokounmpo said. "So then you give him air space to hit a stepback 3 or pull up for a 3. Same thing with Austin Reaves: you have to close out all the way, knowing that somebody has your back in the paint.

"Sometimes, when you don't feel that trust, you kind of hesitate and you go half way. You don't put yourself out there. That's the trust I'm talking about; you've got to do your job. I got to do my job. When they shot goes up, I've got to box out and get the rebound. They've got to trust that I'm going to get them the possession. That's the kind of trust that I'm talking about."

More: Why are there no NBA games today? League promotes the midterm vote

The Heat still have Erik Spoelstra roaming the sidelines. He's a basketball lifer who is widely considered to be the best active coach in the NBA, a coach who does not shy away from in-season adjustments. After the game, he expressed optimism that his group would figure it out, though he acknowledged it would take time.

Losses like these, in their own way, help by showing Miami what it cannot afford to do. Lessons can come from victories, too. The paradox about trust is that, in a sense, you have to let go of individual insecurities for a greater good. You have to yield. That is, of course, easier said than done.

"If you don't want to play defense as a team, you can't do it by yourself," Mitchell said after the game. "It's not surprising. We've got to have a better sense of urgency. We've got to be intentional about our situation and our game plan, and we've got to stick to it."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Heat defense under scrutiny after Lakers rout

#2735. What's next for Connor Bedard, Blackhawks after massive five-year, $75 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks have locked in their franchise cornerstone for the near future. On Saturday, the Blackhawks announced that star center Connor Bedard has signed a five-year contract worth $75 million.

Bedard's $15 million average annual value makes him the third-highest paid player in the NHL for the 2026-27 season. Only Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million) and the newly-signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson ($18 million) are ahead of him.

"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat, but to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has already displayed elite offensive upside, even if his overall game still has work to do. Last season, Bedard posted a career high 75 points in 69 games. In 219 NHL games, Bedard has totaled 75 goals and 128 assists.

The biggest issues for Bedard are durability concerns -- he's played fewer than 70 games in two of three seasons and will miss the first month of the upcoming season with a shoulder injury -- and subpar defense. The defense is a common problem for young centers and should improve in the coming years, but Bedard has now suffered multiple shoulder injuries in his career.

With Bedard's long-term contract finalized, both he and the Blackhawks will try to take the next step toward greatness. For the player, that means refining his game in order to become the $15 million man most believe him to be. For the team, that means surrounding Bedard with an adequate supporting cast for the first time in his career.

First and foremost, Bedard needs to get healthy and stay healthy. After missing 13 games with a shoulder injury last year, Bedard suffered another injury that required surgery to fix, and he will miss roughly a dozen games out of the gate in 2026-27. Those issues may delay his jump into the NHL's elite tier of players.

Once back at full strength, Bedard will have to show improvement defensively. He oozes offensive ability, but if Bedard is going to be a true No. 1 franchise center, he has to thrive at both ends of the ice. With Bedard on the ice at five-on-five last season, Chicago surrendered 3.60 xGA/60, per Natural Stat Trick. That was the second-worst number on the team with rookie Anton Frondell bringing up the rear.

That doesn't necessarily mean Bedard was the Blackhawks' worst defensive player, but it does mean he often struggled when going up against the opposing team's best players. Stars -- especially those raking in $15 million per season -- are expected to drive play for their team regardless of circumstance. Bedard didn't do that last season.

Bedard also needs to show more growth in the face-off circle. To his credit, Bedard has already done that, going from 38.9% as a rookie to 47.1% last season. Still, Chicago would probably like to see Bedard closer to 50%, especially with him taking key draws in big moments. Maybe that number keeps rising as Bedard gets strong and adds more tricks in the dot.

If Bedard can round out his game without the puck, $15 million per season will be a very fair deal, especially as salaries explode across the league.

We've already seen what can happen when a restricted free agent has all the leverage in contract negotiations. The Ducks were essentially backed into a $90 million contract after the Philadelphia Flyers signed Carlsson to a massive offer sheet.

That risk was there for Bedard too, which is why Davidson deserves some credit for signing him at a more reasonable cap hit. Bedard still has work to do in order to reach that price point, but his ceiling is worth at least $15 million per season.

The Blackhawks can help their young star by putting more NHL-caliber players around him. Chicago tore it down to the studs in hopes of landing Bedard in the 2023 draft, and while that plan worked, it also created a roster full of holes around the No. 1overall pick. Over the last three seasons, Bedard has had little help.

Chicago already improved its defense this offseason when it acquired Bowen Byram from the Buffalo Sabres. Say what you will about the acquisition cost or his $75 contract extension, but Byram inarguably makes Chicago better on the blue line. That unit still needs work, but it's a step in the right direction.

The real issue is finding Bedard a quality running mate at the top of the lineup. Outside of Bedard, only one other player topped 50 points in 2025-26, and it was 31-year-old Tyler Bertuzzi. Chicago still has $14.1 million in cap space with which to add some firepower, but some upgrades will have to come internally.

It's conceivable that the Blackhawks' lineup will include seven players selected inside the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

That's an exciting proposition, and fans have reasons to be optimistic about the future. That said, none of those players have really established themselves as future stars, outside of Bedard. Frondell, Nazar and Rinzel seem like the best bets to get there soon, but that's based more on projection than anything tangible.

The first month of the season should be an excellent barometer for the Blackhawks as they assess those players. Bedard will be out of the lineup, and it'll be interesting to see who sinks and who swims until he returns. Once Chicago establishes exactly what it has in its young nucleus, Davidson can then go out and aggressively address needs via trades and free agency.

#2734. Beware of the Lion – TSV 1860 Munich can still mix with the Bundesliga's best

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews) On our excursion to München last weekend, naturally topping the list of priorities was the Bundesliga's famed Der Klassiker as FC Bayern Munich hosted Borussia Dortmund on Saturday, 31 October. One could be forgiven for having tunnel vision.

To that, I would say do that at your own peril. The Friday prior to the bright lights of the Allianz Arena also served up a footballing delight in the vibrant southeastern suburb of Giesing. The might of TSV 1860 Munich taking on Regionalliga Bavaria rivals TSV Buchbach.

Four tier of German football you say? Fear not. A whopping 15,000 fans – of which maybe 1000 are Buchbach supporters – filter into the Grünwalder Stadion. The noise is already reaching fever pitch as we wind our way up the concrete steps of the South Stand.

Shortly after, the whistle blows to get the ball rolling. The football is nothing short of brilliant either. That blend of gritty 50-50 duels with no shirking out, coupled with some technical excellence. Namely, Buchbach's No.10 Tobias Heiland who neatly curled in the opening goal.

𝘋𝘪𝘦 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦𝘯 (The Lions) hit back in a flash. Ex-FC Augsburg star Florian Niederlechner and Felix Weber find the net. Still, Buchbach find a response. Heiland again with a sweet half-volley on the edge of the box before Samed Bahar's drive finds the bottom corner.

In need of a refreshment after a half that ended 3-2 to the guests, we make our way to the kiosk. As if the night couldn't get any more interesting, my colleague Manuel Veth of The Gegenpressing Podcast and I happen to bump into the referee's father there.

Overhearing some 1860 fans mulling over his son's first-half calls, he smiles but you sense a hint of paternal worry. The arbiter in question is 26-year-old Johannes Wagner – it was his first time officiating at this level. Might I add, he went on to do an exemplary job of it too.

Into the catacombs we go for an interval meeting with 1860 president Gernot Mang. There's no fancy murals or glitzy design to the interior. You must duck under the stand's support beams to avoid hitting your head. But that's football. Real football. I find it charming.

Mang is a charismatic, calmly spoken but passionate man who confesses his and the club's aim of returning to the Bundesliga – something they've missed since 2004. This isn't some crazed pipe dream. It's a mission. It may take time, but Giesing wasn't built in a day.

Back to our press box for the second helping of what seemed destined to be inevitable chaos. That's exactly what happens. Both sides had chances but Arian Calderon heads in from six yards for the hosts. We're tired at 3-3 with 8 minutes to play plus injury time.

With the clock hitting 90+4 minutes, space was afforded to Lance Fiedler. Buchbach stood off enabling the left-back to hammer a shot inside the left upright. Cue pandemonium in the terraces. You can't help but get caught up in it. Even the steward beside us delights.

Chants of "𝘌𝘪𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘭 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦, 𝘐𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦" (Once a Lion, forever a Lion) fill the cool Munich air. The three points sees them rise to second in the table. After the emotional rollercoaster, the party continues in Bamboleo – a 𝘒𝘯𝘦𝘪𝘱𝘦 – your unpretentious, cozy local matchday bar.

Sure, the allure of FC Bayern and BVB may have dominated the weekend. But in a way, the 1860 atmosphere is unfiltered and unmatched. One could argue it even surpasses their arch rivals in red and merits a hasty return to Germany's topflight.

Things may not be entirely harmonious behind the scenes after majority shareholder Hasan Ismaik's exit. However, the football drops jaws and the fans remain unwavering. A lion is the king of the jungle. It's fearless, resilient and untamable – TSV 1860 Munich embodies it all.

#2733. Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck requests trade: Where three-time Vezina Trophy winner could land

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After months of speculation about his future in Winnipeg, Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has confirmed his trade request publicly.

Hellebuyck's name has come up in trade rumors since the 2025-26 season ended, and the rumor mill will only pick back up now that he's gone public with his request. NHL training camps will open soon, and Hellebuyck wanted to provide more clarity on the situation.

"Winnipeg has been home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there.

"I have never forgotten June 23, 2012. That's the day Winnipeg took a chance on a goalie playing in Odessa, Texas. I gave everything I had from that moment to prove the Jets made the right decision.

"Several months ago, I privately requested a trade. I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options.

"With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request. My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family.

"I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career and hope a resolution can be reached soon."

In what would become one of the biggest steals in NHL Draft history, the Jets used the No. 130 overall pick to select Hellebucyk in 2012. Just seven years later, Hellebuyck established himself as one of the best goalies in the lea, and he's maintained that level of play for nearly a decade.

A three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck has a legitimate claim as the best goaltender in the world. Over the last three seasons, Hellebucyk has totaled 73.4 goals saved above average, per Natural Stat Trick. That's 20 more than the next closest goaltender -- Andrei Vasilevskiy -- and includes a rather underwhelming 2025-26 campaign.

There have been plenty of years in which Hellebuyck carried mediocre Jets teams, but 2025-26 was not one of them. He actually allowed 0.35 goals above average with a pedestrian 0.895 save percentage. Normally, it would be fair to worry about a 33-year-old goalie with those numbers, but not in Hellebucyk's case.

Hellebuyck backstopped Team USA to its first men's ice hockey gold medal in 46 years at the 2026 Olympics while allowing a total of six goals and boasting a .956 save percentage. He was exceptional in the final against Canada, where he turned away 41 of the 42 shots he faced and made one of the most iconic saves in hockey history.

THAT WAS ONE HELLE-BUYCK OF A STOP. 😳 pic.twitter.com/N3wCimdBGw

The biggest obstacle in a trade might be Hellebucyk's contract. He has five years remaining on his current deal at $8.5 million per season -- and while that may be a lot of term for a goalie his age -- Hellebucyk is worth a lot more than that at his best. The real issue is that he owns a full no-movement clause, which means Hellebuyck controls his fate, and the trade request going public certainly won't improve the team's leverage.

So, where does Hellebucyk land? Without knowing his preferred destinations, it's probably safe to assume that he wants the opportunity to win a Stanley Cup, and the team that acquires him will need the requisite cap space and resources to do so.

With those parameters in mind, here are five teams that could make sense as Hellebuyck trade suitors.

The Sabres were one of two teams frequently connected to Hellebuyck earlier in the offseason, and that makes sense. Buffalo is an ascending team with room to upgrade in the crease. Not to denigrate Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, who were a formidable tandem in 2025-26, but I'm not sure Buffalo can bet on similar performances this upcoming season. Adding Hellebuyck would eliminate that question mark immediately and make the Sabres a favorite to win the Atlantic Division.

In fact, one of Luukkonen or Lyon could go back to Winnipeg to help provide stability in the post-Hellebuyck era. The Sabres also own all their first-round picks for the foreseeable future, and it would probably take at least two of those to pry Hellebuyck from the Jets. Just a year ago, it would be hard to believe that Hellebuyck would waive his no-movement clause to go to Buffalo, but it seems very plausible now.

When the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Florida Panthers in July, I assumed it would only be a matter of time until Hellebuyck was in Newark. To this point, nothing has come to fruition, but New Jersey absolutely needs an NHL-caliber starter. Jake Allen, David Rittich and Nico Daws are on the roster right now, and that won't get the job done.

The Devils were undone by poor goaltending -- and subpar defense -- too much last year. Markstrom allowed 13.7 goals above average, per Natural Stat Trick, and even a diminished version of Hellebuyck would provide a significant upgrade over those numbers. New Jersey has the draft capital to get something done, but it also needs to clear cap space, possibly with a Dougie Hamilton salary dump.

They just won the Stanley Cup with Brandon Bussi in net, so the Hurricanes have proven they don't need elite goaltending to go all the way. Regardless, running it back with Bussi wouldn't be a very safe bet, and adding Hellebuyck would only reinforce Carolina's biggest strength. As we saw in the playoffs, the Hurricanes are already one of the best defensive teams in the league. Put Hellebuyck behind that lineup, and scoring on Carolina becomes a Herculean task.

Thanks to savvy cap management by GM Eric Tulsky, Carolina has the room to add Hellebuyck without jettisoning a current player. Oh, and Carolina has three first-round picks over the next two years. If Tulsky wants to pursue Hellebuyck, he has the resources to do it.

This is more of a longshot, but it would be fun to see the Sharks take a swing if this, assuming Hellebuyck would sign off on a trade to San Jose. Despite the fact that they overpaid for it, the Sharks blue line is better, and there is a wealth of young talent at forward. Another factor here is the current state of the Pacific Division, which is abhorrent. The third playoff spot is up for grabs, and the Sharks could secure it with Hellebuyck in goal.

Superstar Macklin Celebrini is on the final year of his entry-level deal before his $18.8 million salary kicks in next year, so San Jose needs to push the chips in here and figure out the finances next summer. Would the team be willing to trade blue-chip goaltending prospect Yaroslav Askarov to the Jets? San Jose may also need to sweeten a trade package -- or involve a third team -- in order to get Winnipeg to take on Logan Couture's contract.

Yes, Vegas is currently $8.6 million over the salary cap, so there would need to be some impressive maneuvering in order to acquire Hellebuyck. But the Golden Knights have already proven to be cutthroat if a player they covet hits the trade market. Besides, goaltending was optional in Sin City last season. Four goalies combined to allow 23.2 goals above average. Only five teams had a worse save percentage than the Golden Knights.

So, how could the Golden Knights pull off a Hellebuyck blockbuster? Trading an injured Alex Pietrangelo and his contract would help, but that may be costly. Veteran defenseman Brayden McNabb only has a modified no-trade clause, and the same is true for forwards Tomas Hertl, William Karlsson and Ivan Barbashev. Like I said, this would be tough, but the Golden Knights are one team willing to drop the entire egg carton on the floor to make a few omelettes.

#2732. The Chicago Bears are a legitimate Super Bowl contender

The Bears picked up a crucial victory on Monday night, defeating the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks on the road, which is notorious for being one of the toughest places to play in the NFL. They were decisively the better team throughout the evening, picking up a statement 34-17 win in primetime to improve to 6-2 for the season.

It was the first game in which All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons suited up for the Bears, and he certainly made his presence felt. But not only did Chicago's major trade deadline acquisition pay off dividends on Monday, but its offense was also stellar against one of the NFL's best defenses.

Now sitting at 6-2 and firmly in the race for first place in the NFC North, it's reasonable to think that this Bears roster really has a limitless ceiling. Here are some of my other takeaways from their win over Seattle on Monday.

Heading into Monday, no quarterback in the NFL had thrown for over 200 passing yards in a single game against the Seahawks in 2026. Caleb Williams got it done by the third quarter. He was decisive, poised, and accurate against one of the best defenses in the league, throwing for 247 yards, a touchdown, and a 101.0 passer rating. His initial 78.0 grade from the game is enough to keep him ranked No. 6 in the NFL with an 84.0 PFN QB Impact grade so far this season.

The Bears felt the pressure from a very talented Seahawks defense, and that loaded Seattle defensive interior made its presence felt on passing downs and in the ground game; D'Andre Swift averaged just 2.6 yards per carry on Monday. Still, Williams maintained his composure, showing off his trademark elusiveness and sack avoidance to extend the play often and create opportunities for Chicago's offense down the field. This wasn't Williams' best statistical performance of the season, but especially given the context of the situation, it was one of his most impressive.

There was no doubting that Jeffery Simmons was going to be a massive addition to the Bears' defense when they traded for him on Thursday. The only question was whether he would be worth the massive trade package they gave to the Titans in order to acquire him, which included two first-round draft picks. Simmons showed that he was worth every ounce of that deal on Monday night.

He ended the game with six total tackles, two tackles for loss, one pass deflection, one sack, and multiple quarterback pressures. When Simmons got one-on-one opportunities, he rarely lost them, and even when he got double-teamed – which was often – he was still able to make his presence felt. Not only that, but his being double-teamed opened up opportunities for the likes of Austin Booker, Devin Bush, James Lynch, and Montez Sweat, the latter of whom having arguably his best game of 2026. Simmons made everybody around him better, which is exactly what the Bears were hoping for.

Are the Bears a perfect team? Not necessarily. Their cornerback room still remains a major concern, as both Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson had shaky performances. Malik Muhammad will eventually return from injury, but an ideal world would see Johnson sent to the bench if Chicago can get another cornerback before the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

Still, I firmly believe that this Bears team could beat any team in the NFL.

They already had one of the best offenses in the league. They already had one of the best head coaches, as well as one of the best quarterbacks in the league. Those two things feel incredibly weird to say as a Bears fan. But now, they have a genuine force multiplier along their defensive line, which was previously their biggest weakness. Dennis Allen can expect pressure from a four-man rush for once, and he's proven to be one of the better defensive coordinators in the game this season.

After the Bears marched into Seattle, defeated the Super Bowl champions, and picked up their third win in a row, I find myself thinking: why not us?
