#2731. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2730. Warriors' Charles Bassey plays big role in win over Phoenix

SAN FRANCISCO – The Golden State Warriors' biggest concern has been the center position. Charles Bassey showed on Monday, Nov. 2 that he could be a solution for the Warriors with his 'next man up' mentality.

After losing Kristaps Porzingis, the Warriors have had to pivot with different lineups. Amid their five-game winning streak, they've thrown a few small ball lineups out with Draymond Green as the center.

But when Green was ejected from the Warriors' 116-113 win against the Phoenix Suns on Monday, Bassey stepped up and impacted the game with his high-energy and efficiency around the rim, just days after his 26th birthday.

Bassey finished the game with a career-high 19 points and shot 7-of-10 on field goals. He had 8 rebounds and finished with a plus-minus of +10.

"Next man mentality, to be honest. We knew we could get a win," Bassey said. "We started to the game slow.  We got to get better at doing that, you know, last couple games we started slow. We just gotta get rid of doing that. There was a mentality, we felt we could win. Like I said, next man, up, just go in and do your job. That's why I think every player on this team has confidence doing that and as long as you're on this team, you know, like I said, coach Steve (Kerr) gives you all that confidence."

The Warriors got off to a 31-19 deficit after the first quarter. Golden State came out shooting 33% on field goals and went 2-of-15 on 3-point attempts in the first quarter. However, Bassey's hustle stood out to everyone, especially his teammates.

"Bass like... I'm sure he didn't think he was going to play 23 minutes and he was ready for it," Warriors guard Stephen Curry, who scored a game-high 34 points, said about Bassey. "So those are the patterns of what a good team does when night after night, no matter what the combination is you're finding production up and down the bench, and you love it."

"Everybody feeds off the energy when a guy comes in like that with what Bass did tonight, changed the game," Curry added. "Everybody notices. It lifts everybody's spirits and keeps momentum on our side, so it was great."

More: Spike Lee hopes Knicks skip Trump White House visit despite Dolan's wishes

Brandin Podziemski scored 20 points in the win and had high praise for Bassey.

"I thought Charles was great," Podziemski said. "Super efficient, gave us a lob threat, gave us a defensive presence when Dray was out."

Warriors head coach Steve Kerr raved about Bassey after the Warriors' win. One of the things that stood out was the chemistry between Bassey and rookie forward Yaxel Lendeborg.

"Bass was great. What a big night for him," Kerr said. "The rebounding, the scoring. He and Yaxel have a really good connection. The pick and roll game. He gives him a lob threat and Yaxel sees the floor so well and he's so big that he finds him when he's behind the defense."

Bassey feeds off of playmakers like that. His efficiency around the rim makes teammates trust that he'll complete the play. Lendeborg finished the game with 16 points and five assists, four of them went to Bassey for a layup or dunk.

"Since training camp, I'm telling you, man, every time," Bassey said on his continuity with Lendeborg. "We talk about our game, every time. After we played on Sunday, he tells me, you are wide open. When he sees the pass he makes the right play. I love playing with him and I think the coaches, they figured that out too. I mean, everybody knew that."

They have a connection they've established as they've learned each other's game. When Bassey gives Lendeborg a look, he knows whether to set a ghost screen or clear the lane so he can get downhill.

Bassey can be reliable energy guy for the Warriors. A workhorse who provides an offensive spark through his efficiency and an anchor on defense. If comparing to Warriors teams of old, think Festus Ezeli, Kevon Looney, Andrew Bogut or Zaza Pachulia. He's going to scrap, claw and fight for possessions.

Bassey plays physical and the Suns didn't appreciate it. Further pushing and shoving ensued with Bassey after Green's ejection. Suns guard Jalen Green drove to the basket and got tied up with Bassey before Suns players came to Green's aide, including forward Miles Bridges, who was assessed a technical.

"Being physical doesn't mean you have to scuffle with guys, that doesn't mean you're tough" Bassey told USA TODAY Sports.

"Being physical is playing hard every possession, going out there, fighting for rebounds, and doing what I'm doing," he added. "Just being physical, you know, challenging every shot, and going out there you know, two or three guys trying to box me out, me on the offensive end. And that's being physical, still getting the rebound.  But I mean, what they're doing is so fake… That's a fake toughness."

Bassey, Nigerian-born, is no newcomer in the league. He was drafted with the 53rd overall pick of the 2021 NBA Draft by the Philadelphia 76ers out of Western Kentucky. He then bounced around the league, spending time in the G-League, including the Santa Cruz Warriors.

Bassey signed a one-year contract with the Warriors in July. He's looking to make the most of it.

#2728. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2724. NBA scouts missed Yaxel Lendeborg’s greatness with an easy mistake

The high school class of 2020 produced one of the most hyped collections of top-ranked prospects in recent memory. Jalen Green, Terrence Clarke, and Josh Christopher were household names from early in their teenage years for mixtape compilations that drew comparisons to Kobe Bryant and other star scorers. Jalen Suggs was a two-sport stud who bypassed an Ohio State football scholarship because he was better at basketball. Scottie Barnes and Evan Mobley were portable, long-limbed defensive prodigies, and Cade Cunningham shot up to the top of the class after a stirring EYBL run that had him looking like American Luka Doncic.

Yaxel Lendeborg was also in the class of 2020, but while his peers were gracing the cover of SLAM and winning international gold medals, he had yet to play organized basketball. Lendeborg's grades weren't good enough to get on the court back in his hometown of Pennsauken, New Jersey, and he was more interested in playing video games than applying himself to anything that would better his future. It's possible his enormous talent would have slipped through the cracks entirely if not for a junior college on the other side of the country taking a chance on him with its last scholarship in a Covid-shortened season following an impressive weekend at an exposure camp for Dominican players.

Nearly six years later, Lendeborg already looks like something close to an NBA star as a 24-year-old rookie with the Golden State Warriors. His winding journey from Arizona Western College to UAB to Michigan to now playing alongside Stephen Curry has no real analog, but it still offers some valuable insight into how prospect evaluation is changing in a rapidly evolving landscape for young players. Lendeborg is an exception to just about every rule in the sport, but his ascent is no accident, and it could inform similar success stories in the coming years for teams looking hard enough.

What Lendeborg is doing to open this season is nothing short of amazing. He's averaging 22.3 points, 7.3 rebounds, and 3.7 assists on pristine 64.5% true shooting through his first seven games. His 37-point explosion against the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday showed the full extent of his skill set. When he was guarded by the skinnier Derrick Jones Jr., Lendeborg wielded body blows in the paint for easy scoring chances. When Brook Lopez tried to corral him in drop coverage off a pick-and-roll, Lendeborg calmly drained a pull-up three-pointer. He showed impressive body control when attacking downhill, and relentless aggression in punishing a small guard in Darius Garland on switches. With a like-sized defender in Kobe Sanders on him, he ripped mid-range shots like a seasoned pro.

No rookie should be capable of this type of immediate excellence. Then again, Lendeborg is anything but a typical rookie.

The Warriors drafted Lendeborg at No. 11 overall this year, but even they weren't fully convinced he was the player they needed. Golden State reportedly coveted Brayden Burries, who went one pick ahead of them to the Milwaukee Bucks, and they were prepared to select him over Lendeborg. Yaxel's own college coach passed on him for one of his Michigan teammates when the Dallas Mavericks chose Morez Johnson at No. 9 overall days after hiring Dusty May.

It was easy to see the track record of older first round draft picks and immediately write off Lendeborg as a low-ceiling prospect. I never bought that argument. When I ranked Yaxel at No. 5 overall on my final draft board, I wrote "I typically balk at the idea that older prospects are more 'NBA ready' than younger ones who reach the league sooner, but it feels true in Yaxel's case." In reality, he was never that difficult of an evaluation if you could get past his age.

What sold me on Lendeborg was that he was improving in the exact ways you want someone his age to improve, albeit at a lower level than the NBA. When he entered UAB from junior college, he was mostly a rebounding big who provided value by generating extra possessions and protecting the paint. In his second season at UAB, he started to show off his playmaking chops, showing that he could run offense with the ball in his hands by using his own scoring gravity to set up his teammates. He also doubled his three-point makes from the previous season. As his offense was starting to develop, Lendeborg was named AAC Defensive Player of the Year while mostly playing center.

Lendeborg was good enough to get drafted in the first round in 2025 out of UAB. After testing the process at the combine, though, he decided to take a massive NIL bag from Michigan as the top-rated player in the transfer portal. As I was covering the Wolverines during March Madness, I asked Yaxel what he heard from NBA scouts that convinced him to go back to college. His answer showed the self-awareness required to go from good to great on your own timeline.

"(The NBA) wanted to see a lot more three-pointers and a lot more versatility in my defense," Lendeborg told SB Nation. "I tried to be more of three, because in the NBA, I'm not gonna be the superstar. I'm gonna be playing next to somebody like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and he doesn't need me to score for him. He needs me to get stops. I just tried to figure out my role and do whatever I can do to get there."

Michigan's unique team-building strategy forced Lendeborg into the exact role NBA evaluators wanted to see him in. May started three nominal college centers next to each other who were each good enough to have a team built around them on their own. Lendeborg's malleability was the biggest reason it all worked. Forced out to the perimeter full-time for the first time in his brief career, Yaxel showed he could shoot threes with volume, defend away from the paint, and grease the offense with connective passing all without losing his physicality at both ends.

Lendeborg proved he was willing to sacrifice for team success, and he never needed to put up the biggest numbers to answer the NBA's questions. Here was a player with the size to play NBA center after measuring at 6'8.5 without shoes, 235 pounds with a 7'4 wingspan who already showed he could play alongside other bigs while contributing to winning at a high level. He could do the role player stuff of rebounding, setting screens, spacing the floor, and moving the ball as a passer, and he still had an extra gear as an isolation scorer who could leverage his size into more efficient chances. All the while, he kept getting more confident and more accurate as an outside shooter.

The scary thing about Lendeborg is his most impressive flashes haven't translated to sustainable success … yet. Through seven games, he's only making 25% of his pull-up threes on 3.4 attempts per game. If those start falling even at a clip in the low 30s, there's no real cap on his ceiling.

So many young forwards get drafted high in the NBA just because they have the frame, athleticism, and pedigree the league looks for. In the best case scenarios, these players will develop as passers and shooters without losing their physicality in their age-21, age-22, and age-23 seasons. This is exactly what Lendeborg did first at UAB and then at Michigan, and his development curve is made even more impressive by his late start in the sport.

His progression as a player is even more satisfying when juxtaposed against another former Warriors lottery pick who graduated high school in 2020: Jonathan Kuminga. Kuminga was never asked to play a winning role with physicality early in his career when evaluators saw a potential star scorer. He never developed the ball skills or shooting that Lendeborg is showing now. Yaxel's progression shouldn't have been discounted just because it happened in college, not the NBA. In every other way, he was giving scouts everything they wanted.

The two best players in college basketball last year were Yaxel and Cameron Boozer, and no one else was close to him. This is what made Boozer the obvious No. 1 overall pick in my eyes: he was the only player in the country close to Lendeborg's level, and he did it while being five years younger than him. While there's plenty of season left to go, it's no surprise that Lendeborg and Boozer have been the two best rookies to start this season.

Lendeborg checked every box for a role player, and in the NBA, the best role players are truly more valuable than many who get blessed as stars. Yaxel is a premium example of that. The NIL is going to keep good players in school longer before, and don't be surprised if some of the top prospects in the next draft are also multi-year college veterans, if not 24-year-old rookies. It's easy to say progress isn't linear when watching young basketball players, but it's harder to act like it when the chips are on the table. Lendeborg was always running his own race. Right now, he's showing he can still finish first even with a late start.

#2723. Urban Meyer on Ohio State: “It’s Time To Panic”

Former Ohio State coach Urban Meyer told fans it is time to panic. This is not a small criticism after the 30-18 loss to USC. He said the situation is dire for the Buckeyes heading into their next game. Meyer made these comments on Monday while speaking on the Triple Option podcast. His words hit hard because he knows exactly what it takes to win in Columbus.

The loss to USC on Saturday night was a shock to the system. Ohio State had 10 more first downs and over 100 more total yards than the Trojans. Yet they still lost by 12 points. The problem was not the quarterback or the lack of talent. It was discipline. The team committed 11 penalties that cost them the game. Meyer pointed this out directly. "I'll tell you if I'm the head coach and I'm on that staff, I'm so pissed off at the rest of the team," Meyer said, according to Yahoo Sports. He noted that the penalties had nothing to do with the backup quarterback playing his first game.

Meyer did not stop at the USC loss. He turned his eyes to the upcoming matchup against Oregon. The Ducks are a dangerous team with a roster capable of beating Ohio State. Meyer believes the Buckeyes are in deep trouble. "It's 2026, man. It's time to panic. Every day is a panic," he said, according to Yahoo Sports. He added that anyone who thinks Oregon cannot win in Columbus is "out of your mind." This is a stark warning for a program that started the year with championship hopes. The team now sits at 6-2 overall with little room for error.

Ohio State must win its final four games to stay in the playoff hunt. Three of those games are at home. If they win out, they could still make it to Indianapolis for the Big Ten Championship. But the path is narrow. The next test is Oregon on Saturday. Dan Lanning's team has its own issues, including a quarterback change, but they still have the talent to win. Meyer even spoke with Lanning earlier that morning about the logistics of the trip. The former coach knows the stakes are higher than ever.

The margin for error for Ohio State is now zero. They control their own destiny, but only if they play their best version of themselves. Meyer stressed that the message in the locker room must change. The team cannot drop balls or miss tackles if they want to survive. The USC game showed that even with a backup quarterback, the team can move the ball. The problem was self-inflicted wounds. USC coach Lincoln Riley earned the Paul "Bear" Bryant National Coach of the Week award for this win, per reports. That award highlights how well the Trojans played against the second-ranked team.

2011 marks the last time Ohio State suffered two defeats so early in the season. The season started with high expectations and a narrow win over Texas. Five wins in a row made it look like the team was back on track. Then the loss to Indiana happened, and star quarterback Julian Sayin went down with a season-ending injury.

#2722. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2721. Miami Dolphins’ Most Valuable Player | Week Eight | Pressure

The Miami Dolphins took a ten-point lead into halftime against their division rivals, the New England Patriots, on Sunday at Hard Rock Stadium. Unfortunately, they couldn't keep the momentum rolling in the second half — ultimately losing the contest to last year's Super Bowl runner-ups by a score of 24-19.

A big reason why Miami was able to get an early lead against Drake Maye and company was the play of the Dolphins' defense. Through the first two quarters of Sunday's clash, Miami gave up just three points while consistently causing New England's quarterback discomfort in the pocket. One of the main contributors to Miami's pass rush was EDGE player Chop Robinson.

Robinson becomes the first Dolphins player to win my weekly MVP award twice this season.

Robinson had eight pressures and two quarterback sacks on the day. His 47.1% pressure rate against New England, according to Hussam Patel of the 5 Reasons Sports Network, was the second-highest pressure rate of any NFL defender in a single game this season. Miami's young pass rusher now leads the National Football League in pressure rate with a 26.6% mark for the entire year.

Robinson is playing on the third year of his rookie contract, giving the Dolphins club control through next season, at least. From there, Miami's new general manager, Jon-Eric Sullivan, will have the ability to give Robinson the fifth-year option since Chop is a former first round pick of the club. If Robinson continues to maintain this level of production throughout the remainder of the season, don't be surprised of Sullivan looks to get a deal done a year early instead of waiting on the price to rise.

#2719. Luka Dončić's offense is carrying Lakers. Is LA too dependent on its 'showman'?

LOS ANGELES — Luka Dončić earned a standing ovation from the Los Angeles Lakers fans before going on to beat the Miami Heat 138-117 at Crypto.com Arena on Monday, Nov. 2.

Dončić has beocme the early favorite for regular season MVP as the NBA's leader in scoring average (38.3) and 3-pointers made per game (5.9).

The Slovenian point guard is known for his offensive prowess and his ability to score. It's also what makes the Lakers a threat in the Western Conference.

He finished with 42 points, 13 assists and seven rebounds against the Heat on Nov. 2.

More: Heat defense under scrutiny after Lakers rout

Lakers coch JJ Redick praised Dončić's offensive dominance on several occasions in recent weeks, referring to him as a "showman" and a "supernova" while also comparing his rhythm on the court to a theatrical stage.

"He's just making tough shots; averaging 38 points is not easy in this league," Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo said. "He's making tough shots and you just tip your hat off to him."

The two-time scoring champion is averaging 29.3 points per game for his career, which places him third all-time behind Michael Jordan and Wilt Chamberlain. Both players averaged 30.1 ppg for their respective careers.

Dončić has propelled the Lakers to a fast start this season, and his play on Monday was no different. He scored 16 points as Los Angeles led Miami 37-30 in the first quarter.

Dončić is averaging 15 points in the opening quarter, and has scored at least 13 in all but one game this season.

When the six-time All-NBA player is hot, so are the Lakers.

The Lakers have outscored opponents by 113 points when Dončić is on the court during the seven games he's played this season, according to StatMuse.

When Dončić isn't on the floor, things can get tricky for Redick.

Los Angeles' bench nearly blew a 16-point lead with 1:43 left in the fourth quarter on Sunday against the Toronto Raptors.

The Raptors cut the Lakers' lead to make it a five-point game. Toronto scored 11 points in 40 seconds and forced Redick to put Dončić and Austin Reaves back into the game and help secure the victory.

On Monday, Dončić and the Lakers produced 111 points, the team's highest-scoring point total through three quarters this season. This time, the Lakers left very little room for mistakes and refused to give up the lead in the final frame.

Dončić's ability to score isn't the only benefit of having him on the court.

Even if Dončić had a low-scoring night, he will always remain a threat that will keep defenses focused on him. It does free up his teammates for opportunities, who can also benefit from his playmaking and his ability to draw a double team.

That was the case Monday, as the Heat applied double-team looks on Dončić.

"I think at the beginning of the season we didn't execute well with the double team, but today I think we improved a lot," Dončić said. "Everybody was in the right spots, so it's not just me.

"It's everybody, just to be in the right spot and being aggressive and shooting with confidence."

Lakers forward Ziaire Williams has been able to benefit from some of the open looks that come with sharing the floor with Dončić.

"Very easy looks," Williams said. "Way easier than they've been in the past. They're sending two (players) to Luka and two at (Reaves) every time."

Reaves has proven he can be a high-efficiency volume scorer, but he is less likely to thrive without Dončić on the court.

If Dončić were unavailable, opposing game plans would focus on Reaves and he would be challenged by teams' toughest defenders.

Beyond Reaves (23.1 ppg), the Lakers would have to rely on center Walker Kessler (14.3) as a third-scoring option.

Williams (11.3) and Collin Sexton (10.3) could also be options, but neither would be able to guarantee similar production to Dončić on a nightly basis.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Luka Dončić's offense is carrying Lakers. Is LA too dependent on its 'showman'?

#2716. NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 9

The much-anticipated Ravens/Bills Week 8 matchup failed to live up to expectations. Ravens' quarterback Lamar Jackson returned from injury and broke his thumb one play into the game. Buffalo took care of business, and Josh Allen finished 21 of 34 for 289 yards with a pair of passing touchdowns and one rushing touchdown. Buffalo remains at the top of the league with a difficult road matchup against Minnesota on deck.

Chicago went into Seattle and beat up the Seahawks, 34-17. The presence of Jeffery Simmons was felt early and often in this game, as Sam Darnold and the Seahawks struggled offensively. Caleb Williams and the Bears controlled the game, and D'Andre Swift rushed for three touchdowns. Ben Johnson and the Bears are a scary team in the NFC.

Jacksonville beat up an Indianapolis Colts team in fire-sale mode — a 42-7 home win where Jacksonville completely dictated the game.

Minnesota's lack of offense finally caught up to them in Detroit against the Lions, who defeated Kevin O'Connell's crew, 19-15. Kyler Murray threw for 210 yards and two passing touchdowns, but Minnesota couldn't put away Detroit at the end of the game, suffering their first loss of the season..

Denver defeated the Chiefs, 28-24. Bo Nix and the offense took another small step forward, helped by rookie running back Jonah Coleman's 100+ total-yard game. Denver won on a goal-line stand, holding the Chiefs back from securing a victory.

The Chiefs lost 28-24 to the Denver Broncos. Kenneth Walker III was bottled up after exploding in Week 1 against Denver. Patrick Mahomes tried to make magic happen, finishing 30 of 41 for 321 yards wtih three touchdowns, but the Chiefs were stopped on the goal line at the end of the game. Kansas City's lack of weapons on offense is still a major concern; backup running back Emmit Johnson was the leading receiver with five catches for 128 yards and a touchdown

Detroit defeated the — then — undefeated Vikings, 19-15. The Lions got creative in the second half to spark offense against a difficult Brian Flores defense. The Lions totaled 384 yards, including 153 yards on the ground for Jahmyr Gibbs.

The Bengals escaped the Tennessee Titans in overtime with a 42-36 victory. Tennessee pushed Cincinnati, forcing three Joe Burrow interceptions, but the star quarterback went NUCLEAR! Burrow went 38 of 48 for 462 yards with five touchdowns, including several high-level throws. The Bengals escaped with the win, but it was quite hard-fought against a one-win team. Also, Dexter Lawrence had a few difference-making plays, including a late sack of Cam Ward and a fumble recovery.

The Miami Dolphins pushed New England, but the Patriots escaped with a 24-19 win in Miami. Drake Maye threw for 199 yards, and New England rushed for 131 yards (3.6 YPR). Still, it was enough for the Patriots to secure their fifth win of the season.

Seattle could not stop the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. Sam Darnold threw for 188 yards with two touchdowns and an interception, but Chicago controlled the game with their offense. A questionable offensive pass interference call against Jaxon Smith-Njigba helped to suffocate Seattle, which settled for a field goal rather than having a first-and-goal at the 2-yard line in a competitive game. Still, the defending Super Bowl champions are just .500 through eight weeks, and they're underperforming. At least they received reinforcements with the return of Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet to their Rrunning back room.

The Pittsburgh Steelers aren't flashy, but they're strong in the trenches, and they don't beat themselves, although Aaron Rodgers made several questionable checks in this game. Nevertheless, Pittsburgh beat up the Browns, 27-3. Jaylen Warren rushed for 143 yards and a touchdown.

Jordan Love is playing excellent football, and his two star receivers are struggling with drops. Green Bay missed two makeable field goals and lost by three points. The eventual return of Micah Parsons will be welcomed, and the team just got running back Josh Jacobs back.

The Rams defeated the winless Chargers 24-9. Puka Nacua caught 11 of his 12 targets for 80 yards with a score, and Blake Corum led the team with 73 yards on 11 carries; both he and Kyren Williams found paydirt.

The New York Giants were on their bye in Week 8.

Pittsburgh beat up the Browns, 27-3. Cleveland could not get much going on offense, despite DeShaun Watson throwing for 324 yards. Pittsburgh sacked Watson eight times, and the Browns only had 34 yards on the ground. It was a humbling game for Cleveland's offense, but the defense harassed Aaron Rodgers for much of the game. Cleveland is in the mix at the top of the AFC North, but their offense can still be limited.

Tampa Bay has won two games in a row — three of the last four! They just won a game without completing a pass — the first time this has happened since the 1970s! Bucky Irving rushed for 170 yards; Baker Mayfield threw THREE PASSES! Tampa Bay saw a monsoon, and Todd Bowles is seeing his defense play much better.

The Raiders pulled off a resilient late victory against the New York Jets, 38-33. It was Mike Washington Jr. who touted the rock 25 times for 83 yards, as Ashton Jeanty took a backseat to the rookie running back. Kirk Cousins played, tossing three touchdowns and 247 yards in the victory. The defense remains a problem for the Raiders, but first-year head coach Klint Kubiak still has playoffs on his mind, so I wouldn't expect a quarterback change to Fernando Mendoza any time soon.

The Packers beat up the Panthers, 27-19, on Thursday Night Football. Bryce Young was sacked six times, and the offense looked out of sync for much of the game. The NFC South is wide open, so Carolina has to get their game together.

Lamar Jackson returned for one play before suffering a broken thumb — insanely terrible luck. Backup quarterback Snoop Huntley suffered a foot injury shortly after, and UDFA out of UCONN Joe Fagnano came into the game; the offense could not do anything, as the Bills cruised to victory. The Ravens' season is now up in the air with Lamar Jackson being placed on I.R.

The Houston Texans were on their bye in Week 8.

The Falcons were shut out against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The field conditions were very wet, and Tampa Bay's defense and rushing attack dictated the entire game. Atlanta struggled to fit power-rush concepts, and Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions in the loss.

The New Orleans Saints were on their bye in Week 8.

Arizona shocked Dallas with an epic comeback and overtime win that was led by veteran Gardner Minshew II, who is now set to start against Seattle next week. The Cardinals are a feisty team, and Dallas got nothing going on the ground against the Cardinals' front. Arizona's quarterback change led to 23 points in the fourth quarter and overtime, which allowed the Cardinals to secure the victory.

The Dallas Cowboys can't get out of their own way. This week, though, they got Gardner Minshew'd! Dallas led 24-10 at the start of the fourth quarter, and Minshew scored 20 points in the fourth to send the game into overtime, where Dallas' defense capitulated. The Cowboys have talent, but they're a dysfunctional mess, which is just lovely..

Washington beat up a hapless Eagles team led by Tanner McKee. Jayden Daniels completed just 16 passes in the 27-10 victory. Dan Quinn has the defense playing well, but the offense is still a work in progress.

The Jets took a commanding lead on the Las Vegas Raiders at home in Week 8, but ultimately lost 38-33. Geno Smith threw for 290 yards and went 20 of 32 with two passing touchdowns, and Braelon Allen rushed for 147 yards on 21 carries; still, the Jets defense folded to Kirk Cousins, and New York failed to secure the win.

Miami pushed the New England Patriots for four quarters but ultimately lost 24-19. Still, the Dolphins have come out of the bye with a win and a close loss against last year's AFC champs. The offense looks more competent, and Malik Willis looks more comfortable, as Jacob Rodriguez continues to shine as a rookie linebacker.

Philadelphia is injured and has lost six straight games. The Commanders defeated them 27-10 on Sunday Night Football and they host the Giants next week.

The Titans got into a shootout with Joe Burrow and the Bengals. Brian Daboll got a lot out of Cam Ward, but the Titans lost in overtime 43-36. Tennessee was without rookie Carnell Tate in the game. The Titans will hope that Ward continues to play as he did in Cincinnati, where he also forced three Burrow interceptions in the game.

The Colts are another deflated — down-and-out — team shipping valuable assets for future considerations. Daniel Jones looks like the Daniel Jones from the New York Giants, and he was finally benched late in the Colts' blow-out 42-7 loss. However, the Colts are sticking with Jones over Anthony Richardson for now.

The Chargers were defeated 24-9 by their cross-town rival Rams. The Chargers remain winless.

#2713. Rams barely move in Week 9 power rankings

The Los Angeles Rams beat up the crosstown Chargers to draw even on the year at 4-4, but consecutive wins over middling teams weren't enough to vault L.A. back into the top-10 of the expert power rankings we curated.

The Rams won 24-9 but had a hard time dispatching the Chargers until they got the run game going. Even worse, Matthew Stafford didn't look like himself in the win and is dealing with soreness in his throwing arm, which could complicate things for the 38-year-old quarterback.

Sean McVay and company get another nice matchup against the Washington Commanders in Week 9 with the goal of getting back on the winning side of their record with a few games left before the bye.

Here's the full power rankings roundup for Week 9.

If their season wasn't already belatedly taking off, it's about to gain some serious altitude with defensive game wrecker Myles Garrett set to rejoin practice this week.

The defense came up big in the victory over the Chargers. The offense didn't do a ton, but the run game clicked enough to get this team to 4-4.

The Rams officially won the battle of L.A., which of course isn't saying much considering the state of their co-tenants at SoFi Stadium. They gave a pretty middling performance both offensively and defensively, and it was a bit shocking that they trailed 9-3 late in the first half. It's OK to sleepwalk in a game against the Chargers, of course. But it'll take a lot more than that to prove their season is back on track. They better wake up before they face the Packers, Chiefs, 49ers and Seahawks after Thanksgiving.

I don't know what exactly this says or who it compliments, but the Rams defense still has not allowed a first quarter touchdown this season which is wild, potentially insignificant, totally unsustainable and yet, still noteworthy.

At 4-4 after back-to-back wins, the presumptive Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams are finally in a position where a run should be possible.

Prior to the team's Week 11 bye, the Rams face the Washington Commanders and Arizona Cardinals. Both are winnable matchups, even if Los Angeles fell to the Cardinals just two weeks ago.

Plus, help should be on the way. The NFL's reigning Defensive Player of the Year, Myles Garrett, could play as early as this coming weekend. Though another week or two may be a more realistic possibility.

The Rams haven't fielded their intended starting lineup at any point of this season. But Garrett's return should provide a jolt when Los Angeles needs it the most and revive the squad's previous expectations.

The Rams had three kickers active Sunday — a placekicker, a punter and another kicker just for kickoffs (Joshua Karty). It's a sign of how desperate Sean McVay is to get the special teams monkey off his back. It didn't help much. Los Angeles is still last in the league in special teams EPA (minus-41.9) after its fifth-worst special teams performance of the year.

#2710. What Quinnipiac coach Tom Pecora said about Michigan State after loss

On Monday night, Michigan State basketball opened its season with a resounding win over Quinnipiac of the newly rebranded Metro Conference. It was noted by many that Quinnipiac head coach Tom Pecora was a great personality and a class act heading into the matchup (he had a great line about sending Izzo an Italian dinner when the game was scheduled), and that was definitely seen in his post-game press conference, where he was gracious and charismatic.

Below, you can see what Pecora had to say about the Spartans and the lopsided game:

On the importance of a game like this: "I think for our young guys to put them in this kind of environment and when we recruit guys to Quinnipiac, we talk to them about how we're going to go out, we're going to try to play the best teams in the country when we can get those games, and that's one of the reasons why they come."

On MSU's physicality: "You know, it's the old Mike Tyson line. Everyone's got a plan until they get hit... And as a young player, 'Yeah. Yeah. They're going to be physical. Yeah...' And the crazy thing too is like, I tried to explain to them, they're not dirty; they're physical. And when you're young and out of high school, you definitely have never played in an environment like that. I was kidding around with my assistants, and I was a hundred years ago when I was a young teenager. You'd hang around the schoolyard, and we would play, then the older guys would come to play. They tore us off the court in the summer at six o'clock, right? And then once in a while they'd need one, and you would be there dying to get in that game. And then you would realize the basketball is a contact sport. You know, there's a way of doing it properly and no one does it better than Michigan State."

On MSU: "Everyone knows their ability to play physical, solid defense and then rebound... So, I mean, they're really good, and there's a reason why they're ranked where they are."

On MSU's depth: "One thing I always look for when I watch a team like this, when you see a young man like that come off the bench and play that way - he's pissed he's not starting. You want your guys who are coming off the bench to be, hey, I'm going to take somebody's spot up here and to have that level of competition. But they have great depth, and I think that's necessary with the pace that they play at and with the physicality that they play at."

#2709. Biggest questions for World Series Game 5: How will the Rays get enough innings to avoid elimination (again)?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Tampa Bay Rays took their first step toward a baseball miracle with their 12th-inning comeback win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Tuesday's Game 4 of the World Series. That 4-3 victory means the Rays avoided the sweep and cut the Brewers' series lead to 3-1. That sets the stage for Wednesday's Game 5.

Tuesday's escape for the Rays was obviously an essential one, as it was an elimination game. The win also nudged the Rays' chances of winning the series from "all but impossible" to "merely a longshot." Across all of Major League Baseball postseason history, 42 teams have been down 3-0, and only one – the 2004 Boston Red Sox – has come back to win the series in question. That is, history suggests the Rays had a mere 2.4% chance of pulling off the miracle comeback when they were down 3-0. Now, though, they're down 3-1.

In all, 96 teams have been down 3-1 in a best-of-seven MLB postseason series, and 14 of them have clawed back to win the series. That particular data set says the Rays have a 14.6% chance of stunning the Brewers and winning this Fall Classic. Those aren't great odds, obviously, but they're much better than the odds the Rays were facing going into Game 4. Interestingly, teams down 3-1 have a .500 record in Game 5.

Speaking of which, that brings us to three questions for Game 5 – the answers to which will determine whether the Rays can cut the Brewers' advantage to 3-2 and send the series back to Milwaukee. Let's get to it.

Here's the big one. Rays manager Kevin Cash wisely managed Game 4 for what it was: a must-win contest. That means you worry about tomorrow when tomorrow comes and tactically do everything possible to survive the elimination game. Tomorrow, though, has now arrived, and Cash must figure out how to deploy his pitching staff for another elimination game after using seven arms on Tuesday. Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen will be going on short rest in Game 5, but what then?

The most notable Game 4 decision was using Nick Martinez, who had been slated to start Game 5, in relief. Martinez worked two scoreless innings out of the bullpen and threw 33 pitches. It'll be another all-hands-on-deck affair on Wednesday, but just who those hands will be after Rasmussen is another matter. Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay and amassed 74 pitches, which presumably rules him out for Game 5.

As for the traditional relievers, Cole Sulser, Steven Matz, and Garrett Cleavinger did not pitch on Tuesday and thus can probably expect to be used in Game 5. Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly did pitch in Game 4 but they didn't pitch in Monday's Game 3 blowout loss, which means they're presumably available. Ian Seymour also didn't pitch in Game 3, but his 32-pitch workload in Game 4 may rule him out. Tyler Wells and Cameron Booser have each pitched two days in a row, but desperate straits in October may mean they'll be called upon again. As for Rasmussen, he's made short-rest starts before, but he was basically an opener in those outings, the last of which was in 2022. This, then, is something close to virgin territory for him. No doubt, Cash won't lean on Rasmussen for a long start even if he's cruising, but they could use some bulk from him given the shallow and probably tired bullpen. This will be Rasmussen's fifth start of the 2026 postseason. Across his previous four starts, he put up a 2.19 ERA and 2.57 FIP with 27 strikeouts and five walks in 24 ⅔ innings.

In light of the maxed-out stakes involved, anyone who's even a remotely feasible option will probably tell Cash he's willing to pitch. As such, Cash's decisions on whom to trust and whom to assign the plurality of innings will be fascinating and perhaps determinative.

No such dilemmas are to be found for Pat Murphy and the Brewers, at least insofar as their Game 5 starter is concerned. Jacob Misiorowski, the 24-year-old NL Cy Young favorite and the hardest-throwing starting pitcher anyone's ever seen, on Wednesday will make his fourth start of these playoffs. Last time out, Misiorowski in Game 1 against the Rays went five innings and permitted only one run en route to picking up the win. "Miz" also enjoyed a velocity bump compared to his prior run of starts.

However, he was coming off 11 days of rest in that start, and for his Game 5 trip to the bump he'll be on the standard four days of rest. He's well into career-high-workload territory in 2026, so it remains to be seen whether the sizzle he showed in the series opener will be back for Game 5. The Brewers could use some length from him given how hard the bullpen worked in Game 4.

The Rays' best hitter and one of the richest power sources in all of baseball had to exit Game 4 in the 12th inning not long after reaching base on Joey Ortiz's throwing error. He did so because of an injury to his left foot. From afar, this seems like the kind of knock that would earn Caminero a few days off had it occurred in, say, June, but this is very much not June.

"Junior, he's fine and obviously in the lineup today. Really impressive that he went first and third right there, very instinctual play," Cash said on Wednesday.

"He's been dealing with some lower extremity injuries, but there's a lot of guys that are nicked up right now playing through a lot and know that Cammy will be ready to go today."

The heart of the matter is whether Caminero will be in top form less than 24 hours after sustaining the injury. That's worth pondering in light of his ongoing power outage. Caminero this postseason has a respectable .717 OPS, but he has only one home run in 48 at-bats. That's after hitting a whopping 42 homers during the regular season and averaging one every 14.7 at-bats. It's quite possible that the Rays will need some customary thump from the hard-hitting 23-year-old if they're going to extend the series. That we shall see.

#2703. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2702. Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel dies after on-pitch collision with opponent

Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died Tuesday following an in-pitch collision during Monday's game, the team announced. He was 30.

In the closing seconds of Tenerife's game against Andorra, de Miguel was involved in a brutal collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono around midfield.

Owono was immediately handed a red card and began walking off the pitch. De Miguel initially laid with his head and knees on the grass before turning onto his back. He then became motionless, resulting in an opposing player immediately calling to the sideline for help. Once Owono realized the severity of the situation, he stopped walking off the field and turned back to check on de Miguel. Owono faces a suspension for the collision.

The match did not continue. De Miguel was transferred to a hospital and was initially deemed "stable despite the severity of his condition," Tenerife said in a statement after the game. Later in the day, however, the team said de Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically."

On Tuesday morning, Tenerife announced de Miguel's death. The team's statement, which was translated from Spanish to English, read:

In the wake of the news, Andorra also released a statement sending their "most sincere condolences" to de Miguel's family.

Both Real Madrid and FC Barcelona issued statements expressing their condolences and extending support to de Miguel's family. De Miguel was born in Madrid.

Following de Miguel's death, the Royal Spanish Football Federation announced all matches would be suspended Tuesday.

De Miguel began his senior career in 2015 and played for eight different teams. He joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and had 11 goals in 34 appearances with the club.

#2700. The 2026 Brewers were the team of destiny all along -- and now they're World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- Since the 2026 playoffs began, we've been using words like "relentless" and "inevitable" when it comes to the Milwaukee Brewers. As they finished their coronation in Game 5 with a 4-1 victory over the Rays to take the series and win their first title in franchise history, it's pretty clear that the Brewers were the team of destiny from early in the season.

Game 5 on Wednesday never really felt like the Rays' night. Their pitching situation was dire after needing to use Nick Martinez in Game 4. The offense was dealing with Jacob Misiorowski and a full Brewers bullpen of studs. Junior Caminero was compromised and Yandy Díaz would join him. It just never felt like it was going to be their night and it wasn't, because of course it wasn't. It was the Brewers' night. The Brewers' series. The Brewers' season.

It took some longer than others to see it, myself admittedly included. They struggled in two different spans in April, with a six-game losing streak and later a four-game losing streak. That was about it, though. After a loss on May 4 dropped them to 18-16, the Brewers went absolutely bonkers the rest of the season: 85-43. And now they've completed an 11-2 playoff run against stacked competition. That means they finished 96-45. Holy smokes.

It's a misnomer to act like this is some ragtag bunch; a motley crew, island of the misfit toys collection of big-league players. The Brewers have stars. They have a former MVP in Christian Yelich and, though he's past his prime, he was a quality contributor in the playoffs. Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young. Jackson Chourio is an emerging superstar. William Contreras is an All-Star catcher. Brice Turang is arguably the best second baseman in baseball.

The Brewers are such a well-rounded bunch and the front office thrives on winning on the margins, which is why some might slap inappropriate labels on them, such as the little engine that could. That doesn't begin to cover it. They are, in fact, a team of destiny getting contributions from all over the place.

There are more examples, of course. It was just a team full of winners. No matter what obstacle popped up for the Brewers this season, and especially in the playoffs, they reacted by winning. For crying out loud, they scored eight runs with two outs in the World Series. That was off-the-charts outrageous in Game 3.

Then there were the injuries. Yelich and Chourio missed time. Quinn Priester was lost for the season in spring training. Brandon Woodruff missed most of the year before making the World Series roster. With these injuries, in addition to the trade of Peralta, the door was open for players like Drohan, Gasser and Logan Henderson to make the most of their opportunities.

That's just what happens with teams of destiny. It's that ol' "next man up" mentality. The Brewers have been practicing this for years, trading away established veterans before they reach free agency and immediately replacing them with inexperienced players or even retreads like Jake Bauers who are ready to step in. For every player out the door, there's someone else ready to shine.

The Brewers just won 11 playoff games and came from behind to win six times. That's beyond ridiculous. Overall, teams scoring first in the playoffs were 27-13. Milwaukee accounted for six of the losses in there, bludgeoning its opponents even after falling behind.

The "destiny" thumbprints were all over this series. Even in their Game 4 loss, they just kept coming. And they responded to that loss by getting ace-level work from Misiorowski in Game 5 and putting up run-scoring rallies in three of the first six innings. They didn't need any home runs. They strung together winning plays on singles and doubles and sacrifice flies. They can win on home runs, too, as they've done a few times this postseason. They just find ways to win, almost every time. Their starters, bullpen, defense and clutch hitting are just too good. That's what it takes to win, and the Brewers won it all.

I mentioned the early struggles at the start of the season. They closed in opposite fashion. Including the playoffs, the Brewers were 26-5 after Sept. 6. They had established themselves as the best team in baseball from May 4 until early September, and then went into overdrive. How is it even possible for a 103-win team to level up and get better?

Relentless. Inevitable. The team of destiny. Milwaukee Brewers, World Series champions.

#2698. What's next for the Rays? Three questions after World Series loss, including payroll and Junior Caminero

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Tampa Bay Rays' 2026 season is over. Coming off a 98-win regular season, the American League East title, and their third-ever pennant, the Rays were eliminated in five games from the 2026 World Series by the juggernaut Milwaukee Brewers. There's pride to be taken in the Rays' overall body of work this year, but the prevailing reality is that they failed to achieve their ultimate goal. While the Brewers are celebrating their first World Series title, the Rays remain on the list of franchises that have never hoisted the trophy.

This all means that the Rays now turn their attention to 2027 and whether they're likely to make another run at relevance, contention, and perhaps another bite at the championship apple. Let's explore that now by exploring three questions that will define the Rays' coming offseason and their 2027 campaign.

The Rays, across so much of their history, have reliably punched above their weight. The foundation of that has been a level of support and investment from club ownership that's been entirely lacking. The present ownership group, led by Jacksonville real estate something or other Patrick Zalupski, took over in September of 2025, so this is almost wholly an indictment of former owner Stuart Sternberg.

Since the Rays' current run of contention began with their 90-win campaign in 2018, the club has never ranked higher than 24th in Opening Day active roster payroll and never higher than 22nd in luxury tax payroll (basically 40-man roster payroll based on average annual value of contracts). Twice in that span, the Rays have ranked last in year-end 40-man payroll. Given that the current revenue-sharing structure gives small-market teams more than enough to cover cash payrolls, this is all a plain dereliction of duties on the part of Sternberg. One of the canniest front offices in all of sports and the rosters they have assembled deserve more buy-in from ownership.

Maybe now that Zalupski's group is in charge and the Rays finally appear to have a new ballpark – heavily funded by tax dollars – across the finish line, things will change on this front. It'd be a fine time for that, given that the Rays right now are self-evidently capable of vying for a title. This winter, they have a number of key contributors due for arbitration raises, including Shane McClanahan, Jonathan Aranda, Griffin Jax, and Bryan Baker. Yandy Díaz in August triggered a $13 million vesting option for 2027, which, based on prior organizational behavior, might make him a trade candidate. There are also a number of investments needed in the rotation, which we'll get into below.

There's also the matter of what the next collective bargaining agreement will look like once one is agreed to and the forthcoming lockout ends. Signs point to the next CBA being of benefit to teams like the Rays, and that may inform some of their offseason behavior before that owner-implemented lockout likely begins on the night of Dec. 1.

The need for better stewardship from owners will be acutely critical to the makeup of the 2027 rotation. McClanahan's incoming arb raise – which will likely give him the highest salary of any Rays arb-eligible player this offseason — makes him a trade candidate. Freddy Peralta, their stabilizer after he was acquired leading up to the trade deadline, is a free agent. Drew Rasmussen has an $8 million option/$500,000 buyout for 2027. It should be a no-brainer to exercise said option, but, well, you know. There's also Nick Martinez, who has a $20 million mutual option for next season. That likely means he's headed for free agency, but the Rays should still pick up their end of it on principle. That's 80% of the rotation, at least as it was constituted after the trade deadline and before McClanahan's forearm injury. In all, that quartet of starters combined for a 3.03 ERA during the regular season and 42 of the team's 54 quality starts. They also combined for a WAR of 11.2, and that's despite getting just 10 starts from Peralta.

The Rays will need to do a lot of retention work on this front if they're going to again be the best team in the American League next season. As it stands right now, the rotation is the biggest unknown going into the offseason.

The 23-year-old third baseman and emerging superstar is the lineup fulcrum for Tampa Bay. Since his rookie season of 2024, Caminero has improved his OPS+ from 105 to 130 to 144 this past season. His WAR has swollen from 0.7 in 43 games as a rookie to 4.3 in 2025 to 5.7 in 2026.

He hits the ball exceptionally hard, and he has the fastest bat speed in the game. Additionally, Caminero in 2026 made impressive strides in terms of his plate discipline. Prospects these days, thanks to developmental and training advances at the lower levels, are arriving more ready than ever, and some start off at their peak. Caminero, though, has shown improvement on a number of forward-looking fronts, and that raises the compelling possibility that he still has some growth in him. Is a 50-homer season and an MVP award in the offing? That seems quite possible, and given the unbalanced nature of the Rays' lineup, they could use even more from their best player.

#2696. Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 8 loss to the Bills

The Ravens' season took a nosedive on Sunday against the Bills when Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury on his first snap back from a three-week absence. Baltimore's defense did their best to keep the game close, but the unit eventually unraveled against Josh Allen with no help from an offense that was down to its emergency third-string undrafted rookie quarterback.

Roquan Smith: After a week of questions targeted at Baltimore's defense, and specifically the highly-paid leaders of the unit, Smith responded with one of his best games of the season. His 11 total tackles led the Ravens; he also forced a fumble and deflected two passes. Smith finished with a 91.1 grade from Pro Football Focus, the highest on the team and his best since Week 1.

Broderick Washington: Washington's game was otherwise unremarkable, but he did come down with an interception off a dropped pass on Buffalo's third drive. The turnover set the Ravens up at the 17-yard line, leading to a Derrick Henry touchdown a few plays later to cut the lead to 10-7.

T.J. Tampa: Tampa had a strong first game back from injured reserve. The third-year cornerback recovered the fumble forced by Smith while allowing zero catches on one target, according to PFF.

Chidobe Awuzie: Awuzie played 43 snaps on Sunday, his most of the season outside of Marlon Humphrey's Week 4 absence. The veteran made a case for more playing time going forward as he broke up his lone target.

Nate Wiggins: The Bills avoided Wiggins entirely on Sunday. He locked down the right side of the field and was not targeted a single time.

Quarterbacks: Three quarterbacks took snaps for the Ravens against the Bills, and all three suffered injuries of various degrees. Jackson's long-awaited return lasted just one snap, while Tyler Huntley left the game with a toe injury in the second quarter. Rookie undrafted free agent Joe Fagnano — the team's emergency quarterback — finished the game, but he suffered an ankle injury that now puts into question his availability for Thursday's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. The three quarterbacks combined for just 12 completions on 26 attempts for 91 yards, an interception, and two lost fumbles.

Offensive line: Baltimore's offensive line has been a source of frustration all season, and the unit had perhaps its worst outing yet against Buffalo. Jackson had pressure in his face immediately on the play where he injured his thumb, and Huntley and Fagnano dealt with more of the same for the remainder of the game with injuries of their own. According to PFF, the Ravens' offensive line allowed 14 pressures on 31 dropbacks (45.1%). A questionable holding call against Ronnie Stanley wiped out a Henry touchdown as well.

Tyler Loop: Loop started the game off on the wrong foot, no pun intended, by landing the opening kickoff out of bounds. This set the Bills and Josh Allen up at the 40-yard line. Loop later missed a 34-yard field goal that would have pulled the score within three points in the second quarter. Jessie Minter announced on Monday that Loop could go on injured reserve with a groin injury with Jake Moody set to step in for the time being.

Zay Flowers: Flowers' excellent season hit a roadblock in Week 8 as he failed to record a single catch on five targets. What was looking like a potential Offensive Player of the Year caliber season for Flowers could dwindle now with the Ravens' uncertainty at the quarterback position.

Marlon Humphrey: Humphrey allowed the longest catch of the day by giving up a 49-yard completion to D.J. Moore on the opening drive of the second half. He was also flagged for holding on a third down.

#2695. BREAKING: Dodge Returns to NASCAR's Cup Series at the 2027 Daytona 500

Dodge will start the 2027 Daytona 500 on Feb. 21 with a two-car Kaulig Racing team, its first points-paying Cup start since 2012, and the release announcing it names no engine builder, no drivers and no car numbers.

Tim Kuniskis, head of the American Brands, SRT Performance and Direct Connection division at Stellantis North America, shared the news Monday during a preview of the Stellantis display at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas, according to the release Kaulig Racing posted. NASCAR.com's report counts a 14-year gap and calls Dodge the fourth manufacturer in the series alongside Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota, and the first newcomer since Toyota in 2007. We pointed to the SEMA and Homestead dates in our countdown earlier this month.

The engine. NASCAR Event Management president John Probst said on a Monday teleconference that the engine Kaulig will run complies with the rulebook, then left it to Dodge SRT Racing and the team to announce what it is. The release does not mention one.

The drivers. Kaulig will name its 2027 lineup at Homestead-Miami Speedway, where the Cup championship is decided Sunday at 2 p.m. ET on NBC. The two-car count comes from NASCAR.com, not the release, and neither document gives car numbers.

The body. The release says every road-going Charger comes as a two-door coupe or a four-door sedan, and neither document says which shape the race car will wear.

Probst said a brand-new car from a new manufacturer normally goes through about 18 months of CFD and wind tunnel testing, followed by a check of actual production panels to confirm they still fit the performance window. Dodge has passed the wind tunnel portion, he said, and production panels are due in the middle of November, roughly 14 weeks before the Daytona 500. He expects that step to be routine.

Kuniskis put the schedule this way: "Everyone said it was impossible to get back in one year." The release's answer is to plan, test and refine at the same time, on the track instead of ahead of it.

Representative image: Richard Petty's 1976 STP Dodge Charger on display at the International Motorsports Hall of Fame. Photo: BWard 1997 via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

Dodge raced in Cup from 2001 through 2012 and won 57 times in that stretch, per NASCAR.com. Brad Keselowski's 2012 title came with the brand's 217th career Cup win, at Dover that fall, and Dodge left afterward. Ram returned to NASCAR in 2026 in the Truck Series with Kaulig, which fielded five full-time trucks; NASCAR.com lists Tony Stewart, Jamie McMurray and Ryan Newman among its drivers, and we covered Stewart's Daytona truck start in January.

Dodge will reveal the race car on Dec. 4 at the Snowball Derby at Five Flags Speedway in Pensacola, Florida, with a livestream on FloRacing and the NASCAR Channel. The Derby feature runs Dec. 6. The same weekend includes the Dodge Sno-Brawl, a celebrity race in Charger late-model stock cars, with details to come.

The release pairs the racing news with the road-car lineup: a 600-horsepower Charger Super Bee Launch Edition, a 550-horsepower Scat Pack and a 420-horsepower R/T, all with standard all-wheel drive, which the rear-drive Cup car will not share. Our look at Mopar's $10,995 '27 Charger package covers what that lineup costs to dress up.

Sources: Kaulig Racing and Stellantis release, Nov. 2, 2026; NASCAR.com report by Zach Sturniolo, Nov. 2, 2026.

Is a Dodge comeback built in one year, with production panels arriving in November, good for the Cup Series, or a rush the Daytona 500 field will end up paying for?
