#2615. Should Ravens trade for QB after Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley injuries? Possible candidates to watch

The Ravens' quarterback situation went from disappointing to dire to destitute in a hurry Sunday. In his return from an ankle injury that cost him three games, Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury that will require potentially season-ending surgery on Baltimore's first offensive play, and backup Tyler Huntley left shortly thereafter with a toe injury.

That left the Ravens with emergency third quarterback Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie. He went 10-for-21 for 91 yards and an interception, looking very much like an undrafted rookie, as the Ravens went down quietly, 36-10, against the Bills. What looked like a chance to turn the season around now looks like a game that could end Baltimore's season, for all intents and purposes. The Ravens are 4-4 and have lost three straight. Monday, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Huntley will miss extended time with turf toe, a bothersome injury that can last for weeks.

The Ravens have little time to wallow. They play the Jaguars on Thursday night. Currently, Baltimore has one available quarterback on its active roster (Fagnano), and even he was in discomfort late after taking several big hits. The Ravens don't have another quarterback on their active roster or practice squad; Skylar Thompson is on IR.

So where does Baltimore go from here at the position? There are many factors to consider.

Regardless of whether the Ravens can continue to contend or not — and it's very much looking like the latter — they owe it to all parties involved to get a quarterback.

They owe it to the rest of the team, which is still fighting. Baltimore is 4-4, which isn't good, but isn't completely out of it. It's not as if the team is dead in the water, just trying to finish out a completely lost season. There's still Derrick Henry and Zay Flowers on offense and plenty of stars on defense. If there's any hope Jackson can return on the sooner end of the recovery spectrum, Baltimore's players deserve a chance to keep their season afloat.

They owe it to coach Jesse Minter and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, the latter of whom has been excellent this year. Forcing Minter, a first-year head coach, to resort to an undrafted rookie free agent would be extremely difficult. Since 2000, only one team with a rookie head coach has started an undrafted rookie quarterback in multiple games: the Jets with Brady Cook last year. The Ravens do not want to resemble the Jets whatsoever.

They owe it to Fagnano, too. He is a really nice story, someone who started his college career as a walk-on at FCS program Maine and finished it with a superb seventh-year senior season at UConn. He earned a spot on the roster with a stellar showing at rookie tryouts, then throughout the early offseason, and then in training camp and the preseason. But to stick him with an extended starting role would be unfair to him, just as it would be for Minter and Doyle.

And the bottom line is the Ravens have to add someone. They can't have one quarterback on the active roster. Austin Reed makes sense as a temporary solution to join Fagnano, as he was at least with the team this offseason, but he has never taken an NFL snap.

Unfortunately, it's not like capable quarterbacks grow on trees. There's a shortage of passable starting quarterbacks, much less backups or backups to backups. But that doesn't mean it would be impossible to find one.

Rapoport said he'd expect the Ravens to consider quarterback trades. Two names he floated were Bears backup Tyson Bagent and Cardinals recently benched starter Jacoby Brissett.

Bagent, 26, makes sense for a few reasons. First and foremost, he was with Doyle in Chicago last year. Second, it's unclear whether he's even Caleb Williams' primary backup right now. He performed decently in a win over the Jets earlier this year but struggled badly in a loss to the Packers the following week. Overall, he has zero passing touchdowns and three interceptions in three games (two starts) this year.

Case Keenum, on the other hand, played well in his lone start, a win over the Eagles. He got the nod after Bagent had missed much of the week of practice with a concussion, though Bagent returned to primary backup thereafter.

The Bears clearly value Bagent. They gave him a multi-year extension last season. He has shown promise in extremely small sample sizes. He has some creation ability and athleticism, which are helpful in Doyle's offense. All of that also means he wouldn't be cheap, either. There's little reason for Chicago, in a win-now season, to part with Bagent. What if the Bears need a spot start from a backup late in the year? Maybe Baltimore could sweeten the deal by sending a depth piece of their own to Chicago in the deal.

The Ravens must determine how much they want to invest in saving the next few weeks. Bagent would be on the pricier end, and it's not as if his performance this season has inspired much confidence. If Baltimore believes he could eke out a couple of wins, though? Maybe it's worth it.

Brissett has been the Cardinals' de facto bridge starter this year, but he may have lost that position Sunday, when he was benched. In his place, Gardner Minshew threw for three touchdowns in Arizona's stunning 33-30 overtime comeback win over the Cowboys. Mike LaFleur did not commit to Minshew being the starter going forward, but it'd be hard to imagine he's not.

That will be especially true if the Ravens come knocking regarding Brissett. Over the past two seasons, out of 30 quarterbacks, Brissett ranks ...

He is exactly what he has been during his entire career: a low-level starter or high-level backup who has gotten an opportunity to be the starter only when the need arises.

But the need is there for Baltimore, and perhaps Arizona feels the opposite. Minshew is pretty similar in terms of overall player archetype, and the Cardinals also have rookie Carson Beck. If Arizona feels OK with Minshew and Beck, and it can get a solid draft-capital return for Brissett, it could make sense to do so, especially at this point in the Cardinals' long-term timeline.

There are some other names that could be considered, though Bagent and Brissett stand out as more natural/sensical picks. If Baltimore goes elsewhere, though, here are a few names worth mentioning. View this as throwing names at a wall and seeing what sticks.

In the coming days, you'll likely hear Mac Jones' name bandied about in connection to Baltimore.

It doesn't seem particularly realistic. Kyle Shanahan has said many times he wants to keep Jones, and the 49ers, like the Bears, have legitimate Super Bowl aspirations right here, right now. If the 49ers needed a spot start — or even just a few series — from Jones to win a game, it would be worth it. Unlike the Bears, though, the 49ers don't have a second legit backup. Kurtis Rourke has never played an NFL snap.

The Ravens would likely need to blow away the 49ers to have any shot at Jones, and that simply hasn't been Baltimore GM Eric DeCosta's M.O. Instead, Bagent and Brissett seem like top options, with a flyer on a younger, potentially intriguing player also a legitimate route for the Ravens to take.

#2611. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.

#2610. Five bold predictions for 2026 NBA Cup: A new champion, a record for futility, a surprising early exit

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NBA Cup begins on Friday, Oct. 30, as the fourth season of the NBA's in-season competition tips off.

History was made last year when the New York Knicks became the first team to pull off the NBA double, winning the NBA Cup and the NBA championship in the same season -- beating the San Antonio Spurs in both finals. While some still fail to properly respect the Cup, teams are coming around to the idea that it is an early-season proving ground that can build confidence for postseason success.

The 2026 edition will be decided over the next six weeks, with four group-stage games determining the eight teams that reach the knockout rounds, leading to the championship at historic Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis on Dec. 11.

As a refresher, these are the teams that will battle for group stage supremacy over the next four weeks.

Before we get into this year's NBA Cup action, we've got five bold predictions for this year's competition, including some surprising group winners, a pick for the champion and a team that could set a new record for futility.

It took longer than it should have, but the Knicks finally put an NBA Cup banner in the Madison Square Garden rafters. That initial Cup disrespect from James Dolan will have its consequences in 2026.

New York drew a brutal spot in East Group B that includes the 76ers, Cavaliers, Heat and Pacers, and the Knicks are going to continue the streak of defending Cup champs failing to get out of the group stage the following year. The Lakers and Bucks both failed to advance out of the group while defending their Cup crown, and the Knicks will make it three straight years of Cup champs missing out on the knockout stage.

The Spurs are the favorites and the Lakers are a threat, but I think this Blazers team is built for the Cup. An early-season competition is ideal for a Portland team that's still healthy and flying high right now with its star backcourt duo of Damian Lillard and Ja Morant.

I have some questions about the Blazers over the long haul, but right now, they're in a flow state on offense. Lillard has already lifted the Cup once in Milwaukee and will be hungry to help lead his young Blazers teammates to that same glory. They might fall short of that ultimate goal, but I think they can shock Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs in the group and reach the knockouts, where Dame Time gives them a puncher's chance in any matchup.

The Kings have already lost games by 25 and 27 points in four games this season and we have not even reached the portion of the calendar where teams are incentivized to run up the score. The Kings play in West Group C with the Spurs, Lakers, Blazers and Warriors, and each of those teams will see their matchup with Sacramento as an opportunity to get some much-needed point differential help.

The current record for worst point differential in four group stage games belongs to the 2025 Jazz, who finished with an astonishing -85 differential despite winning a game. That might be my favorite NBA Cup fact, but Utah's reign as the worst-performing NBA Cup team -- narrowly beating out the 2024 Wizards (-74) and 2025 Wizards (-77) -- will be short-lived. That's because this Kings team could be on the wrong end of some truly horrible beatdowns in another long season for the Sacramento faithful.

The East will not be decided by the most-discussed teams this summer, but instead the Celtics and Pistons. Boston has a friendly path in East Group C and Detroit's group looks much more manageable with injuries to Paolo Banchero and Kawhi Leonard limiting their top competition.

Both the Pistons and Celtics are off to terrific starts to their seasons and the continuity they have compared to a lot of other East contenders still figuring things out with some new-look squads will help them here. Those two teams will end up battling it out in the semifinals for the right to face the team I think lifts the Cup from the West.

Your 2026 NBA Cup champions will be the Houston Rockets. This is a team on a mission early in the season and even with Alperen Sengun missing a little time to start the group stage with a back injury, they've got a pretty friendly path to the knockout rounds in West Group A (Denver, Phoenix, Dallas and Utah).

Fred VanVleet's return to the lineup has moved everyone back into their ideal roles in Houston, and suddenly the offense runs much more smoothly in the half-court -- which was their downfall last postseason. They've got great defenders, shooters, athletes and Kevin Durant remains one of the NBA's biggest individual mismatches on offense.

Houston also fits the bill for teams that have performed well in the NBA Cup. Almost all past Cup finalists have been teams trying to prove they can win at a high level beyond just regular-season ball. The Lakers, Pacers, Bucks, Thunder, Spurs and Knicks all had something to prove -- either due to falling short of expectations in recent postseasons or trying to show they were ahead of schedule.

Houston is in that same spot after a first-round exit last season, and looks like a team extremely focused on proving it is being slept on in a Western Conference that suddenly looks much more open than initially thought.

The Rockets can use the Cup as a proving ground for this roster in higher-stakes scenarios and should be locked in on that opportunity.

#2609. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2608. MLB rumors: Early favorites for Tarik Skubal emerge, plus Astros eye old friend in hunt for new manager

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is upon us. The Milwaukee Brewers won the belt and the title, and they're now in the process of being feted far and wide. Meantime, an uncertain hot stove season is preparing to unfold. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

Ace and, for now, back-to-back American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is far and away the most coveted free agent within the current class, and he's almost certain to ink a contract well past the $300 million mark and perhaps the largest contract ever for a pitcher.

On that front, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers, who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a deadline trade; the New York Mets; and the Chicago Cubs are expected to be the leading contenders for the lefty's services, ESPN reports. The Cubs, though, may not be willing to go as high as the Dodgers and Mets may be, and of those two, the Mets at this juncture are expected to be the more vigorous in their pursuit of Skubal.

Now that the Houston Astros have a new general manager in Randy Flores, the attention turns to their current managerial vacancy. Joe Espada's contract wasn't renewed after three seasons on the job.

On that front, current Yankees bench coach and former Tigers and Los Angeles Angels manager Brad Ausmus may be a candidate to replace Espada in Houston and was recently at Daikin Park, MLB.com reports. Ausmus, 57, went 314-322 in four seasons as Tigers manager from 2014-17 and one season with the Angels in 2019. His lone playoff appearance as a manager came in his first season in Detroit. There's a strong Houston connection, as Ausmus was the Astros' catcher for 10 of his 18 seasons in the majors.

The Astros are coming off an American League West title in 2026. However, they finished 81-81 with a negative run differential and were swept in the opening round of the postseason.

#2607. NBA's five biggest X-Factors for 2026-27 season: Hopes hinge on Joel Embiid, LaMelo Ball and others

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most important players of a given NBA season are the best ones. Shocker. The 2027 NBA champion will probably hinge first and foremost on the Victor Wembanyamas and Shai Gilgeous-Alexanders of the world. We know they're great. It's not as though the stars cancel each other out, but we take their greatness as a given and make predictions accordingly. Where our predictions are usually wrong, though, is a tier or two down.

A reserve becomes a starter. A starter becomes an All-Star. An All-Star becomes a legend. Someone, or multiple someones, vastly outperforms expectations in a way that pushes his team over the top. These are the X-Factors of a given season, the players whose development or fit or health has a chance to turn a contender into a champion. We've now seen a week of games in the 2026-27 season, and these are the players who stand out as the major swing pieces in the 2027 championship race.

The Oklahoma City Thunder gave 11 players at least 900 minutes last season. Five of those players, due to either trade or injury, are either gone or should not be expected to return this season. The Thunder preemptively replaced Isaiah Joe with Jared McCain in a move that now looks brilliant. The addition of Aday Mara deepens the front-court enough to potentially offset some of the lost wing depth, like Aaron Wiggins.

The defensive losses of Lu Dort and Cason Wallace are substantial. The same is true for Jalen Williams, perhaps more than either, because of his size. Still, the Thunder have an incredible collection of rim-protectors, and they still have Alex Caruso, who can guard anyone on the planet. They'll be able to find a wing defender on the trade market if they want to. Whether it's someone like Derrick Jones Jr. on the lower end or Herb Jones on the pricier one, adding defense is doable given their available assets and salary circumstances.

But replacing Williams-level shot-creation is a much, much taller order, and unless the Thunder are willing to put an amount of draft capital on the table that we can't presently foresee, it's going to have to come internally. The Thunder had no path to good shots against the Spurs last season with Williams and Ajay Mitchell hurt. The offense became mostly contested Shai Gilgeous-Alexander mid-rangers in that series, with a dash of hot shooting from Caruso and McCain barely keeping them afloat.

For now, Mitchell remains healthy, and his volume has soared since Williams went down. The Thunder, for now, will likely treat him as their No. 2 option. The mid-range scoring is there. The finishing and the pull-up shooting -- both necessities for advantage creation against Victor Wembanyama -- have to improve. Mitchell has already grown plenty in two NBA seasons, and the opportunity now in front of him is a tremendous one. He's drawn Jalen Brunson comparisons for the past year. Well... who just slayed Wembanyama in the Finals? Mitchell has a ways to go before he can live up to a name that lofty, but he flashed future stardom in the first two rounds of Oklahoma City's run a year ago. That's where he'll have to go if the Thunder are going to avenge last year's loss to San Antonio.

Ivica Zubac had 15 rebounds on opening night. Do you remember the last time Myles Turner had 15 rebounds in a game? November 2021. Six years ago. For players with relatively similar levels of career accomplishment, you may not find two players who differ so much stylistically at the same position. The Indiana Pacers won the East with five-out spacing and all of the offensive advantages that came with it. Indiana no longer has that. They've traded it in for, well, everything else.

He's the far sturdier defender at this point. Rebounding is, well, something new for Indiana out of its centers. Zubac is a stronger screener and passer than Turner, and he's a more capable interior scorer as well. Figuring out how to integrate all of those skills without letting his lack of 3-point shooting get in the way of everything they already had is going to be a process, and early injuries to both Zubac and Tyrese Haliburton will slow that process.

Zubac and Haliburton have only played 52 minutes together, but the early returns here are positive. It can be hard to find a place to stick non-shooting bigs when two other players run pick-and-roll, but Haliburton's ability to draw two to the ball and Pascal Siakam's ability to attack basically any coverage balances the court comfortably enough for Zubac to feast from the dunker's spot.

When Zubac is screening in these actions, his passing against 4-on-3s fits Indiana should almost always lead to good looks.

The Brooklyn Nets and New Orleans Pelicans in October are hardly the sort of defenses Indiana should expect to see when it counts, but the Pacers will dial up the offensive sophistication as the comfort here grows. For now, everyone is just getting to know each other, but if the Pacers can figure out how to take advantage of all of the new things Zubac brings to the table, their offense is going to be even more diverse for this playoff run than it was in 2025.

The Charlotte Hornets didn't think LaMelo Ball could be their franchise player. The Minnesota Timberwolves didn't need him to be. Putting him next to Anthony Edwards would theoretically amplify the best elements of his game and sand down some of its edges. You don't have to take as many circus shots or try the sort of audacious things that lead to turnovers that Ball has been doing forever when defenses are fixated mostly on someone else. In small doses, those things lead to the sort of "giddiness" that Chris Finch has welcomed. In more concentrated form, well, you get unserious basketball, the sort Charlotte is trying to get away from.

That's what makes this early Edwards injury so enormous for Minnesota. It's not just the absence of his productivity. It's the fact that this is a relatively new and young team still figuring out its identity, and the last team that had Ball decided that the foibles that come with building everything around him were not an identity they wanted to try to sustain. Minnesota looked great in its first four games with Ball and Edwards together.

Ball was dreadful in his first solo star outing, finishing with nearly as many turnovers (6) as he had points (8). His best season in Charlotte, a year ago, came after the arrival of Kon Knueppel and the emergence of Brandon Miller. Before the Hornets could actually support him, well, things were uglier.

That's not exactly exclusive to Ball, but it's the fear Minnesota is facing now. The Timberwolves are deeper than the Hornets teams Ball grew up with, but there's no Knueppel or Miller around anymore. For better or worse, he is going to fully define the next few months of Minnesota's season, and finding the balance between the things that make him special and the things that Charlotte was afraid made him expendable is going to be tricky considering just how much Minnesota now needs out of him. The stakes here are high. Oklahoma City's injuries create vulnerability atop this conference in a way that may not exist in a year. It's hard to imagine Minnesota taking advantage of that from the Play-In Tournament, so winning regular-season games while Edwards is out really matters. Doing so in a way that doesn't compromise the identity of the team Edwards comes back to matters more.

One of the biggest storylines of the 2026 playoffs were the specific ways a handful of centers bothered Wembanyama. Very, very few bigs can genuinely do it offensively. Isaiah Hartenstein did so with his parabolic floater. Karl-Anthony Towns did so with his combination of shooting and driving. The Spurs, with Oklahoma City compromised, are the measuring stick right now. And something we're reminded of every time the Houston Rockets face San Antonio is how much Alperen Sengun seems to relish the challenge of attacking the NBA's best defender.

Sengun shot 17 of 23 with Wembanyama as his primary defender last season, according to NBA.com tracking data. He just posted a 29-point, seven-assist game against Wembanyama a week ago. He has a notable strength advantage over the Defensive Player of the Year, and his game is starting to round out in such a way that he poses many of the problems Towns did, albeit in different ways.

He doesn't have a Hartenstein-level floater, but it's good enough and arcs high enough to force Wembanyama to step away from the rim to try to contest it, which in turn opens up the paint for Sengun as a passer. He's starting to take 3s again too, though we'll see how long that lasts. A year ago, Sengun took 3.4 3s per game in his first 11 appearances and more or less stopped from there. With Fred VanVleet and Steven Adams back, it's probably a skill Sengun leans into a bit more this season, and it's another spot on the floor that Wembanyama has to respect.

Having some sort of answer to the Wembanyama question is a contention prerequisite moving forward. You may not be able to neutralize him completely, but you have to find a way to render him defensively mortal. There are only a handful of bigs in the NBA that can do that. Houston may have one of them, and if that's indeed the case, with the Thunder hobbled, they are probably the single Western Conference team best suited to unseating San Antonio and reaching the Finals.

They may share a uniform, but Joel Embiid and the rest of the Philadelphia 76ers often look as though they play for different teams. Everyone else in the starting lineup and most of the bench wants to run. Between the outlet passing of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown's ability to punish the wrong cross-matches and the sheer athleticism of Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe, Philadelphia should be among the best transition offenses in the NBA. They rank 27th in transition frequency and 21st in transition efficiency, according to Cleaning the Glass. This isn't just an Embiid problem, but he sticks out like a sore thumb in this respect.

This is by no means an insurmountable stylistic clash. Remember, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar played center for the Showtime Lakers. The ability to modulate pace can be a lethal weapon, and Embiid remains a very effective player. Thus far, he's just not the sort of effective center who makes sense on this specific roster. Individual shot-creation is plentiful here. Someone bouncier, someone who uses fewer possessions and makes quicker decisions, probably fits a bit better here. Too bad. Embiid is on a three-year, super max contract that figures to be very difficult to trade. You don't always get the ideal stylistic fit. You make do with what you have.

He's made some concessions on this front. He's holding the ball almost a full second less per possession than he did a year ago. He's in good shape, moving better than he is in years... though still far from where he'll need to be against offenses that can put him in the blender as the New York Knicks did a year ago. He remains an effective rim-protector defensively, though he's closer to a stationary one. It's far too early to judge Philadelphia's defense as a whole. The on-off numbers are deceptive because of how limited Embiid's backups are and how absurdly lucky they've thus far gotten on opponents' 3-pointers when he's played.

It's not as though 2020 Anthony Davis is walking through that door (even if 2026-27 Davis is a popular fake trade target). Embiid is mostly who he is, and the Sixers are going to have to find ways to blend what he does best with what their four other starters actually need out of a center. It'd be nice if he started making his 3s again, a problem that has now persisted several seasons. This is one way the speed disparity here could be beneficial: trailer 3s. His shooting just about everywhere has been down thus far, and that's going to have to correct itself if he's going to justify his volume.

The theory of this roster was less about a specific style than sheer, overwhelming talent. The idea here is that Philadelphia can generate advantages and mismatches so easily with so many high-level players on the floor that even a version of the team that isn't optimized can be great. That's a lot easier in October than in May. Finding the synergies between these very different sorts of players will be the entire point of this regular season for the 76ers.

#2606. 2026 NFL trade deadline QB rankings: Mac Jones, Kirk Cousins lead 10 best targets

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NFL trade deadline is fast approaching, and already some major deals have come down across the league. For instance, the Chicago Bears just made a blockbuster trade, sending multiple picks (including two first-rounders) to the Tennessee Titans for star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. The defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks also landed All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson in a trade with Indianapolis. Those deals may have been the first, but there will certainly be more before the Nov. 10 deadline.

Most of the conversation surrounding the deadline has largely centered around pass rushers, running backs and wide receivers. That said, the quarterback market could also heat up as a few teams across the NFL could be on the hunt for a signal caller. That includes both the Baltimore Ravens and Philadelphia Eagles, who each lost their starting quarterbacks. Then, there's the Minnesota Vikings, who could also eye an upgrade at the position with Kyler Murray struggling despite the team's 6-1 start to the year.

With that in mind, we combed the market and identified 10 veteran quarterbacks who could be available for the right price on the trade market.

Milton is on the active roster of the Eagles after he was signed off of the Cowboys practice squad. He's backing up starter Tanner McKee, who ascended the depth chart in the wake of Jalen Hurts being put on the shelf with blood clots in his lungs. While Philadelphia would lose some depth at the position, Howie Roseman could see shipping away Milton as an opportunity to continue gaining future draft capital, albeit in the Day 3 range.

The 26-year-old was a sixth-round pick of the Patriots in 2024 out of Tennessee and spent his rookie season in New England before he was traded to Dallas in the spring of 2025. He's appeared in five games over the course of his career (one start) and has completed 69.8% of his passes for a 90.4 career passer rating. Milton is still raw, but has ability that could make him an intriguing addition.

Keenum has started games this year for Chicago, so while he may be 38, he has recent starting experience that could be useful for a team looking for a QB. After Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent got hurt for the Bears earlier this year, Keenum started the club's Week 3 matchup against Philadelphia and impressed. He completed 24-of-34 (70.6%) for 247 yards and two touchdowns, while adding another score on the ground in a 27-7 win over the Eagles.

Keenum also saw some action in Week 5, but the results were not as prolific, completing 11-of-19 for 108 yards and an interception. Still, he's shown an ability to come in and play at a serviceable level, which is really all you can ask for at this time of the year when searching for a quarterback.

Dalton is another notable name who could be had, as he's in a crowded quarterback room with the Atlanta Falcons. The 39-year-old began the year with the Philadelphia Eagles, but was released by the team on Oct. 9. He then signed on with the Falcons, who released Cooper Rush to make room for him on the roster. Dalton is currently in a quarterback room that consists of starter Michael Penix Jr., Tua Tagovailoa, and undrafted rookie Jack Strand.

Dalton made a brief appearance in the Eagles' Week 3 loss to the Bears, attempting one pass that was intercepted. While that doesn't exactly instill a ton of confidence, Dalton is a seasoned veteran who has 16 years and 169 career starts under his belt.

The Colts are blowing it up. They already traded away Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and Jonathan Taylor seems like he could be next if the price is right. If Indy is willing to move that caliber of player, trading Anthony Richardson for any sort of return should be on the table even after benching Daniel Jones late in the Week 8 loss to Jacksonville.

Richardson has been a bust so far for the Colts after they selected him with the fourth overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft out of Florida. The 24-year-old is 8-7 as a starter and has a career completion percentage of 50.9% to go along with a 68.0 career passer rating. His raw ability and untapped potential could be of interest for a QB-needy team wanting to pick up a lottery ticket. For a rebuilding team like Indianapolis, extracting any value on the roster -- particularly for a player like Richardson, who is going to be a free agent this offseason --  makes too much sense.

Winston is the backup in New York after he lost the starting job to J.J. McCarthy. After Jaxson Dart went down with a season-ending knee injury, Winston initially got the nod and the 12-year veteran largely struggled, despite a 2-1-1 record as the starter. He completed 57% of his throws and had seven passing touchdowns to go with five interceptions over six games played. Most notably, Winston's arm strength appeared diminished, which helped pave the way for McCarthy -- who they acquired in a trade with Minnesota -- to leapfrog him on the depth chart.

While Winston may be past his prime, he's started 13 games over the past three seasons, so he's not the coldest quarterback on the market.

Minshew might be the new QB1 in Arizona, which could eliminate him from this list. However, the Cardinals should eventually see what they have in rookie Carson Beck, so if they can get value for someone like Minshew, it'd be negligent not to pull the trigger. After coming in for the benched Jacoby Brissett, Minshew helped lead Arizona to a fourth-quarter rally against the Cowboys and pulled off the upset win in overtime. The veteran completed 17-of-23 for 188 yards and three touchdowns in the winning effort.

The 30-year-old began his career as a sixth-round pick of the Jaguars in 2019 and has bounced around the league since being traded out of Jacksonville in 2021. In all, Minshew has made stops in Philadelphia, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, and Kansas City before arriving in Arizona, so he is no stranger to jumping into new systems. He's started 47 games over the course of his career and is 17-30 as a starter.

Brissett could be one of the quarterbacks who is truly available on the trade market, especially after he was benched for Minshew against Dallas last week. The 33-year-old started the first eight games of the season for Arizona, owning a 3-5 record while completing 63.3% of his throws and a 79.7 passer rating. Brissett started 12 games for the Cardinals last year and had a 94.1 passer rating, so his production has slipped rather dramatically in 2026, which has since led to him finishing that Week 8 victory on the bench.

If Arizona is going to turn the keys over to Minshew, it makes Brissett expendable, especially with rookie third-round pick Carson Beck waiting in the wings. Brissett has started in 73 games over the course of his career and is 23-50 in those contests.

Caleb Williams is back healthy, which could make Bagent expendable. He was initially the top backup when Williams went down with a hamstring injury earlier this year, but had to give way to Case Keenum as the Week 3 starter after he landed in concussion protocol. Once he was cleared, Bagent did get the nod in Week 4 against New York, where he completed 25-of-34 for 268 yards and an interception.  The following week, he started against the Packers, but was eventually benched for Keenum after completing 57.1% of his throws and two interceptions.

If Chicago feels comfortable with Keenum serving as the primary backup to Williams, Bagent becomes an intriguing trade chip as he's only 26 years old.

Cousins' future in Las Vegas is directly linked to the development of No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza. If the Raiders believe the rookie is ready to ascend atop the depth chart, Cousins becomes expendable on the trade market and maybe the most sought-after quarterback this deadline. After all, he's 4-4 as the Raiders starter, has thrown 19 passing touchdowns, and has a 101.4 passer rating through eight starts. He's had at least two passing touchdowns in seven of his eight games played this season.

In the right situation, Cousins could help a reeling team -- like Baltimore, who just lost Lamar Jackson due to a right thumb injury -- stay afloat in the playoff race.

It's unlikely that he's moved, but if you're ranking veteran quarterbacks who could be traded by the deadline, you have to at least mention Jones. He's arguably the top backup in the NFL, and given how well he filled in for Brock Purdy last year, the Niners would likely need to be blown away to deal him.

In eight starts last season, Jones owned an 8-3 record while completing 69.6% of his throws and averaging 268.9 passing yards per game. He also had a 97.4 passer rating. The former first-round pick has been mentioned in trade rumors in the past, but San Francisco has held a high price, and it's hard to imagine they'd budge now. Still, if a team is looking to truly make a splash, he would likely be atop their wish list.

#2605. Contemporary Baseball Era Committee unveils eight Hall of Fame candidates: Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Monday announced eight candidates for election on the 2027 Contemporary Baseball Era Committee ballot. The non-player ballot includes four former managers and four former executives: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner, and Bill White.

The non-player ballot includes managers, executives, and umpires. On an alternating basis, the Era Committee also evaluates a ballot consisting of former players. As for the qualifications and criteria, the Hall of Fame describes it thus:

"The eight Contemporary Baseball Era finalists were selected by the BBWAA-appointed Historical Overview Committee from all eligible candidates among managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980. Eligible candidates include managers and umpires with 10 or more major league seasons and retired for at least five years (candidates who are 65 years or older are eligible six months following retirement); and executives retired for at least five years (active executives 70 years or older are eligible for consideration regardless of the position they hold in an organization and regardless of whether their body of work has been completed). All candidates must not be on Baseball's Ineligible List."

As for those figures on the Era Committee ballot for 2027, here's a quick rundown:

Alderson built a powerhouse and won a World Series as general manager of the Oakland A's. He later earned multiple playoff berths and a pennant as GM of the New York Mets.

One of the winningest managers of all time, Baker guided five different clubs to the playoffs and won three pennants and a World Series. His success in the dugout came after a long and distinguished playing career as an MLB outfielder.

Bochy as a manager led three different clubs to the postseason and is one of just six managers ever to win at least four World Series. Three of Bochy's rings came with the San Francisco Giants, and the final one came with the Texas Rangers in 2023.

Maddon won more than 1,300 games as a manager for three different franchises. He also won a pennant as manager of the Tampa Bay Rays, and in 2016, he led the Chicago Cubs to their first World Series title in more than a century.

After an 18-year playing career, Piniella racked up more than 1,800 wins as a big-league manager. He led three different clubs to the playoffs, won a World Series as manager of the 1990 Cincinnati Reds, and in 2001 helmed the Seattle Mariners to a record 116 wins during the regular season.

After filling a key role in the New York Yankees front office, Sabean joined the Giants as their general manager. Under his guidance, the Giants won the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014.

The only posthumous candidate on the ballot, Turner owned the Atlanta Braves for two decades. Along the way, he innovated the distribution of televised baseball games and oversaw a dynasty. Under Turner's stewardship, the Braves claimed 14 straight division titles and won the World Series in 1995.

A five-time All-Star and Gold Glove first baseman as a player, White after his playing days were over served as president of the National League. White was also the first Black play-by-play broadcaster in MLB history, and his leadership of the NL made him the first Black president of a major sports league.

The results of the committee vote will be announced on MLB Network at 8 p.m. ET on Sunday, Dec. 6. As with the BBWAA ballot, a candidate must be named on at least 75% of ballots in order to earn election. A 16-member committee will vote on the candidates.

The more traditional BBWAA ballot, in which candidates are voted on by writers and other media members, will be revealed on Nov. 16. Results of the 2027 BBWAA ballot will be announced in January, at which point we'll know the full Hall of Fame class for 2027.

#2604. Barbra Banda talks a 2021 in which she rose to global prominence and the future

Very few footballers anywhere in the world shot to prominence in 2021 quite like Zambia forward Barbra Banda. A name familiar to those who follow the women’s game in-depth, but perhaps an unknown to many, Banda changed that in the space of four incredible days during the summer Olympic Games in Tokyo.

It was the very first appearance for the Copper Queens at a women’s football tournament, and ranked outside the world’s top 100, few gave them a chance of competing in a group that included China, Brazil and European champions, the Netherlands.

A 10-3 defeat in their opening game against the latter emphasised the gap, but was memorable for the 21-year-old scoring an extraordinary hat-trick, with two or her goals coming in the space of a minute towards the end of the game with the result already beyond doubt.

As if that wasn’t enough, Banda hit another hat-trick just three days later in a thrilling 4-4 draw against China, becoming the first player ever to score back-to-back Olympic hat-tricks.

Sitting in her hotel room in China where she is undergoing mandatory isolation after returning from a national team camp, Banda reflects on a period that propelled into the eyes of the world on the biggest stage available. “I never thought I would represent Zambia on that kind of stage,” she says. “I always told myself it’s about hard work and determination that gets you there and then suddenly I found myself representing my country at an Olympics.”

Throughout our interview, Banda is humble, but more than anything continuously emphasises how her whole career has, and will continue to be, about hard work, about determination, that she hasn’t yet come close to achieving what she wants, even reflecting that the tournament was somewhat of a disappointment despite what they were up against and the personal history she made.

“We didn’t do our level best to go to the second round, but for our team just being there was a great achievement, for our country, for Africa, because we were the only African team there. It was history for us just to qualify for Tokyo. The achievement of scoring those two hat-tricks, it’s just the result of what kind of person I am. I work hard, I am always there for my team and for my country and all I do is aim to do the best for my country.”

Despite only turning 21 this year and having a large part of her career still in front of her, it has been a long and eventful journey for Banda just to get to where she is now, growing up in a country where women’s football was far from prominent.

Banda joined an academy as a youngster and spent over 10 years there, and it was the motivation she got from her dad in particular which inspired her to continue following her dream. “For me, I started very early, I just used to go and play football with my dad. At the academy, that’s when I started playing competitively in a league for women in Zambia.

“Things happened quite quickly. At the age of 13 I was called up for trials for the under 17 national team and ended up doing to play in Costa Rica at the under 17 World Cup in Costa Rica.”

Yes, at the age of just 13, Banda was representing her nation at a major FIFA tournament, where she was incredibly only the second-youngest player behind 12-year-old Ghanaian defender Fuseina Mumuni; a tournament that saw Banda suddenly gracing the same pitches as other promising youngsters such as Deyna Castellanos, Lea Schüller, Jessie Fleming, Patri Guijarro and Aitana Bonmatí.

“After that I moved clubs, went to a bigger club, the Green Buffalos in Zambia. I think that’s when I started with the senior national team and started to become a bit more well-known to people.

“As time went on I was still so inspired by my dad,” she recalls. “He was always there for me in terms of football. It’s interesting because it was really only him who was interested, my mum didn’t want me to play football. I wanted to play and my dad encouraged me, but my mum wanted me to go to school and get an education. But, now they’re both happy with how I’m doing.”

By this time Banda was starting to gain attention from around the world as she looked to take the next step in her career, and found an agent, Anton, who is on the call too, with the pair now having worked together for several years and formed a close working relationship.

Several Spanish clubs in particular were interested in signing Banda in the summer of 2018 but weren’t overly convinced about taking who was then a relatively unknown African striker who hadn’t played football outside Zambia.

There was also the issue of the looming annual COSAFA Cup in Africa, which would take place in September at the very start of the European season, with several interested clubs demanding Banda miss the tournament. One of those who passed up the opportunity was relegated at the end of the season.

In the end, newly-promoted Logroño took the chance on Banda and the teenager went on to score 16 goals in 28 league appearances for the club across a two-year stay in Spain. “That was a great move or me and I always thank Anton, he has always been there for me,” she smiles. “He knows what it takes to have a player and put trust in that player when nobody else believes in you. He believed in me and made it possible for me to move to Spain.

“Many clubs wouldn’t accept African players, they didn’t think we were at that level, but I went there and showed in Africa that we do have good players. Everyone there was happy with me. The players, the management, everyone was happy. I enjoyed Spain, it was competitive, they love football there and every game was very hard and very strong.”

It was not just a big move for Banda on the pitch, but off it. It meant a first move away not just from Zambia, but Africa. At the age of 18, Banda was leaving behind everything and everyone she’d ever known in the search of making football a career for her and to show other young girls in Zambia it could be done.

“Being the first time, my parents were a bit worried, but I think there was a good side as well because they’d got used to me going away for weeks and months with the national team. I think that contributed to them understanding, they had to accept it.”

It wasn’t just her family Banda had to convince either. Extraordinarily, Banda was undergoing mandatory military service in Zambia at the time and had to get permission from the colonel of the Zambian army which she laughs “wasn’t easy” when discussing the story.

“It was so difficult! That’s why I really appreciate Anton, because he worked so hard for me. I was coming from military service, there was a lot of paperwork, a lot of explanations, so it wasn’t easy. The Zambian army commander is now the women’s representative for women’s football in Zambia. She did a lot of good work for me to get permission from the colonel of the army which meant I could go to Spain.”

At the start of 2020, Banda left Spain and indeed Europe and opted to move to China and play for Shanghai Shengli, but her debut had to wait after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic meant a much more condensed season played over the course of just three months towards the end of the year.

Despite fewer games than planned, Banda scored an incredible 18 goals in her debut season, nine clear of the next best, fellow African forward Temwa Chawinga. “It’s a good league,” she says. “I came here, did my best and was the top scorer, which was a great achievement for me.”

Her second year saw her miss a large chunk of the campaign due to her involvement in the Olympic Games, which is still where her most vivid memories remain as she still looks to really take in what she achieved in Tokyo.

“It has been so overwhelming,” she admits. “I think everyone was proud of me, breaking those records is not easy. A lot of people have passed a lot of compliments about me and I’m happy about that, but I can’t be relaxed about what people comment on and the praise they give me. I have to keep focused on working hard and hopefully breaking more records on top of what I did in the summer.

“I still maintain the same aims, the same discipline I have always portrayed. I just have to work even harder now to make sure I still have those nice messages from people in the future.”

It’s a self-image Banda is keen to maintain, wary of the impact she is having not just back home in Zambia, but all around Africa, where she has quickly become one of the most iconic footballers on the continent.

With Zambia now aiming to back up their Olympic Games appearance with a first World Cup in 2023, Banda wants to juggle what she is doing on the pitch with ensuring she remains a role model for young girls off it. “I just have to show a good example to everyone who looks up to me, that’s the most important thing. They look up to me and as their icon I have to show good manners so they copy that.

“As soon as I do something bad, I will become a bad example to everyone. The best way to show myself is to stay out of those things. I just have to focus on doing what I’m doing and keep only inspiring more people in my country and around Africa.”

It’s a role she admits though is “not easy”, especially given the extra reputation she now has off the back of those four incredible days in Tokyo. “I don’t know what to say. I still remember it all the time. I didn’t expect it, I just did my best and I showed what I can do. Like I said, for me, I still want to work hard and just continue what I’m doing.

“Women have not always been supported in Zambia, but you saw people cheering us at the Olympics and it has changed since. There is a Champions League now in Africa, I think we are heading somewhere step by step. We don’t feel like we have everything we need as women, but we have shown we are here, we exist, we play the same football. We get positive messages from fans, they are talking about women’s football in Zambia, we are putting it on the map for people.”

After two years in Spain, it may just be two years in China too, as Banda is looking ahead to the future and what may await her given the attention she has received. While she’s giving little away as to what may lay ahead, it’s clear she has ambitions to make a move to a top team and continue fulfilling her ambitions.

“I always want to try new things experience football in different clubs and different players. I enjoyed playing here, but if anything comes up I want to experience other kinds of football. I am ok here, I enjoy, it’s a good league, better than people think. I’m still very young. My main target is to play in the Champions League – we will see what happens. I just do what I do, I work hard and hope for the best in my future.”

#2603. NBA's 'unprecedented' early season injury crisis has players and coaches searching for answers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Kevin Durant sat in the corner of the small visitor's locker room at Fiserv Forum and rested his chin on his hand as he contemplated the question everyone around the NBA has been asking after a cataclysmic opening week.

"I wish I knew, man. I wish I knew the science behind why all of these injuries are happening," Durant said.

Durant missed the entire 2019-20 season after tearing his Achilles tendon in the 2019 Finals, and knows firsthand the toll that the modern NBA takes on players' bodies. Never has the issue felt as pressing as the past week, as star after star went down with injuries ranging from broken legs to hamstring strains.

"Some people say the game is so fast, some people say more possessions, some people say 82 games," Durant said, listing some of the theories that have become prevalent. "It's unfortunate to have so many great players out with injuries, but I can't put my hand on it, to be honest bro. I wish I knew but I don't know exactly what the reason is. Just hoping all these guys get back healthy."

Here's a quick rundown of some of the most notable injuries that have happened in this first week:

And that doesn't account for preseason injuries, including Ben Simmons tearing his Achilles tendon or Kon Knueppel straining his hamstring. Simmons is out for the season, and Knueppel hasn't played yet.

The rash of injuries, which Rockets coach Ime Udoka called "unprecedented" this early in the season, has already derailed multiple teams' seasons and had a major impact on the title race and major award eligibility.

Injuries are an unfortunate part of sports. There's nothing anyone can do about Williams getting his leg trapped under his body on a bad fall, or Suggs falling onto Banchero's ankle. But the abundance of soft-tissue injuries is a major concern across the league. "It sucks to see this many people going out for this amount of time early in the season," Udoka said.

As Durant noted, there's no shortage of ideas about what's causing the injury crisis.

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr has long been the leading voice on the 82-game season being too long. Indiana Pacers coach Rick Carlisle has repeatedly talked about how much faster the game is now. Udoka and Milwaukee Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins both wondered about the effect of shortening training camp and playing fewer preseason games. "We only had three and some of our guys didn't play in all three of those, and so you can see some things creep up early," Udoka said Wednesday. Jenkins added that league and team personnel are "always studying … what we're doing in preseason and the offseason."

Bucks legend Marques Johnson, a five-time All-Star who led Milwaukee's great teams in the 1980s and now works as a broadcaster, pointed to specific changes in style and the cumulative effect of extensive training.

"Back in the day, we didn't do the full-speed, hard Euro[step], the deceleration stop, that wasn't part of the game back then. Now it's more prevalent in the game, and I think it creates more wear and tear on the lower extremities, just how hard these guys play, the kind of force that they put on those areas of the body. That's my layman's opinion," Johnson told CBS Sports.

"The game is played differently and something's gotta give. The body can only take so much and the floor doesn't give," Johnson continued. "And another thing, the deceleration, the Eurostep, all these things that they're doing nowadays. It's not like they wait for games to practice that. They work on that year-round, so they're doing that constantly. Over and over and over again. I just think at some point the muscles, tendons, joints throw up the white flag and say enough."

Shortening the season has always felt unrealistic from an economic perspective, and how do you legislate the speed at which the game is played, or the moves used to score? Is there actually anything that can be done when players are so big and so strong, and moving with so much force day after day, year after year?

Rockets guard Fred VanVleet, who missed all of last season with a torn ACL, and is now the president of the National Basketball Players Association, doesn't think so.

"There's no prevention. You could look across every league in the world, every age group, this is where we are – in the world, not particular to basketball or the NBA," VanVleet told CBS Sports.

VanVleet added that in his role with the PA, he's been working with the NBA on "different things that we can do to add to the fight because everybody wants everybody out there all the time," which is "one of the few things we all agree on," he said.

CBS Sports reached out to the league about potential injury-prevention measures earlier this week but had not heard back as of Friday afternoon.

Even if preventing injuries isn't possible, VanVleet still wants to see a "real emphasis on player health."

"It's a multi-billion dollar industry, multi-billion dollar business, I just think we could pour some more resources and some more science, and I think the NBA should be the leading experts on some of these things," VanVleet said. "We take stances when we feel like it's righteous in terms of leading. I think we could lead this area."

#2602. Jack Campbell injury updates: Lions LB remains in hospital, but 'indications are positive'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell was strapped to a backboard and carted off the field after appearing to suffer a serious injury during the team's Week 8 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings.

Following the 19-15 victory, Lions coach Dan Campbell told reporters he had no further information on Jack's status, other than that he was receiving medical care. He stayed in the hospital overnight for evaluation, and the team announced it would provide more information when it had it available. Monday afternoon, the team provided the following statement:

Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital. Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.

Shortly after that update, Dan Campbell met with the media, and though he did not share any further updates, he did ask for continued prayers and say he had a chance to visit Jack in the hospital Sunday night and talk with his family.

"It was good, it was positive," Dan Campbell said. "Got to see his parents, talk to his wife, and everybody's in good spirits. It's about the recovery, and it's a small setback. That's the family. They're very positive. So that's good in that regard."

Campbell also said "a lot of people went over there" when asked if teammates were able to visit Jack, though he acknowledged there were lots of tests being run, so not everyone could visit with the linebacker.

On the first play of the fourth quarter, Jack Campbell and teammate Eric O'Neill combined to tackle Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. Campbell then went limp. While lying prone, Campbell was not seen moving before trainers reached him. After about 10 minutes, Campbell was strapped to a backboard and carted off the field.

Prayers up for Jack Campbell. pic.twitter.com/dZsTw6zEj1

The Lions announced that Campbell was transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury.

It was an emotional scene at Ford Field. The entire Lions team went over to see their teammate off, while the defense gathered for a moment to rally after seeing one of their leaders go down.

The Lions defense takes a moment after Jack Campbell was carted off. @ErinAndrews has more. pic.twitter.com/uvy9PfrITI

In seven games this season, Campbell recorded 57 tackles, two QB hits and a fumble recovery. Just six months ago, he signed a four-year, $81 million extension that made him one of the highest-paid off-ball linebackers in the NFL.

Campbell was selected with the No. 18 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft out of Iowa, just six selections after the Lions drafted running back Jahmyr Gibbs. The 26-year-old had a career year in 2025, recording 176 tackles, nine tackles for loss, five sacks, three forced fumbles and four passes defended. He was named a First Team All-Pro and earned his first Pro Bowl bid.

#2601. Demichelis vows to leave RB Leipzig if season targets aren't met

Martin Demichelis has had an inconsistent start as RB Leipzig head coach since replacing Ole Werner in the summer, with several heavy defeats away from home putting him under considerable pressure.

Saturday’s 2-0 win over Schalke 04 at the Veltins-Arena finally delivered Leipzig’s first away league victory of the season, with Demichelis using the occasion to make his position on the club’s expectations clear.

“I know that I have to achieve targets with RB Leipzig; that’s why I’m here. And if we don’t achieve those targets by the end of the season, then I’ll leave myself. That’s how it is. The people who know me know that very well,” Demichelis was quoted as saying by Bild.

While the club’s exact objectives remain unclear, qualifying for the Champions League is likely to be among the key targets.

Saturday’s win should ease some of the pressure on Demichelis, with Leipzig now sitting fourth in the Bundesliga table.

Nevertheless, the Argentine coach was quick to stress that there is still a long way to go this season.

“It was only our first away win. The season is still a long one,” he said.
